The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

This limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Several types of transfers are completely excluded from gift tax rules — no annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required:

The education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single recipient in a year, you must file IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) with your tax return. Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

The current $13.61 million lifetime exemption is scheduled to drop to approximately $7 million per person on January 1, 2026. For high-net-worth families, this creates a narrow window to transfer wealth at the higher exemption level. If you have a taxable estate anywhere near the future threshold, consult an estate planning attorney about accelerating gifts before the sunset takes effect.

A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

Give up to $18,000 per recipient per year with no reporting, no forms, and no impact on your lifetime exemption. Married couples can give $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

Pro tip: There is no limit on the number of recipients. You can give $18,000 each to as many people as you want.

Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

Pro tip: The payment must go directly to the institution — not to the student or patient. Reimbursing someone for tuition they already paid counts as a gift.

Front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts ($90,000 individual, $180,000 married) into a 529 plan in a single year. The full amount starts compounding immediately.

Pro tip: If you die during the 5-year election period, a prorated portion returns to your estate. File Form 709 to report the 5-year election.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

Pro tip: Filing Form 709 is just paperwork — it does not mean you owe tax. It simply tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

If your estate is approaching the lifetime exemption threshold, work with an estate planning attorney. Strategies like GRATs, family LLCs, and intentionally defective grantor trusts can transfer wealth beyond the basic gift tax rules.

Pro tip: With the exemption sunset approaching in 2026, large transfers should be planned now rather than later.

In 2026, you can give up to $18,000 per recipient without any tax consequences or reporting requirements. Above that amount, you file Form 709 but still won't owe tax until you've exceeded your $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Married couples can give up to $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

No. The recipient of a gift never pays income tax or gift tax on the gift. The giver is responsible for any gift tax reporting (Form 709) and any tax that might be owed. Gifts received are not considered taxable income. However, if the gifted asset later generates income (like dividends or interest), that income is taxable to the recipient.

You must file Form 709 with your tax return for that year. The amount above $18,000 reduces your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption ($13.61 million). You won't owe any actual gift tax unless your cumulative lifetime gifts exceed the lifetime exemption. Think of it as paperwork, not a penalty.

Yes, though the amount matters. You can give $18,000 per year with no reporting. You and your spouse together can give $36,000. For larger down payment gifts, you'll file Form 709 and use some of your $13.61 million lifetime exemption — but no tax is owed. Your mortgage lender will require a gift letter confirming the money is a gift, not a loan.

No. The unlimited marital deduction means you can transfer any amount to your US citizen spouse completely free of gift tax and estate tax. No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The recipient does not report the gift on their income tax return either. Gifts are outside the income tax system entirely.

The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

#9130. Molly Bounds "The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins" @ Mrs Gallery, Maspeth, NY

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ New York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her new series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

There are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less important; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

#9129. Deathbed portrait of Vanessa Bell by Duncan Grant discovered

Duncan Grant, Portrait of Vanessa Bell (1961)

A poignant portrait of the artist Vanessa Bell, made within days of her death in 1961 by her sometime lover and lifelong friend Duncan Grant, has been rediscovered among family papers and donated to the famous home of the Bloomsbury Group, Charleston farmhouse in East Sussex.

The drawing in soft pencil and biro, from an angle suggesting Grant was sitting by her bedside, was rediscovered among family papers during research for a forthcoming exhibition of the work of both artists at Tate Britain. It may have been made just after Bell’s death, though she could just be resting peacefully with eyes closed.

Although Grant has dated the drawing “Friday April 14”, Bell actually died at the farmhouse on a week prior. In a statement from Charleston, now a museum and archive, Darren Clarke, head of collections and research, says that in later years, Grant and his friends went through masses of the work in his studio identifying and labelling pictures, so the date may have been added in error years later.

“What seems very likely here is that Duncan knew this drawing had been made around Vanessa’s death and later added a date from memory. He got remarkably close, but apparently not quite close enough. Everything about the drawing itself – its viewpoint, its intimacy and its extraordinary economy – suggests someone sitting quietly beside Vanessa’s bed and drawing the face he had known for half a century.”

The friendship and artistic partnership of Grant and Bell was one of the happiest and longest lasting of the tangled affairs of the group. Although Grant was gay and a former lover of Bell’s brother Adrian, they were lovers for a time and in 1918 had a child, Angelica—who went on to marry David Garnett, another of Grant’s lovers. Grant and Bell lived and worked at the 17th-century farmhouse for decades, covering many of the interiors with striking painted decoration. He outlived her by 17 years, and in 1978 was buried beside her in the churchyard of St Peter’s in Firle, near their home.

Grant was long regarded as the most talented artist of the group, and the first major solo exhibition of Bell’s work came only in 2017 at the Dulwich Picture Gallery. At that time most of her paintings in the Tate collection were languishing in storage, but her reputation has been growing steadily in recent years. The Tate is making amends with a major exhibition of work by both artists, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury (12 November 2026 - 11 April 2027) at Tate Britain.

Although Charleston is the largest lender to the Tate exhibition, including the entire contents of Grant’s studio, the drawing will only be included in the exhibition catalogue. It will go on public display for the first time at Charleston in May 2027, when the studio reopens after major conservation work.

The drawing has been donated to Charleston as part of the 50 for 50 campaign which aims to bring 50 major works by the group back to the farmhouse in time for 2030, the 50th anniversary of the founding of the Charleston Trust, which runs and maintains the museum.

Nathaniel Hepburn, the director and CEO of Charleston, says in a statement on the discovery: “I found this drawing deeply moving when I first saw it. We know Duncan’s drawings of Vanessa so intimately, made over the course of their long friendship, that the discovery of a previously unknown work is remarkable in itself. But there is something incredibly poignant about imagining Duncan sitting beside Vanessa, drawing her after her death.“

A new book and UK exhibition by Charlie Porter explores the sartorial choices of Virginia Woolf, Vanessa Bell and the rest of the Charleston set

British artist Hew Locke has been selected for Tate Britain’s Duveen Galleries commission, while Barbara Hepworth gets a survey at Tate St Ives

#9128. One Dead and Two Critically Injured After a Helicopter Crashed During a Photography Flight

One Dead and Two Critically Injured After a Helicopter Crashed During a Photography Flight

One person has been killed while two others were injured after a helicopter crashed during a photography flight in Miami, Florida.

As ABC News reports, three people were aboard the flight. Passengers were reportedly filming boats on the water when the chartered helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay, just south of downtown Miami.

“Preliminary information indicates it was a photography flight,” the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) reports. NBC 6 South Florida reports that the helicopter is owned by Global Aerials, a Miami-area aerial media services company, and took off from North Perry Airport, just north of Miami.

One man died as a result of the crash, despite the heroic efforts of a good Samaritan who was providing life-saving assistance, according to Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz. The same good Samaritan also sent a mayday call to authorities and may have saved the lives of the other two passengers due to their quick thinking.

The two other men who were aboard the crashed helicopter were rescued from the water and transported by air to Jackson Memorial Hospital’s trauma center, where they are both in critical but stable condition. Authorities say that their conditions after being removed from the water were so severe they required life-flight transportation.

Authorities do not yet know the cause of the crash, although it is under investigation. Heavy storms have hit the area over the last few days, but authorities cannot yet say whether weather conditions contributed to the crash. The helicopter had been flying south in the bay before looping back north shortly prior to crashing.

The Robinson R44 helicopter crashed at around 11:15 AM ET. Rescue workers from various local agencies, the Coast Guard, and even Customs and Border Protection (CBP) all responded to the crash scene, NBC News reports.

Television news video, like the one seen above from NBC 6 South Florida, shows the helicopter upside down in the water, surrounded by rescue personnel.

Less than two months ago, aerial photographer and reporter Eliana Moreno died after an NBC Los Angeles helicopter crashed in L.A. suburbs while the news crew was filming a fatal bus collision scene. Alongside Moreno, the helicopter pilot, George Marciniw, and a person on the ground, Edy Gutiérrez Mejia, who was visiting Los Angeles from Guatemala, also perished.

#9127. The Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift Is the Fastest Tilt-Shift Lens Ever

The Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift Is the Fastest Tilt-Shift Lens Ever

Laowa has officially announced the 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift lens. Built for architectural and commercial photography, the full-frame lens also works on Fujifilm GFX and Hasselblad XCD medium-format cameras thanks to its large image circle.

With its f/2 aperture, the new Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift is an especially fast tilt-shift lens. Canon’s 24mm TS-E Tilt-Shift Lens for EF-mount cameras, for example, is an f/3.5 lens. Nikon’s F-mount PC-E 24mm lens is also f/3.5. Fujifilm’s GF 30mm f/5.6 T/S, which is effectively equivalent to about 24mm, is clearly much slower than the new Laowa lens.

Laowa says that thanks to the 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift’s fast f/2 aperture, the fastest aperture of any tilt-shift lens ever made for any format, it is significantly better-suited to low-light and night-sky photography than any other tilt-shift lens before it.

Despite its fast aperture, it’s also a relatively compact and lightweight lens for its class. The lens is 119 millimeters (4.7 inches) long with a maximum diameter of 93 millimeters (3.7 inches). It weighs 860 grams (1.9 pounds) and accepts 77mm front filters.

The lens features 13 elements arranged across 10 groups. It promises to minimize distortion through optical corrections, hence the “Zero-D” in the model name, and keep lines straight throughout the frame, from center to edge. Laowa also promises high resolution, strong contrast, and minimal reflections and ghosting. PetaPixel will be putting the lens to the test in real-world situations to verify these claims.

The manual focus lens can focus as close as 0.25 meters (9.8 inches), resulting in a maximum magnification of 0.19x. It’s not quite a macro lens, but it should work well enough for foreground elements in a scene.

The shift range is ±12 millimeters, while the tilt range is ±10 degrees. However, Laowa notes that the precise tilt and shift range may vary “slightly” depending on the selected camera mount. Tilt-shift lenses like this often offer reduced ranges on medium-format cameras because of their larger image sensors. However, in this case, Laowa says that the lens retains “its full” range on Fujifilm GFX and Hasselblad XCD medium format cameras.

The Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift lens is available for Sony E, Canon RF, Nikon Z, L-Mount, GFX, and XCD mirrorless camera systems. It is available now for $1,249.

Further, Laowa has also announced that its 55mm and 100mm f/2.8 Tilt-Shift 1x Macro lenses are now available for Hasselblad XCD cameras as well. They are also $1,249 each.

#9126. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#9125. Scrapped marine rope recast as stools that rock like buoys

Rotterdam studio The New Raw has used discarded rope salvaged from the city’s harbour to create a series of 3D-printed public seating for its waterfront.

Called Buoy, the urban furniture project is shortlisted for a 2026 Dezeen Award in the sustainable design category.

To create the stools, The New Raw founder Foteini Setaki collected a series of plastic ropes from Rotterdam harbour, which were formerly used for managing boats and would’ve otherwise gone to waste.

The ropes were then transported to Maastricht, in the south of the Netherlands, where they were cleaned, shredded and mechanically recycled into pellets.

After returning to The New Raw’s Rotterdam studio, the recycled plastic pellets were melted and 3D-printed to create the stools, layer by layer.

“The material fuses as it is deposited, so no separate binder is needed,” Setaki told Dezeen.

Setaki explained that marine ropes are challenging to recycle because they contain a cocktail of materials that accumulate various residues over time.

Careful selection is essential to determine the ropes with the highest polypropylene content to be transformed into recycled plastic pellets, she explained.

While no virgin plastic is used in the creation of the stools, a small percentage of additives support the furniture’s long-term outdoor use, including UV protection.

“These additives are compatible with recycling the material again,” said Setaki.

Each seat features a subtly different hue, which is determined by the colour of the original rope rather than additional pigments or coatings.

The stools were also designed with spinning top-style pointed bases, so that they rock when the user sits down.

This gentle rocking motion was chosen to mimic real buoys bobbing along on the water.

“We wanted the seats to carry a recognisable link to their maritime origin, through both their shape and the slow movement of floating buoys,” explained Setaki.

“Borrowing that movement brings a playful quality to sitting, and the connection to the harbour becomes something you can feel.”

Each unique stool was engraved with its batch and production number, and then placed by Rotterdam harbour.

The project was created as an example of how designers can seek out local, surplus resources in an effort to contextualise their practice with the place that they work.

“Working with a local waste stream is a way of strengthening the relationship between the city and its harbour,” said Setaki.

“The material’s journey and the experience of sitting make that relationship tangible. This approach could also be adapted to other harbour cities, starting with their own discarded materials and local networks.”

Founded in 2016, The New Raw is run by Setaki and Panos Sakkas. The studio 3D prints locally sourced plastic waste to create furniture.

Buoy is nominated alongside a vibrant shortlist of sustainable design projects, including a cement-free architectural material made of waste date pits and lighting for an Australia bookshop made of its own faulty publications rejected due to printing errors.

#9124. iMac With M6 Review: The Best All-in-One Computer for Photographers

iMac With M6 Review: The Best All-in-One Computer for Photographers

The updated iMac with M6 may not bring a new design, display, or major new features, but it is still a competent, straightforward Mac with a lot to offer.

It does its job, looks good doing it, and is about as fuss-free as any computer can be. PetaPixel Score 8/10 ProsPractical and stylish designGood built-in screen for photographyPowerful enough for photo editing and some video editingColor-matched accessoriesConsNo Thunderbolt 5 or SD card slotScreen isn't very bright

It does its job, looks good doing it, and is about as fuss-free as any computer can be.

The first Mac I ever used was an iMac. It wasn’t just just any iMac, either; it was the very first iMac model ever, a graphite iMac G3 with its matching “hockey puck” mouse. At the time, it was running Mac OS 8, I was about eight years old, and I had no idea how computers worked. But importantly, I was hooked. I’ve had Macs ever since.

When it was finally time for me to get my own computer, rather than bogart my older brother’s machine to play games (yes, Macs can play games) and browse the very early web, I ultimately went for a Power Mac and didn’t have any more iMac experience until my parents bought an Intel-powered 21.5-inch unibody iMac over a decade ago. I helped set it up, but that was about it.

Much has changed about the iMac since I puttered around frankly dangerous message boards and forums on the iMac G3 and handled IT on an Intel iMac in the 2010s. In many ways, I think the iMac has lost most of its prominence in the Mac lineup. Older iMac computers were iconic, in homes and school computer labs everywhere. But consumer preferences shift. A lot of people go for laptops now, and I understand why. Professionals and power users might go for a desktop, but typically something like a Mac Studio.

I’m here to tell you that while the iMac may never reclaim its elevated position on the Mac totem pole, people should definitely take a good, long look at the newest M6-powered iMac. It’s relatively affordable and powerful, gorgeous to look at, and very convenient. What’s not to like?

Speaking of “affordable,” while the iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 with two Thunderbolt/USB 4 ports, that’s not the machine I have here for testing. I’m using the iMac with four Thunderbolt 4 ports, which starts at $1,699. The move to more ports also means going from the 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU M6 chip to the M6 with 12 CPU and 12 GPU cores.

It still starts with 16GB of unified memory and a 256GB SSD either way, but the four-port iMac also supports up to 32GB of RAM instead of 24GB and up to a 2TB SSD instead of 1TB. The higher-end starting iMac also has 2.5Gb Ethernet on its power brick.

The exact configuration I’m testing is the four-port iMac with M6, 16GB of unified memory, and a 512GB SSD. It has a beautiful blue finish. It is $1,899.

As mentioned, the iMac can come with either two or four rear Thunderbolt 4 ports. Unfortunately, there’s no Thunderbolt 5 here. While I admit Thunderbolt 5 ports are probably overkill for many prospective iMac buyers, it would be nice to have at least a couple on the higher-spec machine.

If I had to keep levying complaints against the iMac, I might also say that it’d be nice to have a built-in SD card slot somewhere, as we get on the MacBook Pro and Mac Studio. It’d also be nice to have a couple of USB-A slots for older accessories. That’s about where the knocks stop.

There’s a lot going for the iMac, not least of which is that it is pretty pretty to look at. It comes in six different bright colors and a seventh silver option for those who hate fun. In all seriousness, all seven colorways look great. I think the blue version that Apple sent for review is among the best options.

The front has a soft blue finish with a color-matched Touch ID Magic Keyboard (without a number pad) and a blue Magic Mouse. You can also get a color-matched Magic Trackpad instead for an extra $50. I’m generally a Trackpad man, but I wanted to use the blue Magic Mouse to feel fashionable. There’s also an optional color-matched keyboard with the number pad. It’s an extra $30.

The side and rear of the main chassis are a much darker blue, creating a lovely contrasting two-tone look. It even ships with a light blue USB-C cable for charging the keyboard and mouse and a color-matched power cord that connects to the big ol’ power brick.

I suppose I also don’t like that there’s a separate power brick. It houses the 2.5GbE port and is the classic glossy white plastic Apple uses for its bricks. I put the brick on the floor, as I suspect many people will, and it got very scratched almost immediately. Oh well. The cord that connects the iMac to the brick attaches to the computer via magnets, which delivers a super satisfying snap. I thought that might mean the cord would quickly release if I stumbled over the power cable, but it’s too strong a magnet for that. Don’t think of it like MagSafe on a MacBook; it’s not that.

The baby blue stand is well made. It’s very easy to tilt without ever feeling loose or wobbly. Unfortunately, the stand doesn’t have any height adjustment, which some users may find limiting. You can buy the iMac with a VESA Mount Adapter at no additional charge, but that means you don’t get the stand at all.

The iMac has a six-speaker sound system with force-canceling woofers. While not my area of expertise or focus, I find the overall sound quality good, though a bit lacking in the lows. There’s not a lot of bass here, if that’s something you’re into. Fortunately for me, I don’t like bass-forward speakers or sound profiles, so I really enjoyed listening to music on the iMac while working. The speakers don’t sound quite as nice as the ones on the Pro Display XDR I use primarily, but that’s a reasonably high, expensive bar to clear. The iMac’s speakers can also get impressively loud, if that’s what you’re into. The iMac also has a standard 3.5mm headphone jack with high-impedance headphone support on the side.

The iMac has Apple’s fairly standard 12MP Center Stage camera with Desk View and 1080p resolution. I’ve used this camera quite a bit over the years, and it’s serviceable enough for FaceTime and meetings. The same goes for the “studio-quality” three-mic array on the iMac. I’m not sure what “studio-quality” really means, but the mic quality is fine for typical daily use cases. If you want to make high-quality podcasts or videos, you’ll likely want a dedicated external camera and mic setup.

Now to the display. That’s a huge part of why you get an iMac, right? A Mac mini can certainly deliver better value, but you need to get all the accessories and screen. The iMac simplifies things greatly. You unpack it you’re off and running. Baby, you’ve got a stew going.

The iMac has the same 24-inch 4.5K Retina display as before. It has 4480 x 2520 resolution, an LED backlight, 500 nits of maximum brightness, and Wide color (P3) color gamut. This is where the iMac can either win someone over or arguably lose some people.

For me, a photographer, 500 nits of brightness is plenty. Arguably, for those who like to print, like me, even that is way too bright. Something I hoped to be able to do with the iMac is set it to a specific nits brightness, say 120 nits, a good value for printing workflows. However, while you can customize the white point, you cannot set a specific brightness. You can obviously just adjust the screen’s brightness until it seems right or calibrate it with an external device, but with some Mac displays, you can just pick a value and go.

For video editors, especially those working with HDR content, the iMac will prove insufficiently luminous. This is not one of Apple’s high-end panels in terms of brightness.

It’s also not a high-end panel in terms of color rendering, but it’s a genuinely good built-in screen. Black levels leave a bit to be desired compared to a higher-end MiniLED screen or especially an OLED, but the iMac’s Retina display looks good. It’s sharp, vivid, and you can absolutely enjoy looking at photos and watching movies on it.

If you are very serious about photography, I would recommend a dedicated calibration device to really dial things in, but otherwise I’ve had no issues.

By the way, while I don’t mind Apple’s glossy displays in controlled environments like my office, if you do want a nano-texture glass display instead, that’s available on configurations with at least 24GB of unified memory for an extra $200.

Overall, the iMac with M6 looks and feels great. While there are some areas where I think Apple could improve the iMac’s usability, I have zero issues with its aesthetics. Ultimately, style matters, and Apple hits all the high notes there.

Ultimately, the only real upgrade here with the newest-generation iMac is what’s inside. The design and display match the M4 version released in 2024, but the M6 chip is new. I’ve already discussed the M6 quite a bit in my recent Mac mini review, but the gist is that the M6 has Apple’s fastest CPU cores to date and improved performance for AI tasks.

That’s generally great news for photographers because many tasks in industry-standard software like Adobe Lightroom Classic and Photoshop are CPU-reliant and increasingly use AI. Win-win, right?

Generally, yes. Overall, Adobe Lightroom performance is good, about 10% better than the M5 MacBook Pro I tested last year. What’s notable here is that the MacBook Pro in question has twice as much unified memory as this iMac, which does matter. It’s not an entirely fair fight, and yet the M6 chip comes out on top by a healthy margin.

Looking at the category breakdown, we also see something interesting compared to the M6 Mac mini. Whatever was going on with that computer and JPEG exporting is not an issue here on the M6 iMac. To make the charts easier to read, I’ve included one in the gallery below with the Mac mini outlier result removed.

Ultimately, the M6 iMac is really good in Lightroom. It doesn’t export quite as fast as Apple’s higher-end Pro- and Max-series chips, but it barely trails elsewhere. Real-world use feels snappy across the board, too.

Over in Adobe Photoshop, the story remains good. The iMac with M6 is even a bit better than the Mac mini with M6, although not by a huge margin. It’s hard to say whether the iMac’s thermal design is just a bit more efficient under extreme stress than the ultra-compact Mac mini, or whether software is just a little more optimized now than when the Mac mini launched. After all, that was the first M6-powered Mac, and I tested it before public launch. That’s just speculation, though.

What’s not speculative is that the iMac is testing better than the Mac mini in some applications. That’s still true in Premiere, although only barely, and by such a small margin that it falls healthily within the margin of error.

The M6 is a better chip than the M5, all else equal, so you can really see the difference memory can make here, given that the M5 MacBook Pro with 32GB of RAM outperforms the M6 with 16GB in Premiere. If you’re serious about video editing and use Premiere a lot, it is worth considering upgrading to 24GB or 32GB of unified memory.

In our last benchmark, DaVinci Resolve, the M6 iMac really struts its stuff. Again, this could be optimization-related, because Blackmagic Design has updated Resolve since the Mac mini launched, and there’s no big reason the results should be this much better. But hey, don’t stare a gift horse in the mouth, right? These results are impressive.

During all my normal tasks, like importing and editing photos, the iMac stayed entirely silent. The fan never kicked on. It only ever spun up during Premiere and Resolve benchmark tests, and only some of the time. Even then, it was pretty quiet.

The iMac just works. It performs well, handles a wide variety of tasks, and never causes friction. Is it the most performant Mac ever? No, definitely not. I mean, look at the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. Holy cow. But that costs many times more than an iMac, and very few users will ever realize any of the benefits.

The iMac with M6 arrives with everything you need in a single, unified, sleek package. It performs well enough for most photographers, and I suspect many video users, too. It’s not a “professional” Mac, but most of us aren’t professionals with exacting demands at the very cutting edge of computing.

The new Apple iMac with M6 is a quintessential Mac. You unbox it, plug it in, and it works. It does its job, looks good doing it, and is about as fuss-free as any computer can be.

Nearly 30 years ago, when I used my first Macintosh computer, I entered the world of computers as a woefully ignorant child. But the iMac welcomed me in with its friendly, bulbous face, colorful design, and straightforward operating system. It won me over.

And while I eventually graduated beyond the iMac lineup, I truly enjoyed my time with the iMac with M6. It was like sitting down for a coffee with an old friend. We’ve both gone our separate ways, lived our lives, and yet found it so easy to pick up right where we left off.

At their best, Macs always feel accessible and familiar. The iMac certainly does.

While I have zero doubt whatsoever that the iMac is the best all-in-one computer on the market, and certainly the best for photographers, the big PC makers do have some options out there.

HP’s OmniStudio lineup is well respected and offers bigger screens than the iMac. Those are definitely great choices for those who enjoy Windows. Some are extremely cheap but have really subpar processors, so be wary.

Dell makes some that frankly kind of look like knock-off iMac computers. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, and Dell certainly has a wide range of models available at different price points. They are all called “All-in-One Desktop” computers, so you need to carefully look at exactly which model you’re considering.

Other manufacturers, including Acer and Lenovo, are in on the game, too.

Yes. The iMac with M6 is a great all-in-one for people who greatly value simplicity and performance.

#9123. Sydney's new $641m Powerhouse arts and science museum to open amid crisis

The two-wing museum project is counting down to a grand opening Courtesy Powerhouse Studio

Sydney’s Powerhouse, a new arts, design, science and technology museum that the New South Wales government describes as its biggest cultural investment since the city’s Opera House, is due to open on 7 November amid controversy and uncertainty.

The most recent crisis is the departure of Lisa Havilah, the museum’s chief executive, who stepped down in August over allegations of misconduct. Havilah had been the figurehead of the Powerhouse development at Parramatta, located in Sydney’s multicultural western suburbs, since 2019.

Some of Australia’s most powerful and influential arts identities have since signed a petition calling for Havilah to be reinstated immediately. The petition was launched on 27 October by Kon Gouriotis, the editor of Artist Profile magazine.

Among the more than 750 signatories so far are the prominent artist Ben Quilty, the architect and arts patron Penelope Seidler, the commercial gallery owner Anna Schwartz, and Lucy Turnbull, the former lord mayor of Sydney (2003-04) whose husband Malcolm Turnbull was Australia's prime minister (2015-18).

John Graham, the state’s arts minister, also announced that Powerhouse’s chief operating officer, Mark Wilsdon, is on leave while a Sydney law firm, Lander & Rogers, investigates the allegations. Those allegations have not been publicly detailed, but Graham has said they were brought forward by a whistleblower and touch on “governance and procurement”. Graham’s office did not respond before we went to press to a question about whether the inquiry’s findings will be made public.

Powerhouse is part of the broader Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences, which also encompasses a large site in Ultimo, a storage area and discovery centre in Castle Hill, and the Sydney Observatory.

The Ultimo site was the location of the Powerhouse Museum and its half a million objects from 1893 until the state government decided to distribute the city’s cultural assets more equitably across the population base. In 2015, Parramatta, about 20km west of central Sydney, was selected as the new site.

The Ultimo building was closed in 2024 and is now undergoing a A$300m ($210m) heritage revitalisation by the state government.

But a public petition has been launched to save the site following a newspaper report that the government is secretly considering selling part of the Ultimo site to cover the cost of the new Powerhouse.

The closure of the Ultimo site is a cultural “tragedy”, heritage expert and former Powerhouse trustee Kylie Winkworth tells The Art Newspaper. “It’s a globally unprecedented museum demolition,” explains the vocal member of the Powerhouse Museum Alliance pressure group. Located on the banks of the Parramatta River, the new Powerhouse was designed by the Franco-Japanese architectural practice Moreau Kusunoki in collaboration with the Australian firm Genton. Its exhibition spaces cover more than 18,000 sq. m across seven vast, column-free galleries. It also has a rooftop terrace and garden, and temporary accommodation for students, artists and scientists.

Dubbed by some “the milk crate” because of its steel criss-cross design, the Powerhouse is in good company in earning an irreverent nickname: the Sydney Opera House was called a “scrum of nuns” in the 1970s because its sails resembled wimples. While the Opera House was made a Unesco World Heritage Site in 2007, a similarly illustrious future for the Powerhouse, which cost A$915m ($641m) to build, is far from assured.

Even before construction began, experts told a parliamentary inquiry that the museum’s riverfront undercroft would flood in heavy rain. This led to changes in the building’s design.

During a tour around the site in June, before her departure, Havilah told The Art Newspaper that “the whole of Parramatta would be under water” before the Powerhouse flooded. However, Winkworth says she fears people within the building would still be at risk in the event of overland flooding.

Already widely viewed as having consumed a disproportionate share of the state’s arts budget, the Powerhouse has in recent months been the focus of a new funding scandal—the backdrop to Havilah’s departure. The Sydney Morning Herald reported in August that more than A$70m ($46.2m) had been spent in the run-up to the museum’s grand opening, including A$10m ($7m) for LED screens, staging and backdrop for an immersive experience created by the British artist Es Devlin.

Another point of contention was Havilah’s introduction of a five-year “artistic associates” programme, costing A$2.6m ($1.8m), in which external experts were employed to help bring the Powerhouse to fruition. The Public Service Association, a trade union, claimed this sidelined long-serving and knowledgeable Powerhouse curators in favour of outsider non-specialists. The programme was scrapped in May following a review by the state treasury.

After Havilah’s departure, Abbie Galvin, the New South Wales government’s architect, took over as interim chief executive. At the same time, the state appointed former Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron as a “strategic adviser”. Cassandra Wilkinson, a New South Wales treasury executive, took over Wilsdon’s role in July, in an environment of constant media reports about apparent cost blowouts in the lead-up to the launch.

Campaigners are unhappy that key treasures of the Powerhouse collection will not be on display in the new building. The 1785 Boulton & Watt steam engine, the 1855 Locomotive No.1 and the Strasburg Clock model—along with most of the rest of the collection—are stored off-site in a discovery centre that is open to the public only on weekends.

Winkworth says the Ultimo site was “uniquely resonant and appropriate for the display of the Powerhouse Museum’s internationally significant power and transport collections. Now the collections are dismembered at Castle Hill and never to be seen together again.”

She argues that the new Powerhouse was “never intended to be a museum” at all but rather a function and performance centre, helping boost the local nighttime economy.

Five inaugural shows are all scheduled to open on 7 November. Task Eternal, the main draw, traces the history of aviation and space exploration in partnership with the Smithsonian and the British Museum. Es Devlin: The Turning features five major works by the artist and stage designer. The Dark, for children, turns darkness into a “playground of curiosity” through interactive storytelling, a crystal tunnel and 100 borrowed childhood toys.

The fourth show, Overflow, explores the care of salt and freshwater ecosystems around Australia. Finally, The Mall centres on western Sydney’s pioneering role in the global development of shopping malls as part of modern culture and lifestyle.

General admission to the Powerhouse will be free. Over-16s will pay A$30 ($21) for a ticket to Task Eternal. All visitors will pay from A$10 ($7) for James Turrell’s light-based installation, Shangri La (Over the Hump). A 23-day opening festival will feature 179 events including Space Shuttle astronaut Charles Bolden reflecting on leadership in space exploration. Most of the opening events are free.

NSW government scraps controversial billion-dollar relocation plan but faces questions from community groups and parliament

Lisa Havilah had stood aside pending “investigations into governance and procurement”, according to New South Wales’ arts minister

The Art Gallery of New South Wales has been expanded with a new building by Japanese architects SANAA, while new displays will push Australia's Indigenous artists to the fore

#9122. Apple M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Review: Don’t Touch It

Apple M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Review: Don’t Touch It

Apple’s new, highest-end MacBook Pro diverged from the last few launches in that it didn’t focus on performance at all, but rather leaned on a feature the company famously said would never come to macOS: touch control. I get why Apple did this, but touch isn’t at all a reason to get this computer. But to be clear, that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t get this computer. Quite the opposite, in fact.

Setting aside touch capability, Apple's tandem OLED application here results in the best display I've ever tested, full stop. That alone is worth the $400 premium.

As Marques Brownlee pointed out in his day-of reaction video, Steve Jobs said that while touching a laptop screen makes for “a great demo,” it isn’t a feature that most people will actually use every day and those who want to will find themselves fatigued by the ergonomics of the action rather quickly.

And it does make a great demo: that was the focus of Apple’s entire press event in Los Angeles last week. But just because you can touch the display of the new MacBook Pro doesn’t mean you will want to, or even should. I’m quite likely to largely ignore the feature (in fact, I will barely mention it at all in this review), while also lamenting that the device that could actually use macOS with touch control continues to not get it. But I digress.

Apple likely went with the touch aspect because the real reasons to pay the $400 premium for this version of the M5 Max MacBook Pro weren’t worth an event, and the Ternus-led Apple wanted to make a splash. The average computer buyer isn’t going to run to social media to discuss OLED panels and a size and weight reduction. But real users? For them, those are the actual reasons to buy this computer and make that slight price bump entirely worth it.

Shifting up the order of how we typically do things here in computer reviews, I’m going to start with performance because it’s the area of this computer that has not changed at all compared to the M5 Max MacBook Pro I reviewed in March.

I ran the same benchmark tests on this PROLED version and found statistically insignificant differences between the two computers. I’m not even going to post those results here because they’re virtually the same. If you’re curious how a MacBook Pro chassis handles the M5 Max, then I encourage you to read my review from earlier this year.

What is more important than the fact that this computer has identical performance to the computer that came out in March is that it’s getting that same performance despite a slightly smaller overall form factor and a significant drop in weight. I understand that it requires way more words to convey that thought than “you can touch it,” but this advancement is absolutely worth it, especially for photographers who travel with this computer tucked into a bag they carry on their shoulders.

With performance unchanged, let’s instead focus on what is different and why it might matter to you.

As mentioned, Apple made some subtle changes to the chassis of this version of the MacBook Pro. Notice I didn’t say “minor changes,” and that was on purpose. While they are, at first glance, slight, the effects are not minor.

Apple did not remove any of the ports on this version of the computer, leaving all three Thunderbolt 5 ports, an SD card reader, full-size HDMI, 3.5mm headphone jack, and MagSafe charging port. Just like with performance, you sacrifice nothing here by selecting the smaller and lighter build.

Going with the thinner tandem OLED panel versus the previous LCD panel allowed for, as mentioned, a notable weight reduction. The 14-inch model is 15% lighter at three pounds while the 16-inch model (the one I’m using for this review) is 15% lighter at four pounds. Both versions are also thinner at 1.50 centimeters and 1.60 centimeters, respectively.

The four “feet” on the bottom of the laptop are slightly different as well. They feel like they’re made from the same material and do an equally good job of preventing unwanted slipping on slick surfaces; they are just inset and rounded on the edges as opposed to raised on the aluminum surface and flat.

When you look at this new PROLED model side by side with what I’ll call the “standard” model, you’ll also notice that the display is shorter now, and that’s due to the removal of the bezel at the bottom of the display. The corners are all rounded now, instead of having sharp corners at the bottom and rounded corners at the top, which Apple seems to have done just for the sake of consistency here. The actual display area is larger, with the 16-inch model coming in at 16.3 inches, while the 14-inch is 14.2 inches.

What you can’t necessarily see is Apple’s redesigned thermal system. The only evidence that anything has changed is a slightly different, split exhaust port design on the PROLED model. But Apple says there is a lot different on the inside to compensate for the smaller chassis. Given that I cannot see a statistically significant difference in performance between the previous model and the PROLED model, I would say whatever Apple did to mitigate heat was successful.

Another change is the speaker system, which, sure, is better. I think the low end got a very slight boost and yes, it does sound better than it used to when the lid is closed. All that said, the bar for quality was already quite high. MacBook Pro speakers have sounded very, very good for several years now. Unless you’re really craning to hear it and you’re comparing them side by side, you probably would just say, “the speakers sound nice.”

I want to talk a bit about battery life because, as before, it’s pretty impressive. Apple quotes up to 22 hours of video streaming and 14 hours of wireless web browsing on the 14-inch version while the 16-inch version bumps that up slightly to 24 hours of video streaming and 17 hours of web browsing.

Those aren’t particularly useful numbers to me, so I instead wanted to see how well it handled under load. I ran all of the performance benchmarks I mentioned above off battery power and, as is our standard practice, ran all those benchmarks twice. That process took the better part of two hours and really taxed the machine’s CPU, GPU, and fan, resulting in 48% battery when all was said and done. That’s pretty good.

Rounding out the specs, the MacBook Pro with PROLED has Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and can support up to two Studio Display XDR monitors at full 5K resolution and 120Hz refresh rate over a single Thunderbolt 5 connection. The M5 Pro model can support up to a total of three displays while the M5 Max can support up to four.

Oh, and I guess I would be remiss if I didn’t mention that the Apple on the back of the computer glows again. I am fully aware this is entirely meaningless in the grand scheme of things, but I’d be lying if I said this wasn’t cool. I’m glad it’s back, and Apple had to actually go out of its way to add it here since an OLED panel has no backlight, so it isn’t just a happenstance of cutting out a chunk of the backlight backing. Apple had to go in there and put in a specific LED panel to light up the apple, and darn it, I like it. Sue me.

OLED, or organic light-emitting diode, technology produces better colors and contrast ratios than LCD (liquid crystal displays) because each pixel can be individually controlled. Beyond that, each pixel can be turned on and off, so blacks can appear truly black, as there is no light being emitted from those pixels. That means OLED displays, including Apple’s tandem OLED found in the PROLED MacBook Pro, have a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with true black levels and no backlight blooming or haloing artifacts around bright objects.

The PROLED display on this MacBook Pro is not Apple’s first use of the technology: that came with the 11-inch and 13-inch iPad Pro tablets released back in 2024. Apple mentioned that it didn’t immediately bring this technology over to the MacBook — or any other display in its line — because as the display gets larger (in this case, 16-inches), it becomes substantially more difficult to produce a consistent panel.

As a bit of a recap, tandem OLED stacks two electroluminescent-emitting layers that share the current load. The result is reduced stress per layer, yielding higher peak brightness, improved power efficiency, and extended panel longevity compared to single-layer OLEDs. Reading through Apple’s PROLED White Paper, the company says that it is able to get the results this panel produces because of the pairing of hardware and software: hardware-integrated in Apple silicon, the display engine executes real-time compensation algorithms based on real-time content, individual pixel usage history, temperature sensors, and ambient lighting.

To prevent what is colloquially called burn-in (OLEDs don’t actually do this the same way that Plasma panels do, but it’s the best term to describe what people are seeing), the display engine performs active per-pixel uniformity compensation from 1 nit to 1,000 nits and continuously adjusts drive signals.

OLED has excellent viewing angles, too, and Apple rates an 89-degree viewing angle in all directions with minimal off-axis color shift or contrast dip.

The PROLED display can also reproduce over a billion colors and do so accurately. This particular display is also quite bright, which was one of OLED’s drawbacks in its early days. By stacking two panels together, Apple was able to push 1,000 nits of full-screen brightness in SDR and HDR, but up to 2,000 nits peak HDR brightness with four stops of extended dynamic range headroom relative to standard dynamic range. In short, this display is not only extremely color accurate, it also has an incredible contrast ratio and outstanding brightness.

That’s all on paper, though. Real life? That could be a different story.

As a note, my review unit was not equipped with Apple’s Nano Texture. When I looked at these two options side by side last week, I said to myself that I probably wouldn’t pick Nano Texture on this particular model, which is a shift for me from previous years. I typically like the matte display and Apple’s Nano Texture is excellent at rejecting reflections. The thing is, this particular display without Nano Texture is pretty good at blocking them as well. Yes, you will see them, but they’re not overly distracting. I also think that if you’re going to get an OLED panel, you don’t want to do anything that might reduce the perfect contrast that OLED affords you.

Head-on, I couldn’t tell the difference between these two displays when it comes to contrast. However, at an angle, the Nano Texture did degrade it just a little bit. I will rarely be looking at this display at any angle other than head-on, but seeing that was enough for me to want to forgo it this time.

While yes, you can touch this display, that’s not why I think it’s special. When I first saw it in person last week, I knew it was going to be good. What I did not know was that this would be the best display I, or another one of my long-time colleagues, has ever tested.

Apple never promised any gamut coverage in its keynote and even the white paper about this display doesn’t call out sRGB, Adobe RGB, or Display P3 gamut coverage promises. The only number it specifically states is 81% of BT.2020. That number doesn’t mean anything to me, since I live in a world of the “big three” as I call them, so I had to test it for myself.

I ran a display test twice: once with default settings and again after shifting over specifically to the Photography display setting. This is similar to the test I ran when I reviewed the Studio Display XDR. I ran this test at maximum brightness.

Firstly, let’s look at the default color settings. In this mode, the display leans a little heavier on the blues and the reds, while the greens take a slight step back by comparison.

The results are very good. This display hits 137.1% of sRGB, 94.5% of Adobe RGB, and 97.1% of DCI P3 color gamuts with an average Delta E of around 1, which is outstanding. I think if this was the best the display was capable of, I would be very happy. This is a notable step up from the standard display and is better than the Studio Display XDR.

But I had only begun to see how good this display is.

I shifted over to the Photography (P3-D65) setting and re-ran the test. When you select this option, the display resets, locks brightness (it’s much lower than peak 1,000 nits, but is still plenty bright) and it outputs an inversion of the last test: stronger greens with slightly less emphasized reds and blues. The Studio Display XDR does the same thing, and I expected similar results (that is to say, good but nothing unexpected). Instead, I was treated to the best results I’ve seen across any display I’ve reviewed.

The PROLED display hits 148.5% of sRGB, 102.3% of Adobe RGB, and 105.2% of DCI P3 with an average Delta E of 1.08. I have never tested any display — monitor or television — that scored better than 100% coverage in all three of these gamuts. I talked to an industry colleague and he went back through his years of tests and found that he hadn’t either. The best he had previously seen was 100%, 100%, and 99%, respectively. Even as a famous Apple skeptic, he had to give his kudos.

Stacking on top of this impressive result is the fact that this display is remarkably consistent. Panel uniformity evaluation showed pristine performance from edge to edge, top to bottom in our standard 9×5 uniformity test. This panel is flawless.

Given my colleague’s vast experience and combining that with six years of display testing of my own, I have no qualms about making this statement: the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED has the best display you can buy right now. You will not likely find another monitor on the market that will come, out of the box, capable of this level of color accuracy combined with this level of peak brightness, contrast ratio, and panel uniformity, and you certainly will not find another laptop that hits these marks either.

Alright yes, you can touch this display. No, it’s not really very ergonomic to do so. Lack of Apple Pencil support is weird, trying to play the digital piano in Logic Pro with your fingers pointed straight out in front of you is extremely uncomfortable, and the entire experience doesn’t feel like it has been tailored for touch much at all. Sure, you could argue that the improved hinge shows an effort to do something that would make touch feel intentional. Sure, but while the hinge may be stiffer, that stiffness doesn’t prevent it from giving a bit at your touch, resulting in a sort of bouncy experience. I don’t really notice a difference in how it feels in practice and since you can’t fold the display over and allow it to lay flat, I find myself not touching this display ever.

This is not an Apple-specific problem either. I have used and reviewed multiple PCs that support touch and I don’t like touching those either. I’m sorry, but Steve Jobs was right: leaning forward and touching a laptop screen in front of you is not particularly pleasant and you will find yourself with fatigue very quickly.

If there was one argument about touch being thoughtfully implemented, it would be related to the Dynamic Island and closing windows.

I do like the move away from the notch and toward Dynamic Island. I had sort of visually ignored the notch for the last few years and I straight up don’t even see the little oval hole where the webcam is at all since it lives in the darkness of the top menu bar. It’s neat to have some support for the visual flair of dynamic island, but you don’t have to touch it to engage with it and I typically don’t. The experience is not worse when I’m not using my index finger.

Tapping over to the upper-left-hand corner of windows has been optimized for touch because as you might expect, it can be difficult to hit the tiny target that is the red close circle. To that end, Apple made it so that when you tap over there, it doesn’t just immediately perform the action but rather magnifies that corner so it is easier to hit the exact button you want. This does largely prevent you from accidentally closing a window when you want to minimize it.

The benefits of this display aren’t really tied to the fact you can touch it, so none of these quibbles really matter. If you don’t want to touch it, don’t. If you really want to take away the choice, you can straight-up disable touch in Accessibility settings. But a display this good deserves to be crystal clear, and if I’m going to say no to Nano Texture to maximize the viewing experience, I’m going to say no to touching the display and leaving smudges on it, too.

In March, my review of the M5 Max MacBook Pro heaped on the praise, with the two caveats being less than perfect display performance and a complaint about how heavy the 16-inch version is.

I’ve sort of painted myself into a corner here as far as scoring goes, because Apple specifically addressed both those complaints with the PROLED version. This is absolutely a better computer, it just costs $400 more. I don’t want to dismiss that $400 is not a small amount of money, but when you’re looking at spending $2,000 to $3,000 minimum (and you could spend a lot more to maximize performance), it doesn’t seem like a lot to ask for the gravity of the benefits. If those things that bothered me in that last review also bother you, then $400 seems like a reasonable cost to address them.

The last time Apple went out of its way to make the MacBook Pro thinner and lighter, it also introduced the touch bar and the result was objectively the worst MacBook Pro ever made. It took away ports, had abysmal performance, and the biggest feature sucked.

This time, Apple once again made the MacBook Pro thinner and lighter than its predecessor, but the performance didn’t dip and the biggest feature is simply irrelevant. You have to chuckle a little bit at this result, but the broader picture is still a net positive.

Ironically, despite specifically saying the speakers sound better when the lid is closed, if you’re the kind of user who is going to care about how much better the speakers are when the lid is closed, then you probably shouldn’t buy this computer. It’s not giving you $400 of added value acting as a glorified Mac Studio sitting on a desk in your office. That value is only earned if you plan to look at the display.

This is one of those rare times where Apple is giving you a true alternative that you can buy, brand-new, directly from the company’s website. The “standard” MacBook Pro with M5 Max is, performance-wise, identical to this new PROLED version. For $400 off, you are still getting an outstanding computer. It just weighs a bit more, is a just a hair larger, and doesn’t have as good of a display. It also doesn’t have touch control support, if that is meaningful to you.

I do think that this is the exception to what will be a return to the rule, however: do not expect to have both an LCD and OLED option when Apple refreshes the MacBook Pro with M6 Max, either next year or the year after. I think you should fully expect that the $400 premium is going to become the only option. So if you really don’t care about this display or the weight savings, then this might be the last chance you’ll have to get a slightly less expensive, expensive computer.

Yes. The MacBook Pro with M5 Max was already a full recommendation, but Apple went and fixed the two complaints I had about that computer with this new PROLED model. I can’t find a flaw with this machine, and if you can afford it and need the performance it offers, then there is no reason not to take the plunge. And remember: you don’t have to touch it.

#9121. Who Is Responsible for a Camera’s Failure?

Who Is Responsible for a Camera’s Failure?

When news broke that French digital rangefinder maker Pixii had entered liquidation, the response across the photography community was swift and, for PetaPixel, surprisingly personal.

Thank you for helping to destroy prospects for Pixii SAS with your devastating review of the Pixii Max. Awww, you couldn’t get a free trip to Provence to try out the camera in a 5 star resort. What a shame!!!

You should have considered the implications of what a bad review would do to their future prospects. They were already on the brink when you did the review. Now we have one less new entrant in the imaging business. Who knows what they could have become in a couple of years. I would have bought one if they could have ironed out some of the major issues.

THANK YOU, CHRIS! You really did your job exposing this company. And now they are bankrupt and in liquidation.

This and all of the accusations PetaPixel has seen carry a familiar refrain: had Pixii done the song and dance of an international press trip, the coverage of the camera would have been warmer, buying the startup enough runway to survive.

But blaming critical journalism for a company’s commercial collapse misunderstands both the role of editorial oversight and the harsh realities of the camera market.

Every reviewer carries personal bias. Preference in camera design, menu layout, tactile feedback, and image rendering naturally shapes how any photographer evaluates a tool. However, the idea that luxury press trips or manufacturer access dictates whether a review is positive or negative falls apart under scrutiny.

Reviewers — and PetaPixel uses this term specifically to separate them from influencers — regularly attend manufacturer launch events because they provide dedicated environments to test gear under demanding conditions — whether capturing sports, wildlife, or street photography. Yet, at least in PetaPixel‘s case, those experiences do not buy favorable coverage.

For example, consider the Panasonic Lumix S9. PetaPixel traveled to Osaka for the launch, yet offered sharp criticism regarding its lack of an electronic viewfinder and key shooting limitations. Chris has openly said he doesn’t like this camera.

Another example is the Leica SL series. Despite multiple trips to Germany, PetaPixel's reviews consistently questioned whether the performance justified the premium price point.

A third example, perhaps? Consider the Sigma BF. Long-standing professional relationships with Sigma did not prevent honest assessments of ergonomic and operational hurdles.

You need a fourth example? Very well, consider the OM System PEN. The company not only sponsors PetaPixel's Trail Camera series but also brought PetaPixel out to Japan for the review of that camera. Despite this, the final evaluation is among the lowest across the entire industry.

It's worth pointing out that one of the reasons PetaPixel created PixelMeter, a review aggregator designed to surface multiple opinions on a single page, was to further eliminate the perception of bias and to give photographers as much information as possible so they can make informed buying decisions. The goal has always been to encourage readers to compare perspectives rather than relying on a single voice.

A camera reviewer’s primary obligation is to the reader and prospective buyer, not to the manufacturer’s bottom line. When evaluating a product that costs thousands of dollars, ignoring flaws to protect a niche startup does a disservice to the photographers putting up their own money.

The Pixii Max offered genuine novelties, but it also suffered from significant operational and technical hurdles. It had a convoluted, difficult-to-use menu system and showed major issues with image quality (visible banding in shadows), among other problems.

Of note, even those who blame PetaPixel for Pixii's demise often concede that there are issues, noting they would have purchased a Pixii Max if the company had fixed its major flaws. That admission validates the exact points raised in critical reviews: the camera arrived on the market with unaddressed flaws that kept buyers away.

A single review rarely decides the fate of a product, let alone an entire brand. Pixii operated for nearly eight years and released multiple iterations of its digital rangefinder. Yet throughout its lifecycle, the company maintained an unusually closed posture toward the tech press.

Pixii never responded to a single inquiry PetaPixel sent to the company dating back to 2018. It didn't communicate with the wider press pool much at all and, to PetaPixel's knowledge, never sent review units outside of France. In fact, PetaPixel's review of the Pixii Max only happened because a generous reader loaned his personal unit for testing — years after the product had already been on the market.

PetaPixel was not an outlier in its opinions either. No established photo publication or veteran gear reviewer issued an unqualified, glowing endorsement of the Pixii Max, and the broader media consensus ranged from mixed to highly critical.

When a camera brand fails, the root causes lie in product execution, pricing, manufacturing scale, and market demand. Reviewers document those realities — they do not create them. In a media landscape increasingly crowded with sponsored content and brand ambassadorships, transparent and unsparing editorial critique remains vital for keeping the industry honest.

#9120. Sony World Photography Awards Honors James Barnor, Ghana’s First Photojournalist

Sony World Photography Awards Honors James Barnor, Ghana’s First Photojournalist

The Sony World Photography Awards and the World Photography Organization have revealed that photographer James Barnor is the recipient of the Outstanding Contribution to Photography title at the Sony World Photography Awards 2027.

This is a big year for the Sony World Photography Awards, as the renowned international photo competition is celebrating its 20th anniversary with some big changes. Likewise, it’s a significant honor for Barnor, who is considered Ghana’s first photojournalist.

“I am honored to receive this award. I was lucky to be born and brought up in a family of photographers, and I took full advantage of it to absorb as much as I could. When I opened my studio in Accra, I never imagined that my work would take me so far: through Ghana’s independence, to London and back again,” James Barnor says.

“My camera became my companion, and I have never regretted it. Wherever I went, I tried to learn so that I could share what I had learned. Today, that matters more to me than ever. Up and-coming photographers now have every chance to go even further, and I hope this exhibition will inspire them to stay curious, to tell their own stories, and to pass on what they know.”

My camera became my companion, and I have never regretted it.

Born in 1929, Barnor trained under his cousin, portrait photographer J. P. D. Dodoo. In 1950, Barnor became the very first staff photographer at then-new Daily Graphic in Ghana, right as the country was well on its way to winning independence in 1957, a massive societal and cultural shift Barnor captured along the way.

“As a photojournalist, he documented this moment in history through the eyes of those who lived it, from rallies and street parades to Kwame Nkrumah’s declaration of independence,” the Sony World Photography Awards says.

In 1953, Barnor opened the Ever Young studio in Accra’s Jamestown district, where he photographed all members of society, including students, officers, judges, political figures, and more.

He moved to the United Kingdom in 1959 to further study photography at the Medway College of Art in Kent, then worked as a color printer at Color Processing Laboratories, a leading British lab.

Around this time, Barnor also worked for Drum, an influential Black South African lifestyle magazine that was known for its anti-apartheid work. Barnor’s portraits of Black models and celebrities, which often graced covers, helped establish a visual language for the African continent and its diaspora.

A decade later, armed with training from Agfa-Gevaert in Belgium and Germany, Barnor returned home to Ghana and opened the country’s first color processing lab, bringing color photography to a whole new audience. Barnor continued working as a photographer and photojournalist throughout this time, inspiring new generations of photographers in Ghana.

In the early 1990s, Barnor returned to England, where he still lives today. His work has been exhibited worldwide, including at MASI Lugano, the Serpentine in London, the Detroit Institute of Arts, LUMA Arles, FOMU Antwerp, and more. His work has also been featured at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City.

James Barnor joins an impressive list of photographers who have won the Outstanding Contribution to Photography award. Last year, Joel Meyerowitz won the honor, following Susan Meiselas (2025), Sebastião Salgado (2024), Edward Burtynsky (2022), Graciela Iturbide (2021), and Martin Parr (2017).

As part of the celebration, a retrospective of over 50 of James Barnor’s works will be shown at London’s Somerset House as part of the Sony World Photography Awards 2027 exhibition in April.
