#9119. Chris “Daze” Ellis "Orchid Rain on the Underground" @ PPOW Gallery, NYC

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a new series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

Inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor New York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in New York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

#9118. Camp Snap CS-8 Mini Brings Super 8 Retro Video Vibes to Smaller Hands

Camp Snap CS-8 Mini Brings Super 8 Retro Video Vibes to Smaller Hands

Camp Snap is looping back around to its original target market with a miniaturized version of the CS-8 camcorder it launched last year that more easily fits into a child’s hand. The CS-8 Mini is less than half the size of the original and is designed specifically to cater to kids.

The company’s original target market for the first Camp Snap camera was kids at camp—hence the name—though in recent years it expanded to appeal to a broader, adult audience. Today, the company is returning to its roots with the CS-8 Mini.

“Reimagined at less than half the size of the original, the compact, screen-free camcorder is designed for smaller hands and bigger adventures, encouraging kids to capture the world around them rather than consume content on a screen,” the company says.

“Ready to use straight out of the box, the CS-8 Mini combines easy point-and-shoot recording with five film-inspired filters, four aspect ratios, 8x digital zoom, and built-in audio recording. With no playback screen, Wi-Fi, or apps required, young creators can focus on making memories in the moment and reliving them later.”

This new, smaller version of the camera measures 6.0 × 5.6 × 2.0 inches and weighs a scant 0.58 pounds (262 grams).

There really isn’t much different about this camera compared to its larger predecessor. It features the same general design aesthetic, five built-in film filters, four aspect ratios, and a trigger-pull recording style that Camp Snap says is inspired by classic 8mm camcorders. Audio is captured via an integrated microphone, and footage is stored via internal memory that can be accessed via USB-C.

It's not entirely identical to the original CS-8, though. The company says that the retro-inspired battery and storage indicators have been redesigned to fit the Mini's compact body, making it easy to monitor remaining power and recording space.

Another difference is the color options: the CS-8 Mini is available in blue, green, orange, and pink. The standard CS-8 debuted in black, which isn't even an option for this kid-focused model.

The Camp Snap CS-8 Mini is available starting today directly from Camp Snap's website and at Target for $150. For those keeping score, Camp Snap's original CS-8, which is twice as big, launched for that same price.

Do kids (or anyone) really need these? That's a debate the PetaPixel team discussed on this week's podcast.

#9117. The Fifty: VSCO Reveals the Final 25 Photographers in Its Nationwide Billboard Exhibition

The Fifty: VSCO Reveals the Final 25 Photographers in Its Nationwide Billboard Exhibition

VSCO has announced the second half of its The Fifty campaign, a nationwide billboard-based exhibition that is celebrating one photographer in every U.S. state via large-format public displays in their home markets.

Announced in August, The Fifty offered 50 photographers, one from each state, the chance to have their work featured on billboards across the country, licensed, and compensated by the company.

The first 25 photographers were revealed in September and now it is completing its project with the last 25.

Below is a small selection of the chosen photographers and their work:

“For 15 years, VSCO has championed photographers, giving them the tools and community to develop their craft and help them grow,” Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, says. “The Fifty takes that further by putting photographers and their work in front of potential clients and brands with the goal of turning visibility into real job opportunities that help them build the careers they desire.”

VSCO says that The Fifty reflects the many ways photography documents the world, from changing traditions, migration and belonging, environmental challenges, and extraordinary moments found in everyday life.

“It is an honor to be a part of this awesome project that celebrates photography, and that I can represent the great state of New Jersey, and share my personal work with the world,” Ed Kashi, who photographed agricultural workers harvesting crops as part of a larger project examining climate change and labor, says.

“A billboard in California, my home state, and now a billboard in Times Square is truly an experience I will never forget and one I am immensely proud of,” California photographer Lin Bvtcher adds. “I never imagined that my little project featuring women and their cars would take me here but alas, it has. I am still in shock, quite frankly.”

On Saturday, November 7, from 10 AM to 1 PM, VSCO will host a free community event featuring local photographer Nat Segebre who was selected to represent Florida in The Fifty, together with photographers Melina Deya and Deun Ivory. The company says that the three speakers will discuss their journeys from hobby to profession, the challenges they’ve faced and their defining “I made it” moments. The conversation will be moderated by Miami-based Paul Weaver, founder of The Freelance Photographer, VSCO’s professional education platform.

All 50 of the photographers selected can be seen on VSCO’s website.

#9116. As it expands, Provincetown’s Fine Arts Work Center prioritises access and affordability

Fine Arts Work Center visual arts fellow Carlie Trosclair at work in a Provincetown studio Photo: Daisy St. Sauveur

Provincetown, the harbour community perched on the tip of the Cape Cod peninsula in Massachusetts, has a well-earned reputation as a haven for artists, but that status is under threat due to a lack of affordable housing. Geographically secluded and aesthetically distinctive, the town, which experienced an influx of Portuguese sailors in the 1850s, has attracted artists for almost a century, particularly queer painters, writers and poets.

Provincetown’s Fine Arts Work Center(FAWC) has been at the heart of this creative community since it was founded in 1968 by a group that included the painters Robert Motherwell, Myron Stout, Jack Tworkov and Fritz Bultman. The painter Sam Messer and Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Mary Oliver were among the centre’s early residents, followed in ensuing decades by artists including Lisa Yuskavage, Jack Pierson, Ellen Gallagher, Jeffrey Gibson, Firelei Báez, Elliot Hundley, Jacolby Satterwhite and Jennifer Packer.

Miguel Braceli, True love Kiss: a Queer Fairy Tale in Provincetown, 2024 Courtesy the artist

Today, the non-profit grants artists access and community in a town that is among the most expensive in New England during the summer season. Providing room and support for queer artists remains a priority. The Venezuelan artist Miguel Braceli, for instance, completed his 2024 residency by orchestrating the public performance True Love’s Kiss, in which strangers were invited to lock lips at the granite breakwater on the shore’s very western tip.

Located in the Provincetown’s residential east end, the FAWC is best known for its residency programme, which provides ten artist fellows and ten writers with lodging and studio space for seven months every year, between October and April. Among this year’s artist residents are Abigail Dudley, Alina Perez, Nasim Hantehzadeh and L.J. Roberts.

The Fine Arts Works Center's 1979-80 fellows in the studios Courtesy the Fine Arts Works Center, Provincetown, Massachusetts

“People have come here for generations to live their identities to the fullest and they have heavily contributed to the artistic creativity that makes Provincetown what is,” Sharon Polli , the centre’s executive director, tells The Art Newspaper. “The unique experience residents feel the second they drive down Route 6 or step off the ferry comes out in the work created here.”

The centre has been in a continuous state of expansion and renovation for much of its 58-year history. What was once the longtime Provincetown resident Hans Hoffman’s studio is now a fraction of the centre’s main grounds, named Days Lumberyard, which includes multiple living units, studios, offices, an auditorium, a gallery space, an outdoor area and a printshop that still houses Motherwell’s own press. The centre acquired a heating supply building in 1972 for around $120,000 and has gradually transformed its coal bins and other disused or dilapidated areas into its main hub.

The Days Lumberyard building at the Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown, Massachusetts, date unknown Courtesy Fine Arts Work Center, Provincetown, Massachusetts

Polli says the lumberyard’s growth and importance to the community are proof of “Provincetown being a place where there has always been room for artists and writers who maintain the town’s cultural identity” since the middle of the 20th century. The centre operates on an annual budget of around $3m, $600,000 of which this year was raised at its annual summer gala at the Pilgrim Monument at the Provincetown Museum.

The centre’s core role in maintaining the town’s artistic and intellectual identity has recently been officially acknowledged. The municipal board made a pledge this past summer to grant the centre $1.5m toward a planned $12m transformation of its 4 Brewster Street building. Located around the corner from the main FAWC complex, the lot the centre acquired in 1997 is in line for a totally new build. The Boston-based firm Hacin Architects was selected to double the housing square footage for fellows and staff, while adding a community space and a rooftop garden.

The main Fine Arts Work Center complex in Provincetown, Massachusetts Photo: Robert Benson

“We are hoping that the municipal support will help us leverage private funding,” Polli says. She and her team of 12 full-time employees keep the conversation and cultural exchange active throughout the off-seasons by offering a community-oriented programming. The year-round calendar includes FAWC Fridays, group exhibitions with past fellows, Queer Week, workshops and public talks with artists such as Catherine Opie, Ilana Savdie and Doron Langberg.

Polli says the centre’s off-season programming is even “more important than anything we do rest of the year because we give people a place to engage with high-calibre dialogues where many locals have working practices”.

#9115. Wandrd Reimagined the Magnetic Camera Strap

Wandrd Reimagined the Magnetic Camera Strap

Wandrd’s new Magnetic Camera Strap System is now available, bringing a redesigned approach to how photographers attach and switch camera straps.

The system uses magnetic alignment and mechanical locking hardware to let users connect or release a camera with one hand. In contrast, its modular design lets users move a strap between multiple camera bodies without repeatedly changing attachment hardware.

The collection is the result of more than two and a half years of development, Wandrd says. Instead of simply introducing another camera strap with quick-release clips, the company has developed its own connector hardware, webbing, and attachment components. The lineup includes two neck straps, a wrist strap, and a conversion kit for photographers who want to use the system with an existing strap.

Quick-release camera straps aren’t new, but Wandrd’s approach combines magnetic guidance with a separate mechanical locking mechanism. Its Magnetic CoreLock uses an internal magnet to draw a Torus Link into the correct position, where a self-centering design helps guide the connector into place. Spring-loaded locking buttons then secure the connection under tension.

The release mechanism requires a dual-pinch action, meaning photographers must deliberately press both sides of the connector to detach it. This separates the convenience of magnetic alignment from the mechanism that actually holds the camera.

Wandrd opted for PA66 fiberglass-reinforced nylon for the CoreLock instead of metal. The company says the material offers strength without adding unnecessary weight or introducing hard metal surfaces that could scratch camera equipment.

The connector is one part of a larger hardware redesign. Wandrd also developed custom Liquid Nylon Tubular Webbing, plus its own Torus Links and Torus Mount components, rather than building the system around readily available strap hardware.

One of the more practical aspects of the system is its approach to photographers who regularly work with multiple camera bodies. Each neck strap comes with four Torus Links, which can remain attached to individual cameras. Once the connectors are installed, photographers can move the same strap between bodies by engaging or releasing the CoreLock.

For wildlife and sports photographers, for example, this could make it easier to switch between different focal-length setups without transferring strap attachments each time. It also offers flexibility for photographers who use separate camera bodies for photography and video.

The Torus Links include a built-in wear indicator intended to help users identify when a connector needs replacing. The cord has three visual zones: black indicates that it is in good condition, yellow signals that replacement is needed, and red indicates that it should no longer be used.

Wandrd describes the links as low-profile connectors designed to remain on the camera rather than becoming another piece of hardware photographers need to remove between uses.

Rather than limiting the system to a single strap design, Wandrd is introducing three options for different camera setups and carrying preferences.

The Magnetic Camera Strap is the widest option at 30mm (1.2 inches) and is intended for heavier camera equipment and extended shooting sessions. The Magnetic Camera Strap Lite narrows the webbing to 15mm (0.6 inches), providing a slimmer option for compact cameras and lighter everyday setups.

For photographers who prefer a wrist-based connection, the Magnetic Wrist Strap also measures 15mm (0.6 inches). All three models use the same CoreLock attachment system and are available in Black, Wasatch Green, and Wandrd Red.

Both neck strap versions also include on-body storage, allowing the strap to clip to itself when it is not connected to a camera. This lets photographers keep the strap secured and out of the way while shooting handheld.

Photographers who already own a preferred strap do not necessarily have to replace it to use Wandrd’s new attachment system. The company is also introducing a DIY Magnetic Kit designed to convert compatible third-party straps to the CoreLock system.

Wandrd says the kit works with many leather straps, original equipment manufacturer camera straps, and other existing designs. This extends the system beyond its own collection and lets photographers keep their preferred strap material or design while changing how it attaches to a camera. Pricing for the DIY kit has not yet been announced.

Additional Torus Links are available separately in packs of four for $13, giving photographers more attachment points for multiple cameras or strap configurations.

Wandrd’s Magnetic Camera Strap System is now available through the company’s website. The 30mm Magnetic Camera Strap costs $69, the 15mm Magnetic Camera Strap Lite costs $49, and the Magnetic Wrist Strap costs $39. Additional Torus Links cost $13 per pack of four, and the DIY Magnetic Kit is $29.

All three strap models are offered in Black, Wasatch Green, and Wandrd Red.

#9114. Dezeen's favourite furniture and homeware from October

The first piece of furniture by architecture office Studio Hagen Hall and a pleated cabinet by Didi Ng Wing Yin feature in this roundup of design pieces spotted by Dezeen’s Jane Englefield over the last month.

Louis Hagen Hall of London-based Studio Hagen Hall has made his first foray into furniture with this sculptural coffee table, delivered as two legs and a weighty glass tabletop that require no mechanical fixings.

Hagen Hall originally designed the asymmetric piece for Pine Heath, a modernist Hampstead renovation with a corner sofa that required a bespoke coffee table to offset the negative space left by the seating.

Cherry veneer legs are paired with recyclable brown smoked glass to create the made-to-order piece, informed by the design philosophy of modernist American architect John Lautner.

Austrian, Netherlands-based designer Flora Lechner originally caught the attention of London’s Max Radford Gallery with her alternative aluminium chandeliers that look like ornate robots

Lechner has now translated her distinctive style into an unusual vase, composed of aluminium clips held together by stainless steel bolts. Stems can be slotted into the clips, which are supported by a base that can be filled with water.

“Exo 01 approaches the vase more as a support structure than as a container,” explained Lechner. “Inspired by braces used to hold and align parts of the body, the work applies this principle to flowers.”

Anne Holtrop is known for his rough-hewn furniture pieces, which conjure images of volcanic craters and mountainous landscapes.

For his inaugrual exhibition with Carpenter’s Workshop Gallery in London, the Dutch architect and designer is showing off his Low-relief collection of tables made from cast glass.

Their unrefined legs were informed by stone reliefs Holtrop visited in Aswan, Egypt.

Helsinki designer Didi Ng Wing Yin is known for his distinctively pleated wooden furniture, which he makes from locally sourced Finnish timber.

Last week, the designer debuted his first cabinet at Paris’s Spazio Nobile Gallery. Made from a mixture of fir and pine, finished with tung oil, the cabinet features a delicately pleated door made using Ng’s combined splitting, brushing and carving technique.

“I wanted to explore the dynamic contrast between form and texture,” Ng told Dezeen.

“The chunky pedestal base is built from straightforward architectural beams that retain their natural knots and raw characteristics, providing a heavy, structural anchor for the light, organic silhouette of the pleated cabinet door.”

One of many design events in October was PAD London, a collectible fair that takes place annually in Mayfair’s Berkley Square.

Among this year’s exhibitors was Mexico-based Manu Bañó, who showed a duo of striking patinated brass chairs formed from stacked, sculptural slabs of metal.

The chairs are a continuation of Bañó’s existing brass and stainless steel furniture, and were presented as part of the Objects with Narratives exhibition.

South Korean designer Seungjin Yang has been making playful furniture shaped like balloons for years, using colourful epoxy resin.

At PAD London, Yang showed his most recent balloon-like creations in the form of a sofa, two armchairs and two stools.

The designer coats real balloons in resin, painstakingly building their strength. Each piece is complete after around two weeks of delicate testing.

Don’t be misled by the intriguingly delicate appearance of Yang’s finished pieces, which are solid enough to be sat on.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you plan to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Company). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage (67 cents per mile), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $72,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

ChooseFI has partnered with CardRatings for our coverage of credit card products. ChooseFI and CardRatings may receive a commission from card issuers.

The biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

The 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

The decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the important thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

The most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and company handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $72,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP quickly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

#9111. Wandrd Magnetic Camera Straps Review: A Substantive Reinvention of the Humble Camera Strap?

Wandrd Magnetic Camera Straps Review: A Substantive Reinvention of the Humble Camera Strap?

Camera straps are one of those accessories that don’t always get much attention until something about them becomes inconvenient. Switching between straps, dealing with attachment hardware, or having buckles knock against camera equipment can all become minor annoyances over time. Wandrd’s new Magnetic Camera Strap System takes a different approach, using magnetic alignment and a mechanical locking mechanism to make connecting and removing a camera quicker.

The straps are solid, the hardware has some thoughtful design touches, and the magnetic release mechanism is genuinely enjoyable to use.

Wandrd sent over the 30mm Magnetic Camera Strap in Wasatch Green and the Magnetic Wrist Strap in Black to try out the new system. Both offer a familiar approach to carrying a camera, but the redesigned connection hardware adds an interesting twist. After spending some time with them, there are a few details that stand out, particularly the tactile release mechanism and some of the smaller design choices that make the straps pleasant to use.

The straps feel solid and well-constructed, with a straightforward design that doesn’t stray far from what you’d expect from a camera strap. The biggest difference is the Magnetic CoreLock system, which replaces more traditional attachment hardware with a magnetic quick-connect mechanism.

One detail I particularly appreciate is the use of plastic hardware rather than metal buckles. When packing away a camera or storing the strap, there is no metal clanging against the camera body or other equipment. It is a small consideration, but it makes sense for photographers who regularly pack gear into camera bags or carry multiple accessories.

On the 30mm version, the faux leather material is used specifically where the nylon webbing meets the magnetic release hardware. It has a subtle texture that feels smooth to the touch but still offers some grip. Rather than covering large sections of the strap, the material is limited to the transition area around the connector, adding contrast to the otherwise nylon construction.

The most interesting part of the system is undoubtedly the Magnetic CoreLock. Instead of threading or clipping a traditional strap attachment into place, the connector uses an internal magnet to guide the Torus Link into position. Once aligned, the spring-loaded locking mechanism engages, securing the connection under tension.

Releasing it requires pinching both sides of the connector. The action works just as Wandrd demonstrates, and it quickly becomes intuitive. The mechanism is particularly satisfying, to the point that I occasionally play with it like a fidget toy while hiking. It is a small thing, but the tactile action makes the system enjoyable to use beyond its intended purpose.

The combination of magnetic alignment and mechanical locking is also an interesting design choice. The magnet helps guide the connection, while the physical locking mechanism keeps everything secure. It is a more thoughtful approach than simply relying on magnets to hold a camera in place.

The 30mm Magnetic Camera Strap is the wider of the two neck strap options and is designed for photographers carrying larger camera setups. The Wasatch Green color adds some personality without being overly flashy, and the wider nylon webbing gives it a substantial feel.

The strap keeps a familiar design, with the magnetic connection hardware as the main departure from conventional camera straps. Its 30mm width makes it the more substantial option in the collection, particularly for photographers who prefer a wider strap when carrying their equipment.

Both neck strap models share one useful feature: integrated on-body storage. This lets the strap clip to itself when it is not attached to a camera, giving photographers a way to keep it secure rather than leaving loose strap ends hanging around while shooting.

The Magnetic Wrist Strap uses the same connection concept in a more compact form. The black version has a minimalist appearance, with the same quick-connect hardware used throughout the collection.

Wrist straps can be useful when working handheld, especially when you want to keep a camera readily accessible without wearing a full neck strap. The same magnetic attachment system means photographers can switch between the wrist strap and neck strap without an entirely different connection setup.

This is also where the collection’s modular nature becomes more interesting. Rather than treating each strap as an independent accessory, Wandrd has created a shared attachment system that allows different carrying options to work together.

One of the more interesting aspects of Wandrd’s approach is that the system isn’t limited to its own straps. The company also offers a DIY Magnetic Kit intended to adapt compatible existing camera straps to the Magnetic CoreLock hardware. Additional Torus Links are available separately, allowing photographers to outfit multiple camera bodies with their own connection points.

For photographers who regularly switch between cameras, this could be a convenient way to keep one strap compatible with several bodies. It also opens the door to using different carrying styles depending on the type of photography being done.

Overall, I like what Wandrd has put together. The straps are solid, the hardware has some thoughtful design touches, and the magnetic release mechanism is genuinely enjoyable to use. It is a neat system that offers a different approach to a familiar camera accessory, and I’m interested to see whether Wandrd develops the concept further and what other applications it might find for the technology.

As a woman who spends a lot of time hiking with a camera, I find carrying it this way considerably more comfortable than having it hang around my neck. Being able to switch between a traditional neck strap and a sling-style carry with little effort is a meaningful advantage for how I work outdoors.

That flexibility is what ultimately makes the system stand out to me. A camera strap might seem like a relatively simple accessory, but how it carries and moves with you can make a noticeable difference over a long day of shooting. The Wandrd system makes changing how I carry my camera straightforward, and the quick-release hardware adds another layer of convenience.

Peak Design remains a strong alternative, and photographers who prefer to avoid magnetic hardware may be more comfortable with its approach. But for my own use, Wandrd has taken the lead. I like the overall design, appreciate the smaller details, and find the ability to move between neck and crossbody carrying especially useful.

I’m looking forward to seeing what else Wandrd does with this system and whether the concept expands into other camera accessories.

Wandrd isn’t the first company to rethink how photographers attach and remove camera straps. Peak Design has built a popular lineup around its Anchor Link quick-connect system, and having used straps from both companies, I think they are both great options. They approach the same everyday problem differently, though, and a few details could make one more appealing than the other depending on personal preference.

One thing I have never particularly liked about the Peak Design hardware is its metal components. The metal buckle and adjustment hardware can knock against other equipment and potentially scratch camera surfaces if they come into contact. I’ve also had the hardware catch in my hair when I wear it down, which is surprisingly irritating when carrying a camera for extended periods. These aren’t dealbreakers, but they are small inconveniences I notice in regular use.

Wandrd avoids some of those issues by using plastic hardware for its CoreLock connector. There is no metal buckle clanging against equipment, and the overall connection feels more streamlined. However, the magnetic alignment introduces a different consideration. While the mechanical lock secures the camera, the system still uses magnets, and some photographers may prefer not to have magnets near their cameras or other electronics. That concern may not be an issue for everyone, but it is worth considering if you are uncomfortable with magnetic accessories.

Another detail I noticed is the difference in the strap materials. Wandrd’s webbing feels softer and silkier, while Peak Design’s has a noticeably stiffer texture. I prefer the feel of Wandrd’s material against my neck, although the difference is subtle enough that I probably wouldn’t have noticed it without having both straps side by side.

Both systems are strong contenders, and which is best for you comes down to personal preference. Peak Design has an established, versatile attachment system, while Wandrd takes a different approach that I find particularly appealing in everyday use. The choice ultimately comes down to which hardware and carrying style you prefer.

Yes. After spending more time with the Wandrd strap, it has become my preferred option among comparable camera straps, largely because of how easily I can wear it crossbody.

#9110. PixelMeter Now Lets You Compare Specs and Scores on Cameras and Lenses

PixelMeter Now Lets You Compare Specs and Scores on Cameras and Lenses

PixelMeter, the first and only review aggregator for cameras, lenses, smartphones, and more, has been updated with the most-requested feature since it launched last month: the ability to directly compare products.

“When we created PixelMeter, our goal was to give photographers and videographers a place to quickly gauge how reviewers across the internet feel about a camera or lens at a glance, while still offering easy access to full reviews for those wanting deeper context behind a rating,” Michael Zhang, publisher and founder of PetaPixel, says.

“As many readers pointed out, the next logical step was enabling side-by-side comparisons—allowing users to compare gear head-to-head, review consensus on pros and cons, and evaluate key specifications to make informed decisions much more easily. We now deliver that.”

The new comparison tool can be accessed in a couple of ways. First, while on any PixelMeter category page, an option to “Compare” will appear in the upper left-hand corner when hovering over any product listing. Clicking this option will start a comparison page, and users can then add more products to the comparison as they see fit.

Comparisons can also be started from any PixelMeter product page, directly to the right of the product name.

Camera and lens specifications are extremely tricky to get 100% correct, as specifications vary in how they are presented even on dealer product pages. If there is an issue with a particular specification, you can suggest a correction (via an option right above the specifications section on any product page), and we’ll double-check the issue and make any necessary edits. We greatly appreciate your help in making sure PixelMeter is a reliable, useful resource.

PixelMeter is still growing and improving. We encourage users to suggest products to be added (this can be done by clicking the small + icon right above the “What Reviewers Say” section of any product page). We also welcome feedback on the platform, so please leave comments below with any suggestions or bugs that come up while using PixelMeter.

We’d love to hear what feature you would like to see next on PixelMeter! Let us know what you think in the comments below. Also, as a reminder, PetaPixel Members can browse PixelMeter with no ads ever.

#9109. Hong Kong artists create a poetic moment in Venice

Kingsley Ng’s installation Laundry Nocturne (2026) Photo © Hong Kong Museum of Art

For Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, the Hong Kong-born artists Kingsley Ng and Angel Hui are training visitors’ attention on the quiet moments and subtle details connecting both cities. The exhibition, marking the 25th anniversary of Hong Kong’s first participation in the Venice Biennale, is curated by the Hong Kong Museum of Art (HKMoA) and continues until 22 November. It is housed in a historic Venetian residential building in the floating city’s Campo della Tana neighbourhood, a setting that underlines the meditative, lived-in quality to the works.

“What we hope visitors take away from the exhibition is a moment of reflection,” says Dr Maria Mok, the director of the HKMoA. “Through Kingsley and Angel’s attention to everyday details, we hope visitors feel invited to slow down and become more attentive to their surroundings, even within the hustle and intensity of urban life.”

One of Kingsley Ng’s installations, for instance, Laundry Nocturne (2026), consists of a projection and soundscape that evoke the play of light across laundry hung between buildings. It was inspired by the artist’s experience visiting Venice, where billowing laundry on clotheslines is still common, though for Ng it also evoked memories of Hong Kong.

Kingsley Ng in Venice Photo © Hong Kong Museum of Art

“The laundry becomes a point of entry into a wider soundscape of nighttime labour: recordings from a wastewater treatment plant, a newspaper-printing facility and a postal sorting centre evoke the work that continues while much of the city sleeps,” Ng says. “These modest, often overlooked processes that keep a city alive do not only connect Venice and Hong Kong. They are like a low hum in almost every city, to be picked up by an ear that doesn’t only listen to loud grandeur.”

For her installations, Angel Hui shines a spotlight on humble features of Hong Kong’s everyday life, including goldfish in plastic bags and a neighbour’s ornate but faded window frame. In her magical rendering, glowing plastic bags embroidered with goldfish motifs are suspended overhead, while a handwrought iron window made by Hui and traditional metalsmiths rotates slowly in the gallery.

“In Hong Kong, a goldfish bag is an everyday object; in Venice, it seemed almost precious—delicate and exposed,” Hui says. “The experience reminded me that a work does not need to be grand to hold meaning. Sometimes, its poetry lies in inviting us to look more attentively, and to meet the familiar with tenderness.”

Angel Hui’s installation I Would Like to Open a Window for You (2026) Photo © Hong Kong Museum of Art

Both artists, through their site-specific installations, encourage visitors to mark a pause while heightening their attention to details of light, sound, colour and texture. This invitation to contemplation is echoed in the exhibition’s title, Fermata, which is a type of musical symbol instructing a performer to hold a note or a pause for an extra moment, and the term for the places where Venetian vaporettos stop to let off and pick up passengers. For Hui, this title and its dual meanings resonate across the exhibition’s disparate locales.

“The difference in pace is pronounced: Hong Kong often presses forward, while Venice seems to make room for pause,” she says. “This is why Fermata—a moment of stopping, of stillness—felt so resonant. In both cities, the ordinary endures, and in that endurance, everyday objects acquire a quiet radiance.”

The exhibition’s title and installations also complement the theme of this year’s Venice Biennale, In Minor Keys, set by the late curator Koyo Kouoh.

Angel Hui in Venice Photo © Hong Kong Museum of Art

“I come to see the works as experiences to return to and live alongside,” Ng says. “For me, that is one meaning of In Minor Keys: making time for the ordinary and immediate—the air, light and weather around us—and becoming more attentive to our presence within them.”

The artists’ ability to turn familiar objects and moments into tableaux where time pauses and senses are heightened is key to the exhibition’s power. It allows their installations to resonate across localities, from the Venetian Lagoon to Hong Kong’s cityscape.

“The artworks merge into the Venetian neighbourhood, from laundry hanging across nearby alleys and above our courtyard exhibition space to the view of the neighbourhood outside Kingsley’s Laundry Nocturne gallery, to wrought-iron windows that echo Angel’s work,” Dr Mok says. “All these details are blurring the boundary between the exhibition and its surroundings. They also show how small moments of daily life can quietly synchronise across different cities and audiences.”

#9108. Nat Geo Explorer Bertie Gregory Deeply Cares About the Wolves He Has Followed for Seven Years

Nat Geo Explorer Bertie Gregory Deeply Cares About the Wolves He Has Followed for Seven Years

In National Geographic’s newest television program, Wolves Up Close With Bertie Gregory, the eponymous British wildlife filmmaker, acclaimed photographer, and ardent environmentalist heads to Hudson Bay, Canada, to film wolves in their harsh Arctic habitat. Gregory chatted with PetaPixel about filming the new documentary.

While the focus of the new documentary is clearly on wolves, a specific wolf pack in particular that Gregory has followed for seven years, Wolves Up Close is a smorgasbord of Arctic wildlife in general. There are polar bears, red foxes, and moose, each beautifully filmed.

“One of the best parts about filming nature, and also the most annoying part, is that it doesn’t read the script,” Gregory laughs. “I always joke with the production team that we often go out with this make-believe script that we’ve written and then nature on day one is like, ‘Nope.’ And that’s the frustrating part, but on the positive part of it, it means that you never know what’s gonna happen.”

In one sequence, a pair of polar bears gets awfully close to Gregory and the rest of his small crew, which is admittedly a bit nerve-wracking for viewers. Gregory brushes off the dangers of wildlife filmmaking, thanks in large part to the local guides he worked with, including Mike Reimer and Albert “Butch” Saunders.

Gregory says he never felt nervous at all about the wolves, which likewise would saunter up to the crew to check things out, but what about the polar bears and moose?

“They’re potentially dangerous animals,” Gregory admits. “But humans are really dangerous animals. You know, statistically much more dangerous than a polar bear or a moose. Just like with humans, you’ve got to read body language to stay safe. But I work with great people, like Butch and Mike, our local guides, and they were really key to keeping everyone safe.”

Besides, Gregory might have been too busy feeling cold to feel fear.

“Any time during the episode, I was cold. I was feeling cold.”

The veteran filmmaker didn’t just experience physical closeness to some of his subjects — again, he’s a trained professional — but also emotional closeness, especially to the wolves. Bertie has followed this same pack of wolves for seven years, and over that time, he argues it’s impossible not to feel a bond.

In contrast to old-school wildlife documentary practices, which effectively demand that filmmakers remain entirely detached from the nature they experience and shoot, Gregory doesn’t fight the natural urge to feel something about his subjects.

“I mean, we’re trained not to,” he admits. “We’re told not to get attached because you can’t get involved, but I think that’s BS. I think there’s no way you can follow a pack of animals, an animal family, for seven years and not care about them.

I think if you don’t care about them, you’re pretty weird.

“I think if you don’t care about them, you’re pretty weird.”

Gregory says he isn’t actively trying to forge any bond, something he is fully aware would be a one-way street since the wolves “don’t care about us,” but he says, “I care about them.”

“There are two strategies when filming animals. You can either hide from the animals and they don’t know you’re there, or in the case of these wolves, you can have them know you’re there and be accepting of your presence. That’s an amazing relationship to have. They see us as kind of a part of the landscape.”

Viewers can truly feel through the screen how much Gregory cares about and loves these wolves. It shapes the way he films them, which I think is undeniably a good thing.

“You know when someone makes you like a bowl or a pot, or when you’ve got kids, they draw you a picture? There’s something intangible about the quality of the work and how much you like it when you know it’s been made with love,” Gregory explains.

There’s something intangible about the quality of the work and how much you like it when you know it’s been made with love.

He believes, rightly, that there’s something special too about wildlife documentaries that have been crafted with “real immense care and admiration for the animal.”

“I don’t think you need to try too hard to illustrate that. It just comes through naturally.”

For Gregory, wolves are easy to care about. He can’t help but wonder why such beautiful, intelligent creatures that are so much like the pet dogs many people love like they’re members of the family are treated so poorly and feared excessively.

As an example, the federal government is weighing a move right now to delist gray wolves and Mexican wolves from the Endangered Species Act, potentially removing the very protections that helped wolves rebound in the United States.

“That’s just so dumb on so many levels,” Gregory says. “So if you care about wolves, make your voice heard. Tell politicians, tell people with influence, tell them to shout about this stuff because it’s important. Not only are wolves important for wild places, but they’re representative of who we are as a species.

So if you care about wolves, make your voice heard.

“It’s so weird that we value their closest living relative, the domestic dog, in such high regard that we let them come into our houses and sleep in our beds, but yet we’re so horrible to the wild version of them,” Gregory says somberly.

On a much more positive note, Gregory and his crew got to experience something extremely special out in the field, filming a pack of wolves chasing down a moose from their drone. It’s moments like these that inspire wildlife filmmakers like Bertie Gregory.

National Geographic graciously shared a clip from the incredible sequence with PetaPixel.

“I realized I was seeing something very special and something that no human in that area had ever seen before,” Gregory says. “Mike says on camera, he’s been watching wolves for 30 years and never seen that.

“We combined amazing traditional knowledge with new technology. That’s the dream combo. Old school with new school, working together.

“I knew we were seeing something special.”

To make it even more special, it was a wolf Gregory has watched grow into a leader over the years, named Kona by “Butch” Saunders, that tried to take down the moose, latching onto one of its rear legs.

“I was like, ‘No one’s ever gonna believe this.’ It’s too good of a story,” Gregory says. “Then it dawned on me that I didn’t think Kona was going to survive it. The toll on his body. It just goes to show how tough these animals are.”

Kona survived the encounter, but there’s a poignant moment during the show when Gregory looks at the aging wolf and reflects on his age. Life in the Arctic is hard, and before you know it, the long, challenging winters have flown by.

Kona may not have many winters left, certainly not as the leader of the pack. But for a beautiful moment, Kona looked every bit the apex predator.

Wolves Up Close With Bertie Gregory premieres tomorrow, November 6, on National Geographic and will stream the following day on Hulu and Disney+.

#9107. It’s Interesting That Neither Sony Nor Tamron Have Said Anything Regarding Acquisition

It’s Interesting That Neither Sony Nor Tamron Have Said Anything Regarding Acquisition

In late July, news broke that Sony was trying to acquire Tamron, a fact Tamron itself confirmed shortly after. However, since then, it’s been crickets.

Both Sony and Tamron released their financial results as scheduled today, a date I circled on my calendar in hopes that one or both companies might comment again on Sony’s attempted takeover of Tamron. However, neither company said anything about it at all. Sometimes the lack of news is itself news.

Back in July, Tamron said it had established a “special committee” to explore “various options for enhancing corporate value,” while acknowledging that reports were “true” that Tamron had received a “non-binding proposal from Sony Corporation to make [Tamron] a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Sony Group.”

Since that statement on July 30, Tamron has said nothing else.

Sony has likewise been silent since July.

On the same day Tamron acknowledged Sony’s proposal, Sony itself told Reuters that it believed its offer to Tamron would help develop Sony’s imaging business and also enhance Tamron’s corporate value.

Sony was Tamron’s largest outside shareholder, with a 15.35% stake, until Singaporean investment firm Effissimo Capital aggressively increased its stake earlier this year to nearly 17.4%, pushing Sony to second place.

On the topic of Tamron’s corporate value, as Nikkei reported in September, Sony’s acquisition attempt has only helped Tamron so far.

“Investors seem to be pricing in a premium for Tamron shares following Sony’s proposal, counting on it going through,” Nikkei wrote.

That seems to be the smart bet. The fact that neither Tamron nor Sony has said anything about Sony’s acquisition offer since the two companies simultaneously acknowledged its existence, including in either of the two financial reports since, strongly signals that negotiations remain ongoing. If Sony hasn’t pulled out and Tamron hasn’t declined the offer outright by now, it sure seems like wheels are very much in motion.

Sony’s non-binding proposal was reportedly 200 billion yen, or nearly $1.3 billion. Again, Sony already owns over 15% of Tamron, so the 200 billion yen would be for the remaining 85%.

Tamron’s market cap on June 30 was about 224 billion yen. It’s now about 233.7 billion yen. The company’s share price skyrocketed as soon as reports about Sony’s proposal were published, and it hasn’t dropped back down to pre-proposal levels.

For reference, Tamron’s operating profit is up year over year compared to Q3 FY2026, and Sony likewise grew profits in both imaging and image sensor segments compared to the same quarter last year.

#9106. Stare Straight Into Your Subject’s Soul With This Strange New Camera

Stare Straight Into Your Subject’s Soul With This Strange New Camera

South Korean consumer electronics startup Lutra Inc. has launched a camera brand, Humans of Authenticity (HOA). HOA’s first camera, the HOA A1, looks weird as hell.

Like the widely-panned Godox C100, the HOA A1 says “no, thank you” to a viewfinder and, for that matter, a screen. The HOA A1’s rectangular frame itself is the viewfinder. If that sounds strange, it’s probably because it is.

"Frame is designed to be a viewfinder," HOA says. "Look through it with both eyes open, and feel the air. You can capture the scene just as you see."

As the company's few in-situ product photos show, the user winds up looking rather unusual, staring just over the top of the built-in lens at their subject.

Speaking of the built-in lens, HOA says it is a 26mm equivalent f/1.75 prime lens. It is paired with a 16-megapixel Sony IMX image sensor. The output images, presumably JPEG only since RAW isn't mentioned, are 4656 x 3104, which is about 14.5 megapixels.

Gratefully, HOA shares the sensor's size, which is a rather unusual move in the broader "odd digital camera" segment. It is a Type 1/2.53 image sensor, which delivers around a six-times crop factor. So while an f/1.75 aperture sounds fast, users should not expect a shallow depth of field by any stretch of the imagination.

That said, it's impossible to say anything about the HOA A1's image quality right now because HOA isn't sharing any sample photos, citing the need to "fine-tune the camera's color and tone in collaboration with photographers."

Time is running out, given that the company says the camera launches on December 21, "just in time for Christmas." Whether it's a fantastic present or a camera-shaped (?) piece of coal remains to be seen.

The camera's built-in battery offers up to eight hours of standby or 90 minutes of continuous shooting, per HOA.

Now is a good time to mention that Lutra Inc. also has extensive experience with blockchain and digital asset authentication. A core tenet of HOA's debut camera is celebrating authenticity. Subjects can see the photographer's face while they shoot; after all, this is about building connection to reality.

The camera authenticates every photo with "ShootProof," which creates a certificate that binds "image and data" at the time of capture. The certificate is recorded on a public blockchain. It's also anonymous, unlike some similar authentication technologies.

"ShootProof proves a photo is real," says HOA.

"Photography is endangered. Generated images are everywhere, making it hard to trust what you see," the company says. Fair point.

"That’s where ShootProof matters. It proves images are captured, not generated -- protecting photography’s credibility."

Photographers can also sign their photos through a "signature mode." Basically, photographers create a signature in an accompanying app; whether it's a legitimate one or a goofy little illustration is up to them, and the camera then slaps that signature onto the corner of every shot.

There's no way to know what this will look like yet, but it's an interesting idea. The smartphone integration goes far beyond this mode. The user's phone is the only way to view photos, although exactly how it works hasn't been detailed yet. Photographers will tap their phone on the back of the camera, and then some wireless transfer will occur. Photos can be captured without any connectivity, but Wi-Fi is required for viewing. HOA adds that the network is required to "safely authenticate" photos.

The HOA A1 First Edition launches on December 21. The first batch, comprising just 100 units, will be engraved with numbers from 001-100. Customers can reserve a specific number on a first-come, first-served basis. The HOA A1 is 360,000 KRW, or $289 USD. Preorders haven't opened yet, and interested buyers are advised to follow the company on Instagram to learn more.

#9105. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.

#9104. Glyph Continues Its Expansion into Creator Support with New Card Readers

Glyph Continues Its Expansion into Creator Support with New Card Readers

Earlier this year, Glyph pushed hard into the creator space with the launch of new SSDs and a line of CFexpress memory cards. It is continuing that trend with the announcement of memory card readers.

The series includes two new additions: the Glyph Capture+ CFexpress Type A USB4 Memory Card Reader and the Glyph Capture+ Dual SD Memory Card Reader. The company says these are designed to meet “the rigorous demands of modern film, photography, and audio workflows” and combine its SteadyIO technology (which is Glyph’s term for fan-less thermal sinking) with support for SD and CFexpress Type A cards, specifically targeting Sony photographers and filmmakers.

While Glyph currently doesn’t make any SD cards or CFexpress Type A cards, it recognizes that Sony photographers represent a huge part of the market. As such, the Glyph Capture+ CFexpress Type A USB4 Memory Card Reader promises what it characterizes as next-generation offload efficiency thanks to USB4 Type-C (40Gbps) connectivity. It can achieve transfer speeds of up to 5,000 MB/s, which Glyph says allows for data ingest up to 3x faster than traditional readers.

The Glyph Capture+ Dual SD Memory Card Reader features two SD card slots and can function as a dual-ingest device. But that versatility does come at a slight speed cost: this reader uses USB 3.2 Gen 2 (10Gbps) connectivity with transfer speeds up to 1,000 MB/s. That is likely fast enough for most photographers using SD cards in their workflows, since the cards can’t operate at speeds any higher than that anyway.

The readers are constructed of a solid aluminum shell with an increased thermal ceiling and a protective soft composite bumper. Compact and bus-powered, Glyph says both models fit seamlessly into desktop and field setups across Mac and Windows environments.

Both the Glyph Capture+ CFexpress Type A USB4 Memory Card Reader and the Glyph Capture+ Dual SD Memory Card Reader will begin shipping in November, but availability may slip into December depending on demand. Both readers will be available directly from Glyph and authorized resellers. The Dual SD reader retails for $120, while the Type A reader will cost $150—the same price as Glyph’s existing Type B reader.

#9103. Charles Dickens’s writing chalet and Hastings Castle added to list of English heritage sites at risk

Left: Charles Dickens' Writing Chalet, Rochester, Kent. Right: Hastings Castle

Dickens’ chalet: Photo: Nick Johnson - The Imageworks. Hastings Castle: © Historic England Archive

The cabin where Charles Dickens spent the last day of his life, the home in Stratford-upon-Avon of William Shakespeare’s daughter Susanna and the castle built by William the Conqueror high on the cliffs above the town of Hastings are among 197 buildings and sites added to Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register today (5 November).

The list identifies sites such as buildings, parks, battlefields and shipwrecks that are threatened by decay, neglect or inappropriate development. There are now 4,991 entries on the register, all of which are labelled as of national importance. This encompasses 197 sites that were added this year.

The miniature Swiss chalet which became the writing retreat of Charles Dickens was a Christmas gift to the author in 1864, arrived flat packed in 94 pieces, and was put together by a theatre carpenter after Dickens and his house guests failed. Dickens placed it at the furthest end of the garden, reached by a tunnel he built under the road at his last home, Gad’s Hill, near Rochester in Kent. He spent much of 9 June 1870 working in the chalet on The Mystery of Edwin Drood, before returning to the house where he died that night, aged just 58.The house, now a school, and tunnel survive, but the chalet was moved in the 1960s to the garden of Eastgate House in Rochester, where it is now too fragile for public access.

Hall’s Croft, an imposing timber-framed building dating from 1613, was the home of Susanna Shakespeare and her husband John Hall. After many uses, and residents including the playwright George Bernard Shaw and the bestselling Victorian romantic novelist Marie Corelli, it was acquired by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and opened to the public in 1951. It had already been closed for several years for extensive conservation work when, in October 2025, a car reversed into the facade and caused further serious damage. The playwright Ken Ludwig has donated £1m to the work but major fundraising will still be needed.

Hall’s Croft, Old Town, Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire

Hastings Castle was one of the first three such sites built by William the Conqueror after his victory in the famous battle—and is depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry. The site, with a sweeping view across a stretch of the coast, has a long history, with remains of an Iron Age fort having been discovered there. The castle’s commanding site has made it very vulnerable to storms and coastal erosion and there have already been urgent works to stabilise its ruins. Future plans for the site include the creation of a new visitor centre and cafe.

Along with the sites that have been added this year there is good news: 85 sites for which solutions have been found, and which have now been removed from the register. They include the storm-lashed Newlyn Harbour in Cornwall and a little hut in the Gloucestershire garden of Edward Jenner, in which, in 1796, he performed the first-ever vaccinations.

A pair of elegant Georgian houses in east London, built around 1715 and Grade II* listed, had an unusual saviour: Tottenham Hotspur Football Club, which has converted them—with help from the Lottery Heritage Fund—into artists studios, gallery spaces, and a cafe. The space is run by Sarabande Foundation, which was founded by the late fashion designer Lee Alexander McQueen.

The Georgian terraced house saved from dereliction by Tottenham Hotspur FC. The house is now home to artists’ studios, galleries and café run by Sarabande Foundation, which was established by Lee Alexander McQueen

Rescue grants available include the Heritage at Risk Capital Fund and the Places of Worship Renewal Fund, both funded by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and administered by Historic England, and the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service.

The UK’s heritage minister Baroness Twycross said in a statement that the register has a crucial role in identifying historic places in need of support. “Every part of the UK is bursting with history, so it is vital we protect the heritage sites at the heart of communities which help tell the stories of our nation.”

Claudia Kenyatta and Emma Squire, the joint chief executives of Historic England, said the most effective way of protecting the sites was to bring them back into use.“The sites saved and removed from the Register this year show what can be achieved when partners and communities work together to deliver positive lasting change.”
