Last year, it seemed that some of the biggest brands had declared the death of the opulent, magical holiday advert. AI slop would do, they decided.

Coca-Cola's AI Christmas ad was one of the most controversial, while McDonald's pulled its festive effort due to the backlash. This year, it seems we're seeing a strong counter movement, with big brands making a point of their commitment to handcrafted art.

First, there was the glorious Prada Christmas ad, directed by former Disney animator John Pomeroy. Now Levi's has pulled out the stops for a very different animated gem, showing that it's not just luxury brands that see the value of human craftsmanship in advertising.

Levi's Let’s Get Fuzzy stop-motion holiday campaign was produced by the London-based production studio Blinkink . The animation begins as a play on horror movies, making it a fun segue from Halloween. A monster interrupts a group of friends' cosy festive retreat in a snow-covered cabin. But Fuzzyeti's discovery of festive jumpers makes him quickly succumb to the holiday spirit.

The medium of painstaking stop-motion animation was chosen to highlight Levi's heritage of craftsmanship. As shown in the making of video below, a six-person team spent more than 2,000 hours over six and a half weeks building and painting the sets, including three cabins at different scales, along with 400 miniature trees, and four faces for each character.

The clothes are miniature replicas of real Levi's products – a stylist was on hand to ensure accuracy. They were moved for every frame of the animation to make them feel life like, but requiring four hours of work of every second of animation.

A reference edit was made with actors and the directors themselves acting out the roles (including a specialist monster actor for Fuzzyyeti). This was then used as the guide for the animators.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Levi's has form in animation, from the psychedelic 2D short The Stranger in 1971 to Clayman with Shaggy’s Boombastic in claymation in 1995. Today, the decision to use such a laborious handcrafted process makes a bigger statement, creating added distinction and value amid so much AI-generated content.

Your local food truck might not worry about their ugly AI flyers if they can do the job for cheap. But for big brands, proof of work like the behind-the-scenes video above has become as important as the finished advert. Avoiding the embarrassment of an 'AI content' label isn't enough, they're taking steps to proactively signal that an advert was human made.

Hermès and Ralph Lauren are just two fashion brands that have been doing this by mentioning the people behind their ads in the captions on social media. Naming the creative team behind a campaign has become a signal of craftsmanship, and the implication is clear: human-made art is seen as a sign of a premium brand.

A post shared by Ralph Lauren (@ralphlauren)

Apple's also been on the trend with its embroidered logo and the stop-motion ad for Apple Games, which was also made by Blinklink. The resurgence of interest in stop motion is likely to continue to grow with Laika's Wildwood doing well at the box office.

#9077. Art Collaboration Kyoto fair celebrates five years of matchmaking galleries

The fifth edition of Art Collaboration Kyoto includes 52 galleries in the main section and 11 galleries in the Kyoto Meetings section Courtesy Art Collaboration Kyoto

This year marks the fifth edition of Art Collaboration Kyoto (ACK), the fair that pairs Japanese commercial galleries with international peers to collaborate on shared stands. The fair will take place from 7 to 9 November at the Kyoto International Conference Center. The event has become known for its distinctive exhibitor model, which has proved popular with exhibitors and fair attendees alike.

“We thought, ‘If we are going to do this, why not create a fair that galleries and artists themselves would find exciting and genuinely want to be part of?’” Miho Doi, ACK’s director of experiences, tells The Art Newspaper about the fair’s founding.

This year’s edition includes a number of high-profile Western galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Jeffrey Deitch and Carlos Ishikawa, alongside Asian galleries such as Seoul’s Gallery Hyundai.

The collaborative format is intended to give both Japanese and international galleries an opportunity to work together and introduce their artists and programmes to new audiences. Pairing domestic and foreign galleries has been key for the success of the fair, organisers say, especially for dealers without experience in Japan.

“For an overseas gallery, participating independently in an art fair in a country it is entering for the first time is by no means easy,” Doi says. “We have heard from participating galleries that, for a variety of reasons, taking part in a Japanese fair entirely on their own would not have been realistic.”

The fair’s main section will bring together 52 galleries. Taro Nasu from Tokyo will join forces with Hauser & Wirth for a presentation focused on text in contemporary art, including works by Louise Bourgeois, Jenny Holzer, David Horvitz and Glenn Ligon, among others. Nanzuka from Tokyo will work alongside Jeffrey Deitch, while Tokyo Gallery + BTAP will team up with Gallery Hyundai for a presentation pairing post-war Japanese and Korean experimental practices, including the Korean artist Seung-taek Lee in dialogue with the Japanese artist Kishio Suga.

“Some participating galleries have even described ACK as a ‘fair built on friendship’ rather than a place for competition,” Doi says.

Another section of the fair is dedicated to presentations from 11 individual galleries with strong connections to Kyoto. Mendes Wood DM, for instance, will present works by Tomie Ohtake—who was born in Kyoto and later relocated to São Paulo, which is home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan—among other artists. Hong Kong’s Kiang Malingue will show works by Yang Chi-Chuan and Faye Wei Wei, whose sculptures and paintings respond to Kyoto’s landscapes and urban environment.

A joint stand with Nonaka-Hill and Hoffman Donahue galleries Courtesy Art Collaboration Kyoto

The fair also coincides with a programme of special exhibitions and projects across Kyoto. This year, the Scottish painter Andrew Cranston will present an installation at Ryosokuin Temple, a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto’s historic Gion district. The exhibition is organised by Modern Art and Ingleby. Elsewhere, Carlos Ishikawa will stage a presentation of work by Evelyn Taocheng Wang and Issy Wood at Korin-in Temple.

This edition of ACK takes place under a new leadership committee structure, introduced earlier this year. Rather than being led by a single fair director, ACK is now guided by a seven-member committee with expertise spanning art consulting, cultural foundations, Kyoto cultural policy, fair production, education, partnerships and collector relations. The former fair director, Yukako Yamashita, now leads the fair’s ambassador programme.

As for ACK’s next five years, Doi says the leadership committee aims to develop the fair into a platform that “connects the art scenes of Japan and the world and generates a virtuous cycle between cultural and commercial value”.

The fifth edition of the fair, where Japanese galleries invited international ones to share stands, welcomed 72 exhibitors

#9076. Solid cork forms walls of pavilion dedicated to silence at Casa No Tempo in Alentejo

Photography by Mercês Tomaz Gomes

Antwerp-based studio Corkinho has unveiled its latest “still room”, a pavilion with walls of solid cork, which is installed in the grounds of a vacation villa designed by Manuel Aires Mateus.

The still room is a space dedicated to silent and introspective activities, such as reading, yoga, tea ceremonies or meditation.

Corkinho installed it in the grounds of Casa No Tempo, a former farmhouse in southern Portugal, which architect Aires Mateus converted into a holiday home in 2014 for hospitality entrepreneur João Rodrigues.

Lead designer Cédric Etienne devised the building’s innovative structure, which is fully demountable, with the help of architect and master carpenter Gonçalo Madeira Marrote of Madeiguincho.

The floor slab is a timber deck, built over a foundation of removable concrete blocks.

Above this, solid blocks of cork are stacked up like giant bricks to form the building’s walls and secured with metal rods that thread through milled channels.

The pavilion is topped by a timber roof, described by Etienne as “like a hat with four screws”, which helps to weigh down the cork blocks.

“I wanted it to be zero waste and carbon-neutral,” the designer told Dezeen.

“If we need to dismantle it, we can place it somewhere else. There is no glue and no screws,” he said.

“It’s like the Japanese way of building teahouses, with total respect of the local materials and no harm to the land.”

As the name suggests, Corkinho is a studio that specialises in objects and spaces built from cork.

The studio first launched the still room concept in 2020, when it moved its office into the former Noorderpershuis power station in Antwerp and transformed one of the rooms into a silent sanctuary.

Etienne defines a still room as any space where you can pause your mind and be still.

“It’s a place where you disconnect from noise and distractions and invite a deeper sense of presence,” he said.

After consulting with various hotel brands keen to adopt the concept, Etienne pitched the idea to Rodrigues and his company, Silent Living.

The company has five properties, all designed by Aires Mateus and all with a focus on slow living.

“I had been to Casa No Tempo many times, so I knew the place like an inner home,” the designer said.

“It felt so aligned in terms of feeling and senses, so I thought it could be a really beautiful challenge to move the concept forward in this place,” he continued.

The room can be used by guests staying at the villa, but it can also accommodate curated programmes.

Etienne has been hosting four-day silent retreats, allowing groups of designers and hospitality professionals to learn more about the still room concept.

The cork blocks, supplied by locally based company Sofalca, were heat-treated to improve their durability. The material gives the building impressive sensorial and thermal qualities, Etienne said.

“All the technical properties of cork – the acoustics, the scent, the softness – all become architectural conditions,” he stated.

“You really feel like you’re coming into a womb. Even when it’s 40 degrees outside, the temperature inside is around 22 or 23.”

Other pavilions recently featured in Dezeen include a wildlife pavilion informed by rippling water and a jigsaw-like pavilion made of mass-timber scrap.

Photography by Mercês Tomaz Gomes

#9075. Met Gala's New Theme Is the Biggest Recession Indicator Yet

Brace yourself for A-listers strutting down the red carpet in everyday garb like jeans, T-shirts, and "humble, even 'disposable' materials."

Two months after British fashion designer John Galliano bowed out of his 2027 Met Gala and Costume Institute exhibition due to backlash over his racist past, organizers have decided to play it safe with the new theme announced today, November 5.

In perhaps the biggest recession indicator yet, extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday will see A-listers and Hollywood's finest strutting down the red carpet in everyday garb like jeans, T-shirts, and "humble, even 'disposable' materials."

When The Met announced the Costume Institute exhibition John Galliano: Horizons in July, intense scrutiny resurfaced around the designer, who was convicted of antisemitic and anti-Asian hate speech directed at a French couple in February 2011, and fined for a torrent of antisemitic slurs against a woman the same year. A separate video of Galliano declaring “I love Hitler” caused Dior to fire the designer from his post as creative director in March 2011. Amid the renewed backlash, Galliano withdrew his exhibition on August 31.

#9073. It’s Time to Talk About Classism in the Art World

In his memoiristic new book, photographer Mark Alice Durant weaves his personal experiences into a larger rebuke of the economic inequality that governs the art world.

For something that determines so much — about the art we make, the art we get to see or not, the art that may never be made at all — the issue of class is rarely discussed in the art world. Breaking the silence, artist and writer Mark Alice Durant speaks up in his memoir-cum-rebuke, Confessions of a Working Class Artist (2026). It reads both like a Künstlerroman and an updated version of the seminal guide for the aspiring artist, Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet (1929), for our dystopian neo-Gilded Age.

For Durant, also the author of the moving photographic memoir Summer of the White Fox, and After (2024) and publisher at Saint Lucy Books, which released both titles, choosing to become an artist was an act of self-exile. He writes that he psychically uprooted himself from the working-class precincts of Boston where he grew up as well as from his extended family, with the exception of his mother, unusually open-minded and supportive of her son. Perhaps she saw herself in his youthful gift of a framed reproduction of Jules Breton’s 1884 painting of a field worker, “The Song of the Lark.” After deciding on this path, Durant writes, “I could never return home on some level.”

What do you mean Mr Monopoly doesn't have a monocle?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most of us have been playing Monopoly since we were kids, so it's one of the most recallable logos out there, right? Of course, I'm talking about Mr Monopoly, also known as Rich Uncle Pennybags, who is kitted out as a very fancy gentleman with a moustache, top hat, cane and monocle. Except he doesn't have a monocle. Seriously.

This is just one of the many logos subject to the Mandela effect, a psychological and social phenomenon that convinces us of visual elements that simply don't exist. A few years ago, we reported that scholars at the University of Chicago studied the effect and found that people share the same false memories of a range of logos and icons. The very best logos are memorable, but some of them have false additions in the minds of many people.

We decided to revisit this study after a chat in the office brought up the design details that actually don't exist in real life – and we want to know, have you been subject to the Mandela effect in these cases? If so, let us know in the comments. And if you have any other logos you've misremembered, can you draw your version and upload them in the comments?

Neuroscientist Wilma Bainbridge and lab manager Deepasri Prasad at the University of Chicago's Brain Bridge Lab found that people have confident and consistent false memories of famous icons. The team trawled internet discussions for logos and characters people commonly misremember, then added their own picks and made small tweaks to see if people could spot the real thing. In total there were 40 images, including the logos for Apple, Bic, Disney, Fruits of the Loom, Ralph Lauren and Volkswagen, plus the Bluetooth symbol, Pikachu, C-3PO, Wally and Curious George.

Participants had to pick the correct version from three options. Apple and Ralph Lauren did well, with around 80 per cent getting them right. Monopoly, Volkswagen and Fruits of the Loom did not: only 20 to 30 per cent chose the real logo. Most people also insisted Pikachu’s tail has a black tip. It doesn’t.

It wasn’t just a multiple-choice problem either. When asked to draw the images from memory, people made the same mistakes unprompted. Bainbridge says it’s a strong effect: people hold a false memory of an image they’ve never actually seen.

Nobody knows yet. The study doesn’t identify a cause. One suggestion is schema theory, where our brains add details that fit the theme. A monocle says ‘wealthy Victorian gent’, so in it goes.

Sign up to the design newsletter from Creative Bloq, brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of graphic design, branding, typography and more.

That doesn’t explain everything, though. A cornucopia isn’t an obvious addition to a plate of fruit, which is the problem with using schema theory to explain the Fruits of the Loom logo. (The scene does exist in art, but that’s a stretch.)

The researchers say the findings could matter for logo design and for choosing images in education and advertising, where accurate memory is the whole point. Bainbridge also linked it to wider questions about the images used in the media.

It’s a useful reminder that ‘memorable’ and ‘remembered correctly’ aren’t the same thing.

The pieces are the smart idea here. Board’s PieceSense tech identifies each piece, where it is, and how it’s moving, so kids who’d fumble a standard controller can pick up a plastic spaceship and fly it straight away. That active interaction gives Board an old-fashioned Nintendo appeal.

#9070. Many London architecture firms not paying London Living Wage

The majority of the London-based studios in The Pay 100‘s fifth annual salary survey are not paying Part I architectural assistants the London Living Wage, as required by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA).

An engineering firm has topped the leaderboard for the average salaries for UK architects, according to a survey conducted by the anonymous group The Pay 100.

Engineering firm tops architect salary leaderboard

Published over the weekend, the survey provides rough figures only based on the mean figures submitted by respondents. This year’s data collected the annual salary of 127 firms in the UK and the mean number of hours of unpaid overtime per week.

Topping the leaderboard with the highest average annual salary for architects with less than five years’ experience is BakerHicks, an engineering and design firm, which paid £72,000, according to the survey.

Second on the list is London studio Hawkins\Brown at £63,700, and joint third at £56,300 are London practices Samuel Chisholm Studio and Thomas Alexander Design.

The survey also presented figures for Part I and Part II architectural assistants. Transport for London had the highest wage for Part II roles at £44,000, followed by Foster + Partners at £42,000.

Majority of London firms not paying London Living Wage

The results for Part I roles included salaries from 30 studios, 21 of which were based in Greater London.

Only the top four studios on the leaderboard – Haworth Tompkins, Allford Hall Monaghan Morris, Studio McW and Studio PDP – paid more than the London Living Wage of £32,136, which RIBA declared a requirement for relevant offices.

Twelve of the 30 studios were paying Part I roles less than the £29,328 UK Living Wage.

Low wages “a threat to the future of the profession”

Alongside its survey data, The Pay 100 wrote an open letter to RIBA, asking it to take action on the financial wellbeing of those working in the architecture industry and to ensure the long-term future of the profession.

“Our aim has always been to create tangible financial incentives for employers to improve pay, empower employees to make informed career decisions, and encourage a healthier, more sustainable profession,” said The Pay 100 in the letter.

“We recognise that architecture practices operate within a highly competitive market, often under significant financial pressure themselves,” it continued. “Nevertheless, the commercial challenges facing practices should not prevent the profession from addressing the deteriorating conditions experienced by many employees.”

“Poor financial conditions for staff are not merely an employment issue; they are a threat to the long-term health, resilience and future of the profession.”

It went on to set out two courses of action it called for RIBA to take: establishing “meaningful minimum salaries” for RIBA chartered practices, and taking full ownership of The Pay 100 and its annual salary survey.

The Pay 100 said a framework of minimum salary levels should be established across different architecture roles, increasing year-on-year in line with inflation.

“A profession cannot sustainably advocate for the value of its services while leaving the financial conditions of its workforce to market pressures alone,” it said. “The RIBA should take a leading role in addressing this imbalance.”

After five years of aiming to improve pay transparency with its annual surveys, The Pay 100 wants RIBA to take ownership of the survey and commit resources to it, developing it into an industry-wide initiative.

“We believe that improving pay transparency across UK architecture should be a core responsibility of the profession’s leading membership body,” said The Pay 100.

“Under the RIBA’s stewardship, the survey could benefit from significantly greater reach, sustained institutional support and broader participation across the profession,” it continued.

“This would provide a foundation for more comprehensive salary data, stronger engagement between employers and employees, and meaningful progress towards better financial conditions throughout the industry.”

The Pay 100 ended its letter by asking for a public response from RIBA by 1 December

#9069. Comment | John Berger at 100: why the writer and artist's legacy is as vital as ever

Tom Overton's biography John Berger: From Life was published in August this year

John Berger was born on 5 November 1926, making this year his centenary. Next year will be the tenth anniversary of his death. It seems a good time to look back and take stock of one of the 20th century’s most persuasive and challenging voices in art and literature, and one of only two writers on art who also wrote a Booker Prize-winning novel (the other was Anita Brookner).

The story of Berger’s 1972 Booker Prize speech, after winning for his novel G., is told by Tom Overton in his thoroughly engaging biography, John Berger: From Life, published in August this year. To a stunned and affronted audience at the prize ceremony, Berger announced he was donating half the considerable prize money to a British chapter of the Black Panthers, as a protest against the labour exploitation in British Guiana that had made the Booker McConnell fortune. It is hard to imagine an acceptance speech nowadays without acknowledgment of the reputation-laundering that is still widespread in cultural sponsorship. Berger’s bravery in making such a stand, which can hardly have been easy, is one aspect of his legacy worth remembering.

This legacy—why Berger matters—is the subject of the smattering of centenary events but is also brought into focus by their dearth. The only anniversary exhibition in Britain devoted to Berger is a small display of his drawings at Mandell’s Gallery in Norwich (until 21 November), co-curated by the artists John Christie and Martin Battye. Berger’s drawings are those of a writer intent on seeing the world around him, gathering images and experiences, but also of an artist who knows that the best way to look is to draw.

Berger’s popular legacy lies with his 1972 book Ways of Seeing, which remains, quite remarkably, a bestseller—“one of the most stimulating and influential books on art in any language”, says its publisher, Penguin. Anyone rereading the book now might pause at such a description. Berger was hardly the first to show how images are constructed by viewers, and reflect their prejudices, but he was the first to publish a book that communicated this idea so effectively, combining relentless polemic with brilliant design (thanks to Richard Hollis). It also helped that the book was based on a successful television series and contained numerous pin-up images to back up the argument that Old Master painting, through patterns of privilege and possession, relates directly to contemporary advertising.

Yet the arguments feel dated and even slack, quite unlike Berger’s later writing on art. His attacks on Seymour Slive’s interpretation of Frans Hals, and on Kenneth Clark’s book The Nude, are grounded in a personal dislike of art historians. What Gen Z art students will make of his attack on the “disingenuousness that bedevils the subject of art history”, picking apart Lawrence Gowing’s nitty argument that the figures in Gainsborough’s Mr and Mrs Andrews (around 1750) are not just enjoying nature but being philosophical about it, is anybody’s guess.

And yet the questions Berger asks about how we value works of art, and how they exist as part of our lives and the world in which we live, are still utterly relevant. They are part of what Overton describes as the idea central to all his writing: how we live with the dead, how the past surrounds us and keeps us company. Berger spent his life tilting against a world “ordered with the logic of profit, always looking forward, never back”, Overton writes, a world therefore bent on neglecting the past and forgetting the dead.

It is an idea explored in Berger’s short story The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol, from the novel Pig Earth, about peasant life in France at the turn of the 20th century. And it appears in the leaps of imagination and connections he draws between art from different periods in the writings collected in Portraits: John Berger on Artists: on Fayum portraits seen from a century of exile and emigration, or his description of drawing Antonello da Messina’s astonishing 1475 Christ Crucified in the National Gallery, while recalling hearing pianist Myra Hess playing in the same gallery in 1942 (before being thrown out for swearing at a security guard), or his account of Jean-François Millet, “a moralist in the only way a great artist can be, by the power of his identification with his subjects”, in his case the experience of peasants working the land.

Berger’s legacy is his remarkable ability to link art with the most important questions of our time, and so to redeem it from the clutches of the market and specialists alike.

• John-Paul Stonard is an author and art historian

#9066. Stolen Picasso Prints Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Riviera Apartment

Six stolen prints by Pablo Picasso have been safely recovered from an apartment in the French Riviera, where, according to investigators, the works were stowed beneath a pile of clothes and toolboxes, not too far from the restaurant from which they were pilfered.

The theft happened almost exactly one month before French investigators found the prints, which regularly hang in the restaurant L’Amandier, located in Mougins, the village where Picasso famously resided at the time of his death in 1973. Related Articles A Seagram Heir, a Bankrupt Hedge Funder, and More: Consignors for the November Marquee Sales Revealed Police Recover Three Religious Artworks Stolen From Spanish Churches

At around 2 a.m. on October 1, two men, both wearing gloves and masks, entered the restaurant through a door and stole the prints in under a minute. In the morning, the restaurant’s owner, Matthieu Autant, discovered the works were missing and proceeded alert local authorities, which assigned the task of retrieving the stolen art to officers in nearby Cannes.

La Libre, a Belgian outlet, reported that the prints were worth the equivalent of a little more than $112,000—not much, as far as Picassos go. But, speaking to the French publication Le Monde, lieutenant colonel Guillaume Plaidy said that the works “were not easy works to sell,” all the more so because lacked the know-how required to find a buyer for these works. Instead, these men were “known more for drug and weapons offenses,” Plaidy said.

Still, Plaidy added, “We had to act quickly: Works like these carry a high risk of being resold and never returning to the art market.”

On November 3, 40 gendarmes searched two apartments and found the works in the process. Seven men, all aged between 18 and 30, were subsequently arrested. Those men include three burglars and four accomplices, per Le Monde.

Though the theft of the prints may be relatively minor, it gained notice because it comes at a moment of heightened attention to art theft in Europe. Following the storied Louvre heist of 2025, works have been stolen from institutions ranging from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, France, to the Magnani Rocca Foundation, near Parma, Italy.

Within France, the quick recovery of the Picasso prints seemed to inspire hope. Leisa Paoli, head of the Female Artists Museum of Mougins, said, “We are delighted to be able to recover them; I thought they might have already left the country.”

Autant, the owner of L’Amandier, seemed both relieved and a little exasperated. He told the channel France 2, “We may have to rethink the security arrangements.”

#9064. One museum visit a month could improve health, new report finds

The author Daisy Fancourt and Jenny Waldman, the Art Fund's director, view the ‘Recommended Dose of Art: A Prescription for Health and Wellbeing’ report at London’s Wallace Collection

David Parry/Assignments/Press Association

Visiting a museum or art gallery for just one hour a month could significantly improve people's physical and mental health, according to a new report which calls for cultural engagement to become as routine as exercise and healthy eating.

The research, commissioned by the charity Art Fund in partnership with University College London professor Daisy Fancourt, recommends that people spend at least 60 minutes with art in museums and galleries every month.

However, the survey of 2,000 UK adults found that 89% fail to meet this proposed target, equivalent to an estimated 49.5 million people.

The report, “The Recommended Dose of Art: A Prescription for Health and Wellbeing”, draws together scientific evidence suggesting that regular cultural engagement can reduce stress, improve cognitive health and potentially extend life expectancy.

Previous studies have shown that regular museum and gallery visits could nearly halve the risk of developing depression over the following decade. Other studies have linked cultural participation with reduced dementia risk and lower levels of loneliness.

Viewing original artworks in galleries was also associated with a 22% greater reduction in the stress hormone cortisol compared with viewing reproductions.

Fancourt, whose book Art Cure on the scientific benefits of art came out earlier this year, says regular engagement with art should be considered a health-promoting behaviour alongside exercise, a balanced diet and spending time outdoors.

“Guidelines like eating our 5-a-day of fruit and vegetables and getting our 10,000 steps have proven effective in helping us to prioritise other health-promoting behaviours in our busy lives,” she says in a statement. “Adding regular arts engagement to this list could be a simple and joyful way of investing further in our health and wellbeing.”

But the findings also raise questions about whether Britain's struggling museums have the resources to encourage more frequent visits. Jenny Waldman, the director of Art Fund, tells The Art Newspaper that the research strengthens the case for sustained public investment in museums, including protecting free admission at national institutions and supporting local and regional collections.

“We want to see sustained, long-term public investment across the museum sector, so that all museums have the resources to care for their collections and welcome the widest possible audiences,” she says.

Waldman acknowledged that removing admission charges alone would not overcome barriers to visiting museums, including accessibility and the resources available to institutions.

She says Art Fund's research among museum directors found that 36% of museums had reduced their opening hours because of insufficient funding and staffing.

“If we want museums to play a greater role in supporting public health, we must invest in the sector and give them the means to do so,” she adds.

Waldman also points to international developments, including Greece's introduction of arts prescribing into its national healthcare system and growing recognition of cultural organisations as public health assets. She also notes efforts closer to home: “Scotland's Chief Medical Officer, Sir Gregor Smith, recently published a report recognising arts organisations as important public health assets and calling for arts and culture to be embedded more widely in Scotland's approach to public health.”

The approximately $9m project included modernising 20,000 sq. ft of galleries and bringing key objects out of storage for public display for the first time

The museum has been praised for the ambitious way it has shared its collections and for its social outreach

#9063. Brick bathhouse by Kengo Kuma nears completion in Copenhagen

Pyramidal towers frame pools at the Kai Water Culture House by Japanese studio Kengo Kuma & Associates, which is nearing completion in Copenhagen.

Set to open on the city’s harbour in December, the 5,800-square-metre aquatic centre will contain ten indoor and outdoor pools, alongside wellness facilities and cultural spaces.

Kengo Kuma & Associates was commissioned alongside Danish firms Cornelius Vöge, Søren Jensen and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects to realise the new cultural and recreational facility on the city’s artificial island of Christiansholm – known locally as Papirøen, or Paper Island.

Photos revealed ahead of the opening show the facility’s five staggered buildings perched atop a glazed base and fronted by a wooden pier that provides direct access to the sea.

“The Water Culture House is a significant new landmark on Copenhagen’s waterfront,” Kengo Kuma & Associates lead architect Yuki Ikeguchi said. “It is part of the story of the city and the harbour’s transformation from an industrial to a cultural harbour.”

“As the cultural cornerstone of Papirøen, the house is a gathering place with water and community as its focal point, embraced by a public harbour bath,” Ikeguchi added.

Constructed from 300,000 handmade bricks, the tapered volumes are punctuated by triangular and square openings that filter dappled light into the indoor pools.

“The bricks are arranged in a staggered, stepped pattern, giving the building its distinctive texture and sculptural character,” Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects said.

“A total of 403 windows of varying sizes act as viewing apertures, framing the surroundings and creating captivating experiences of natural light as it shifts throughout the day,” it added.

The tallest of the five volumes, dubbed the Culture Tower, houses the centre’s cultural programmes, which include a third-floor events space. Meanwhile, the other four towers each house lofty indoor pools.

Nestled between the five brick volumes on the first floor is an outdoor pool, framed by the building’s sloped facades, and an open-air Onsen – a Japanese-style hot spring – that overlooks the harbour.

The Kai Water Culture House is set to open to the public on 5 December, with its wooden pier slated for completion early next year.

The facility sits among a wider redevelopment of Copenhagen’s Paper Island led by Danish studio COBE. Recent projects on the island include a 20,000-square-metre apartment complex informed by the area’s 300-year-old warehouses.

#9062. Rana Hadid on Taking the Zaha Hadid Foundation Into the Future

Last October 31 marked what would have been Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid’s 76th birthday, as well as the 10-year anniversary of her death. Rana Hadid, Hadid’s niece and chair of the trustees of the Zaha Hadid Foundation, said that the time is right for a proper celebration of her aunt’s legacy.

Last week, the Zaha Hadid Foundation reopened its doors at 10 Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell, the architect’s former headquarters. Meanwhile at the Architectural Association’s campus on Bedford Square, the foundation, together with the architecture school and the Serpentine, held a two-day symposium in Hadid’s honor. Titled “89 Degrees of Zaha Hadid,” the event celebrated her legacy, including talks on her beginnings in Baghdad and Beirut, her student years at the Architectural Association, and generally grand nature of projects and personality. (One talk is titled “Would they call me a diva if I were a guy?: Being Zaha.”) Related Articles The Zaha Hadid Foundation Is Reopening the Late Architect's Former HQ as a Public Arts Space Pritzker Prize Defends Jury Independence After Tom Pritzker's Epstein Ties Surface

Rana, who was present at the symposium, told ARTnews that she raised her hand during some talks to correct misconceptions. “I get really upset when I hear things that are not true. We all have our own perceptions of how things happen, and after someone dies, it becomes very easy to change it,” said Rana. She took over as chairman and trustee of the Zaha Hadid Foundation in 2025 from Brian Clarke, artist and Hadid’s close collaborator, who died in July last year. Earlier, in 2020, the foundation settled a four-year legal and personal battle over the architect’s $133 million estate.

“When Zaha passed away, I discovered that I was an executor and trustee of her estate. She had never told me that I was either of these, and straight after her passing, we just had to deal with all of the legal matters.”

The Zaha Hadid Foundation encompasses 300,000 objects from the late architect’s life, from paintings, architectural models, sketchbooks, letters and even her wardrobe (which includes Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto pieces).

“Our greatest asset is the archive she left behind, and it goes beyond architecture. We can see the way that Zaha thought and how her methodology evolved, resulting in her designs and architecture,” said Rana, revealing that although she doesn’t necessarily believe in a 10-year plan for the future, the next two years are enough to keep her busy with international retrospectives in the works at major institutions. She added that there has been “huge interest” in Hadid’s paintings and wardrobe. An exhibition titled “Zaha Hadid: Visionary Museum Designs” will open next year at the Sir John Soane’s Museum in London, running from March 24 to June 20, 2027.

Rana wants Hadid’s archive to travel beyond the UK just like her architecture. The foundation has been offered exhibitions in Iraq and other countries in the Middle East. “We will be going to Iraq,” said Rana, who grew up in Beirut. She’s never visited Iraq, but said she still “feels Iraqi.”

“Zaha was first and foremost always Iraqi; she always credited the Iraqi part in her for who she was. She had a huge pride of place for Iraq,” said Rana. She recounted how Hadid used to make “the best leg of lamb, the Iraqi way, simmering over a fire for almost 20 hours” with rice. The Iraqi dialect would slip into her Arabic, too, with colloquialism like “Shaku maku?” (What’s there? What’s not there?)

Hadid’s exuberance was well documented, and to honor a decade of her death, Rana had to think like her late aunt, which is what inspired the two-day symposium.

“Zaha was really big on birthdays and she’d always like to make a big thing about her birthday. She would always say to me, ‘I hate surprises and I hate someone throwing me a surprise birthday party, so I may as well assume it, invite everyone and be in control,’” said Rana. A great number of Hadid’s friends and admirers attended the symposium, from Hans Ulrich Obrist and Deyan Sudjic to Aric Chen and Francesco Vezzoli.

“Symbolically, it’s been a very rough 10 years with legal disputes, and we’ve only been a foundation for four years,” explained Rana. “To turn Zaha’s office of 35 years into a foundation was very important to her because it was a former Victorian schoolhouse—and now people can come to learn and it serves everyone.”

The newly refurbished headquarters includes galleries, a learning space, lecture hall and collection display. The spaces will be used to host exhibitions, talks, workshops and creative residencies—the space has been inaugurated with an exhibition, “Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance,” curated by Catherine Howe and Libby Sellers, tracing the stage and set designs Hadid imagined for contemporary dance, classical opera and pop music.

Rana describes the Zaha Hadid Foundation as a platform for Hadid’s connections: “We’ve inherited a lot of friends, supporters and clients who became friends and family. Zaha had this amazing way of connecting with people and people loved her—without all of their help, we wouldn’t be here today.”

It's time to finally do something about my dingy home office.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've been through enough UK winters to know that things can get dark – and I don't just mean the incessant torment of existence (who's with me?!)

I mean working from home in a home office that is actually a spare room. And a spare room with crap light to boot. But there's a bit of tech for that, and over the last month or so I've been working with a SAD lamp right next to me. And it's had a massive positive impact on my day.

So I looked around and found the best SAD lamps from the best manufacturers in the US, all of which are on Amazon. As I explain below, you really can't go wrong with any of these, and as long as they're emitting 10,000 lux of brightness, you're only really paying more for the design and features of the lamp. For me, I really like the idea of having a magic pyramid on my desk!

This is the cheapest of the four SAD lamps here, but it absolutely does the job. It gives you the 10,000 lux that you need to smile, while also being a UV-free LED (which is standard). For $40, this is an easy recommendation.

With a more standard desk lamp aesthetic, the Halo lamp also offers wired and wireless phone charging features. I'm not the biggest fan of the design, but for $56, it's still a tempting bit of kit.

This is where the design of the SAD lamp comes into play – and the price tag goes UP! Foe me, this is definitely the most visually pleasing of all the four SAD lamps on the list. But then having a bit of futuristic ancient Egypt on hand is a bit of me.

The Clinical Light also boasts a striking design, and this and the Max version are both quite tall (18 and 22 inches). I feel like this might be too big to sit on your desk, but if you've got a spot for it to live, it will make you smile in return.

In a nutshell, SAD lamps mimic morning sunlight to balance internal body clocks. As their light enters our eyes it stimulates retinal cells. These cells then send signals to the brain to decrease melatonin (the sleepy hormone) and increase serotonin (the neurotransmitter that regulates happiness and energy). And this isn't all just vibes-based. Clinical trials confirm light therapy treats winter depression. I've had one for the last month, and I have absolutely felt the benefits.

For SAD lamps to be effective, they need to be able to pump out 10,000 lux of brightness from a normal sitting distances. All the lamps on this list achieve that. What's most interesting is that the more expensive lamps offer zero additional mood benefit. Budget boxes with certified output match luxury models, so you're just paying for design aesthetics and features (which admittedly are important).

A note on the light temperature – therapeutic lamps emit cool white light, so you won't be getting lovely honey-warm light with these. Blue wavelengths stimulate circadian photoreceptors in the retina. Warm white bulbs lack that blue spectrum and fail to trigger the internal wakefulness response, so keep that in mind before you click 'buy'.

Blizzard’s artists and engineers explain how volumetric fog, moonlit forests and flowing rivers will make the original Azeroth feel as players remember it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When we return to a game after years away, we tend to remember it as bigger and more vivid than it ever looked on screen. The forests, the mountains, and the little settlements along the way to somewhere more exciting all grow a little in memory. Blizzard Entertainment is building World of Warcraft: Forever around that effect.

WoW: Forever, the new version of the iconic MMORPG, released today, takes players back to the original Azeroth, with reworked environments, lighting and atmosphere. It won’t get a full visual overhaul or take on the look of the recent expansions. Blizzard wants it to feel like coming home to a place that’s more alive. That's a tricky task, given that World of Warcraft is one of the defining video game art styles many look to and love.

“We believe WoW Classic’s art style is timeless,” says Matt Heyman, lead environment artist at Blizzard Entertainment. “Which is why our focus was not on changing the game art but on small ways we could push specifically things like the environmental effects. Such as the way rivers now flow in Elwynn Forest, or the way the fog rolls in the Duskwood at night. Or the way the moonlight breaks through the leaves in the Ashenvale. It’s the same original Azeroth that players fell in love with all those years ago, with just a few small but powerful effects and updates to make it more immersive than ever.”

World of Warcraft: Forever is designed as a permanent home alongside modern and Classic WoW. It returns players to the original continents and the level 1-60 journey while adding new stories and experiences, and Blizzard says it will keep expanding this version of Azeroth over time.

For this unique release, the team needed to build something new without disturbing the memories players already hold. The work covers around 40 existing zones, new locations such as Zephras Isle, home of the new Skyborne race, and changes to familiar places including Dalaran.

“We asked ourselves, ‘What does it mean to evolve a timeless world?’” says Heyman. “We wanted to take that original ‘Vanilla’ version of Azeroth and combine it with the version that lives in our heads. Where our experiences, nostalgia and imagination all shape the ways we remember it.”

Each zone has its own colour palette, mood and atmosphere. “We often talk about the world as the main character of World of Warcraft, but I like to imagine it as a cast of characters,” he says.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Duskwood shows the problem well. Players remember a gloomy forest full of spiders, wolves, undead and skeletons, with the Night Watch patrolling Darkshire by torchlight. “However, while it’s an awesome and iconic zone, it’s probably not as dark and creepy as people remember,” says Heyman.

For WoW: Forever, the team is leaning into the remembered version, with moonlight cutting through the branches around Darkshire and fog drifting through the graveyards.

New tools can tempt artists to change things just because they can, so Blizzard has set a guiding rule. “Changing a world that players have cherished for such a long time has risks. We approach it carefully and responsibly,” Heyman explains. “We developed a central artistic principle that everything must be authentic. That’s both authentic to our world but, most importantly, authentic to the memories we have of Azeroth when the journey began in WoW.”

He points to Durotar, the arid, vibrant homeland of the Orcs. A cool blue atmosphere would look natural and realistic there, he says, but it wouldn’t be authentic. “The correct approach is to go in with purpose and to lean in and push the fantasy that the region already has.”

Most of the changes sit in the rendering technology, according to lead software engineer Jason Scott, who describes work on fog, lighting and water. Fog has been part of WoW’s look since the beginning, creating depth and gloomy vistas. Blizzard has replaced the original distant fog with volumetric technology, which gives artists much more control.

“We can control fog like we never have before,” says Scott. “Now we can increase the sense of creepiness in Dustwallow Marsh, and we can see the effect of wind in a zone. The texture of dust as it sweeps across plains.” It also extends sightlines across the map, which adds to the sense of scale.

Lighting has changed too. Until now, the sun and moons didn’t cast light into the world, a gap that would have been obvious once volumetric fog went in. Light now shines through the fog in a process called scattering, with the size and shape of the rays set by whatever blocks it, whether trees, mountains or other terrain.

“Now in WoW: Forever, when the sun comes up at dawn, there are streams of light that now cascade down the mountains, and we created similar rays for the moons as well,” says Scott.

To make that work, the team had to be sure the world properly blocked light and that the sun and moons lined up with the illumination on the ground. “There are still creative and artistic choices that we make, but it altogether makes the world feel much more alive,” he adds.

Rivers used to move simply, without resembling a river. For Forever, Scott says, the team studied how water moves, how wind and waves affect its surface, and how light interacts with its colour, transparency, and reflections. Rivers now follow their course, bend around rocks and produce foam where they hit them. Artists have full control over the effects, so different kinds of water can be tuned to look the way the team wants.

The models and textures remain the foundation of Warcraft’s look, even though the style has shifted with each expansion. Heyman says Forever is deliberately holding on to the character of the original assets.

“There’s an edge and grittiness to the way those assets look, and it just feels like Warcraft,” he says. “It’s a little bit of old, and a little bit of new. It’s maintaining that timeless iconic look matched with new rendering updates that breathe life into the world.”

World of Warcraft: Forever is available from today on Mac and PC (Pacific Time).

#9059. Paul Hamlyn Foundation announces recipients of £75,000 Awards for Artists

Award winners left to right: Hayley Tompkins, Daudi Matsiko, Bushra El-Turk, Linda Bell, Olivia Chaney, Rory Pilgrim, Ayanna Witter-Johnson, Georgina Starr, Charlotte Keeffe, (Racheal Crowther not present).Photo credit: Emile Holba

The Turner prize nominee Rory Pilgrim and the Venice Biennale artist Hayley Tompkins are among the recipients of this year’s Paul Hamlyn Foundation’s Awards for Artists. The £75,000 awards were granted to five artists and five composers.

In the wake of the ongoing cost of living crisis, the awards are timely. “Unique in its no-strings-attached funding model, the [Hamlyn] awards for artists allows recipients to use their award as they wish, providing them the freedom to develop their creative ideas, alleviating the pressures they may be facing,” says a press statement.

Tompkins was part of a trio of artists, alongside Corin Sworn and Duncan Campbell, who showed works in the Scotland + Venice exhibition in 2013. Her installations combine painting with a variety of other media, including found objects, digital films, photography and furniture. “It still hasn’t felt real yet, but I do know with more resources there will be room for me to feel and move a bit differently now,” she says in a statement.

Pilgrim’s work explores how “activism, spirituality and music can create spaces for connection”, adds the statement. Bristol-born Pilgrim was nominated for the Turner Prize in 2023 for their commission RAFTS at Serpentine Galleries and Barking Town Hall. “After working on many intensive processes, [the award] gives invaluable breathing space, autonomy and financial security to find joy and excitement in creativity,” Pilgrim says.

The other successful artists this year are Georgina Starr, who is known for performance works such as Androgynous Egg (2017), Dublin-born artist Racheal Crowther and the learning disabled artist Linda Bell. Judges include Joe Hill, the director of Yorkshire Sculpture Park, Melissa Blanchflower, a senior curator at Turner Contemporary in Margate, and Sheryll Catto, the artistic director of ActionSpace.

Since 1994, Paul Hamlyn Foundation has made 377 awards to artists with over £12m in funding; Phyllida Barlow, Yinka Shonibare and Alberta Whittle are among the previous recipients. Five composers including Daudi Matsiko and Ayanna Witter-Johnson were also recognised.

#9058. Jaguar designs Knightsbridge flagship to be "physical expression" of Type 01 electric car

Photography courtesy of Jaguar Land Rover

British car brand Jaguar has redesigned its flagship store in Knightsbridge, London, which is the only place in the world where the public can see the recently unveiled Type 01 electric car.

Jaguar overhauled itp show in central London to align its aesthetic with its latest electric car, which was created as the first car in a new era for the brand. It aimed for the flagship store to be a clear departure from the traditional car showroom.

“[We wanted] to create a physical expression of the new Jaguar,” said Jaguar Land Rover spatial brand design team senior manager Nick Rolls, whose team was responsible for overhauling the store.

“Rather than a traditional showroom, we wanted to design a destination where architecture, culture, hospitality and craftsmanship come together – and London felt like a natural home for that vision,” he continued.

“The space has been purpose-designed from the ground up to embody the brand’s new identity – it gave us the opportunity to truly rethink what a Jaguar destination could be outside traditional conventions.”

The showroom has space for two cars to be displayed, one of which is currently the Type 01, with the showroom being the only place in the world where it is on display to the public.

However, the majority of the ground floor of the space is occupied by a restaurant.

Named Café Eighty-One, the restaurant by Michelin-starred chef Michael O’Hare was finished in rich red fabric.

Upholstered benches run around the space, while a series of booths line the front facade of the showroom.

“Food is one of the most universal forms of connection,” said Rolls. “We wanted Café Eighty-One to be a welcoming space where people could spend time, meet friends or discover something new.

“It’s designed to be a destination in its own right, helping make Jaguar at Knightsbridge part of London’s cultural and hospitality landscape,” he continued.

According to Rolls, the extensive use of red was a nod to the surrounding brick architecture in central London.

“Jaguar’s design philosophy is exuberant modernism, so colour plays an important role in creating emotion, atmosphere and a sense of occasion,” he said.

“The rich reds within Café Eighty-One were inspired by London’s iconic red-brick architecture, which is so prevalent throughout Knightsbridge and the surrounding neighbourhoods,” he continued. “It was a way of connecting the interior to its setting while creating a warm, vibrant environment that feels distinctly London.”

Through the rest of the spaces, the materials and colours were chosen to directly evoke the interiors of the Type 01 electric car.

“The relationship is deliberate,” said Rolls. “The interiors share the same emphasis on materiality, craftsmanship and bold, contemporary form that defines Type 01.”

“Materials such as travertine, tactile textiles and warm brass reference the vehicle’s interior, while the use of sculptural shapes, carefully composed lighting and strong geometric forms reflects the same creative philosophy behind the car,” he continued.

While the public restaurant and showroom space are on the ground floor, a lower level contains more private spaces for sales, meetings and for discussions about customisation.

One of these, called the Design Vault, was entirely finished in rich navy blues.

Overall, Rolls hopes that the revamped space will help people understand the current, major rethink that the brand is embarking on.

“I hope people leave with a deeper understanding of Jaguar,” he concluded.

“Every element of the destination has been designed to reflect craftsmanship, creativity and bold design. We want people to feel a genuine connection to the brand and to see Jaguar through a new lens.”

The creation of the showroom follows the launch of Jaguar’s second electric car earlier this year, the Type 01. The car is the production version of the much-discussed Type 00 concept car, which drew much attention in 2024 when it was unveiled following a rebrand for the car company, which was described as a “complete reset”.

Artists and creatives are familiar with the fear of AI. Illustrators and graphic designers have watched in dismay as increasing numbers of businesses decide that AI slop is good enough for their branding and marketing needs. And many put the blame on companies like Canva and Adobe, who have been aggressively rolling out AI tools in their software.

Canva's just revealed another side of the story: the tech companies driving the change aren't immune to its impact. The Australian design software giant has announced the biggest restructuring in its 12 years of history, with plans to eliminate or relocate more than 1,200 jobs. That's almost a quarter of its global workforce, and it will include staff who helped to build the platform.

Canva aims to “collapse layers” in its organisation and bring “more teams together in person”. It's handling the layoffs in the classiest way possible, promising six months of salary and 12 months of healthcare to those affected, alongside career support, a fund for those who want to start their own business – and it's letting people keep their MacBooks.

But the layoffs highlight an inescapable contradiction. Even those responsible for the ubiquity of AI image generation are suffering from its expansion. Rather than a push for growth and innovation, Adobe and Canva's rollout of AI tools feels more their own desperate fight for survival, and it's a fight they might not be able to win.

"Success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next," Canva CEO Melanie Perkins writes in an update to staff. "This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade."

There's been talk of an “SaaS-pocalypse” as AI becomes advanced enough to make specialised software redundant. We've already seen the release of an open-source vibe-coded Adobe alternative, and it works to an extent. Generating your own software is only going to get easier, as is asking an AI bot to generate design assets directly.

Despite its heavy investment in AI, Adobe's stock price has fallen by around 25% in the past year and over 60% in the past five years. It's not clear that even AI leaders like OpenAI and Anthropic, the makers of ChatGPT and Claude, can become profitable as Chinese rivals emerge delivering similar technology at a cheaper price.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Some creatives opposed to AI might feel a twinge of satisfaction at seeing a prominent proponent floundering. But Canva has also been a positive force, even if you don't use it's AI tools. As well as its premium platform, it has one of the best free Adobe alternatives in its free Affinity app, providing much-needed competition.

Creatives using the app might have cause to worry about how long it will be offered as a loss leader. Canva's shown a strong commitment to it so far, recently adding new raw editing tools and an iPad app. But its recent decision to pull the previously free Remove.bg into its paid suite shows that the structure and availability of creative software is constantly in flux as developers try to work out how to respond to competition from AI.

A primary beneficiary is the person or entity you designate to receive an asset — such as a life insurance policy, 401(k), IRA, or bank account — when you die. If you name multiple primary beneficiaries, they split the asset according to the percentages you specify. A contingent beneficiary (also called a secondary or backup beneficiary) receives the asset only if all primary beneficiaries are unable to inherit, either because they predeceased you, disclaimed the inheritance, or cannot be located.

This layered system exists because life is unpredictable. If you name your spouse as primary beneficiary on your life insurance and you both die in the same accident, the contingent beneficiary ensures the proceeds go where you intended rather than into your general estate where they become subject to probate.

You can name individuals, trusts, charities, or even your estate as a beneficiary. However, naming your estate is generally a poor choice because it forces the asset through probate, exposing it to creditors, delays, and court costs. The entire purpose of a beneficiary designation is to transfer assets outside of probate — naming your estate defeats that advantage.

When naming multiple beneficiaries, you must choose a distribution method that determines what happens if one beneficiary dies before you. This choice is critical and frequently misunderstood.

Per stirpes (Latin for "by the branch") means each branch of your family tree receives its designated share. If your son predeceases you, his share passes down to his children (your grandchildren) in equal portions. The family branch stays intact.

Per capita (Latin for "by the head") means assets are divided equally among surviving beneficiaries only. If your son predeceases you, his share is redistributed among your other surviving beneficiaries — his children receive nothing.

For most families, per stirpes is the safer default because it prevents accidental disinheritance of grandchildren. If you want surviving beneficiaries to absorb the shares of those who predecease you, per capita achieves that — but make sure that outcome aligns with your actual wishes.

Some financial institutions also offer per capita at each generation, which distributes equally among the nearest living generation first, then passes remaining shares equally to the next generation. This hybrid approach is less common but available at some custodians.

Beneficiary designations are deceptively simple forms that create binding legal consequences. The most expensive mistakes happen not from malice but from neglect.

In most states, a divorce does not automatically remove your ex-spouse from beneficiary designations on retirement accounts or life insurance policies. Federal law (ERISA) governs employer-sponsored plans like 401(k)s, and ERISA does not recognize state divorce revocation statutes. If you divorce and never update your 401(k) beneficiary, your ex-spouse can legally claim the entire balance — even if your will leaves everything to your new spouse.

Minor children cannot legally receive life insurance proceeds or retirement account distributions. If you name a 5-year-old as beneficiary, the insurance company will not release funds until a court appoints a guardian or conservator of the child's property. This process costs $2,000 to $5,000 in legal fees, takes months, and requires ongoing court reporting. Instead, name a trust for the benefit of the child or use your state's Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) custodial designation.

If you leave the beneficiary field blank or all named beneficiaries predecease you without a contingent, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This triggers probate, adds 6 to 18 months of delay, and exposes the asset to estate creditors. Always name at least one contingent beneficiary.

Your beneficiary designations and your will can contradict each other. The beneficiary designation always wins. If your will says your daughter gets your IRA but the IRA beneficiary form still names your brother, your brother gets the IRA. Review both documents together annually.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Set a recurring calendar reminder to review every beneficiary designation once per year — ideally alongside your tax preparation. Pull statements from your 401(k), IRA, life insurance, bank accounts, and brokerage accounts. Verify that primary and contingent designations match your current wishes. This 30-minute annual review prevents the kind of outdated-beneficiary disasters that lead to costly litigation and assets going to unintended recipients.

Yes. You can name multiple primary beneficiaries and assign a percentage to each. For example, you could name three children as primary beneficiaries at 33.3% each. The percentages must total 100%.

If all primary beneficiaries predecease you and no contingent is named, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This forces the asset through probate, where it is subject to creditor claims, court costs, and delays of 6 to 18 months.

For state-law-governed accounts like IRAs and life insurance, some states have revocation-upon-divorce statutes — but not all. For ERISA-governed accounts like employer 401(k)s, federal law does not recognize state divorce revocation. You must manually update the beneficiary form after divorce to be safe.

Yes. A beneficiary can file a qualified disclaimer within 9 months of the account holder's death. The disclaimed asset then passes to the contingent beneficiary or according to the plan's default rules. Disclaimers are sometimes used for tax planning purposes.

Naming a trust provides control over how and when assets are distributed — especially useful for minor children, spendthrift beneficiaries, or blended families. However, trusts named as IRA beneficiaries must meet specific IRS requirements to qualify for stretch distributions under the SECURE Act. Consult an estate planning attorney before naming a trust as retirement account beneficiary.

A POD designation on a bank account functions exactly like a beneficiary designation. The named person receives the account balance upon your death without going through probate. You maintain full control of the account during your lifetime and can change the POD beneficiary at any time.

Primary and contingent beneficiary designations are among the most powerful — and most overlooked — estate planning tools. They transfer assets instantly upon death, bypass probate entirely, and override your will in every state. The 30 minutes it takes to review and update your designations after every major life event can save your family months of legal proceedings, thousands in attorney fees, and the heartbreak of assets going to unintended recipients.

#9054. Two More Vienna Galleries Close, Citing ‘No New Collectors’ and ‘Challenging’ Financial Landscape

Two more galleries in Vienna are closing or changing their models amid market challenges, reports the Art Newspaper (TAN).

Zeller van Almsick and Exile cite high costs and unreliable sales. This development comes after Zurich’s Eva Presenhuber is closing the Vienna outpost she has operated since 2022, as she told ARTnews in October, and Emanuel Layr changing his operating model.

Exile is calling it quits after some 18 years, with founder Christian Siekmeier telling TAN that “there are simply no new collectors emerging.” The gallery was founded in Berlin in 2008 and moved to Vienna after a decade, showing older generations including Alvin Baltrop and Nathalie du Pasquier as well as younger artists such as David Gruber and Katharina Marszewski. Related Articles Prairie, Chicago Gallery That Put Conceptualism Ahead of Commercialism, Closes After Nearly a Decade New York's Massey Klein Gallery Closes Its Doors and Goes Nomadic After Nine Years

Zeller van Almsick is shuttering after a decade. “There is no point in sugarcoating the fact that the past two years have been financially extremely challenging,” cofounder Magdalena Zeller told TAN. The gallery showed younger Austrian artists including Dejan Dukic, Carsten Fock, and Bianca Phos.

Layr, meanwhile, will go nomadic, while keeping a smaller, by-appointment showroom in the capital, as the founder revealed in September. “The gallery model as we know it is increasingly reaching its limits,” said Layr, who mounted his first show in 2011, at the time, while also saying that “financial reasons played no part” in the decision. The gallery’s roster includes such well-known artists as Julien Bismuth, Lili Reynaud-Dewar, and Leah Ke Yi Zheng.

He now tells TAN, “It’s harder to sell some things, costs are getting higher, then there’s a big art fair coming and taking another €100,000. I had to be more realistic, and think, ‘How much profit do I get? How much does the artist get?’”

These troubles come despite the fact that the city, whose metro area is home to 2.9 million, is rich with both historical and contemporary art institutions, as Art in America’s Emily Watlington wrote in 2025 after a dozen visits, calling it “Europe’s best art city.” But Zeller tells TAN that there is “a significant gap” between the city’s cultural heft and the level of activity among its collectors.

In a contrasting signal of the local market’s potential, a number of top Vienna galleries have banded together to launch a new fair, Astoria Artshow, which had its inaugural outing in September. That followed troubles at both the Spark Art Fair Vienna and Vienna Contemporary.

Longtime contemporary art collector Eva Frey tells TAN that there are not enough collectors in her age cohort (over 70) to sustain the city’s galleries. At the same time, she says there are not enough collectors in the 45 to 55 range, formerly the principal group supporting contemporary art, who are “established in a profession.”

Nintendo has worked its magic on a 28-year-old classic.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early reviews of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time are out, and most reviewers are certain this one has avoided the pitfalls of some remakes – no weird visual redesigns here. Our review will come a little later, but for now, let's look at what some are saying about how Nintendo's 1998 Nintendo 64 adventure, often held up as one of the greatest games ever made, has made it to the Switch 2.

The response has been pretty spectacular. The remake is sitting at 96 on Metacritic, with a hefty collection of perfect scores and very few critics finding much to complain about. That's quite an achievement for a game whose original version already has such a place in gaming history.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launches on 5 November, and Nintendo has done rather more than give Link a fresh coat of paint. Hyrule has been rebuilt with a striking new visual style (while staying tonally true), the soundtrack has been re-orchestrated, and the original's occasionally clunky controls have been updated. Now it offers free jumping, a modern camera, and fully voiced cutscenes, alongside redesigned dungeons and expanded character interactions.

It's a substantial overhaul, even if the adventure itself remains reassuringly familiar to those who grew up on this classic Nintendo game. If you're a fan, take our Ultimate Zelda quiz and test your knowledge.

GamesRadar+ awards the remake five stars, calling it "a remake for the ages". Reviewer Anna Koselke is particularly taken with how Nintendo has brought Hyrule to life without losing the original's charm, praising its "stunning visuals" and newly voiced dialogue.

TechRadar is equally impressed, awarding five stars and describing the remake as "a thoroughly well-thought-out retelling of one of the most loved video games of all time". Reviewer Josephine Watson highlights the redesigned locations, enemies and puzzles, as well as the refreshed soundtrack. There is a little caution, though, with TechRadar suggesting the remake could have been more ambitious and that some of the original's difficulty has been lost along the way.

Game Informer awards the remake 9.25/10, describing it as "a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one." Reviewer Kyle Hilliard likes the visual overhaul and improved camera but feels Nintendo has played it relatively safe with the changes. It looks new, he argues, without necessarily feeling like an entirely new adventure.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Shacknews is considerably more enthusiastic, awarding a perfect 10/10 and calling the remake "a tour de force that redefines what remakes can be". Its review highlights how Nintendo has made familiar mechanics feel fresh, from the reworked combat to the redesigned dungeons. It also singles out Navi, who has been given a much bigger role as a companion rather than simply popping up to shout "Hey! Listen!"

Destructoid also hands out a 10/10, calling it "one of the best examples of how to properly reimagine an enduring masterpiece". The review praises the improved visuals, 60fps performance, and updated controls, though it agrees the remake can feel a little too easy in places.

The Guardian's Keza MacDonald is similarly impressed, scoring the game five stars and describing the remake as "a dream come true". Her review makes an interesting observation about the new art direction, comparing Hyrule to detailed theatre scenery and Link to a handmade doll, with his equipment looking like exaggerated props. It's a more stylised approach than simply chasing photorealism, and one that suits the fairytale quality of the original.

Reviewers are highlighting the lack of Master Quest is a notable omission for returning players wanting a tougher adventure, while the more generous clues and quality-of-life improvements have softened some of the original's challenge.

GamesRadar+ also flags the absence of Master Quest and the single-save-file restriction as drawbacks. Game Informer, meanwhile, feels the remake could have been a little more adventurous in how it reinterprets the original.

These aren't deal-breakers, but they're worth considering if you've spent years exploring Hyrule and know the N64 version inside out.

For anyone who grew up with the original Nintendo 64, this remake is clearly wrapped in an enormous amount of nostalgia. But Ocarina of Time is more than a fond memory for those of us who played it back in 1998. It helped establish the language of 3D adventure games, from lock-on combat to sprawling interconnected dungeons, and its influence still runs through modern game design.

Nintendo has had to do a lot of work to bring the adventure up to date, but it hasn't had to fix what made it special in the first place. The world design, the sense of discovery, and that slightly odd fairy-tale atmosphere are all still there, only now with the visual detail and fluidity the original hardware could never manage.

And Nintendo is very good at this too, with the recent Star Fox remake also proving popular on Switch 2, and the many Metroid and Mario updates and remasters proving a reason to buy Nintendo Online.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches on Nintendo Switch 2 on 5 November.

#9052. Arches create “animated silhouette” at red-brick apartment block in King’s Cross

Two-storey-tall arches frame entrances to Cadence, a mixed-use apartment block in King’s Cross, London, which has been completed by local studio Alison Brooks Architects.

Positioned at the northern end of Lewis Cubitt Park, the prominent red-brick building combines 163 apartments alongside commercial and social spaces organised around an open-air courtyard.

Signposted by its two towers, the building by Alison Brooks Architects forms part of the wider King’s Cross redevelopment and is complete with views overlooking Heatherwick Studios’ Coal Drops Yard to the south.

According to studio founder Alison Brooks, the building’s red-brick exterior was chosen to pay homage to the nearby St Pancras Station, while its arched openings draw on the area’s neo-gothic architecture and were conceived as a “civic welcoming gesture”.

“The main concept of the project was to make a clear statement of welcome and arrival in King’s Cross, but from the north end of the master plan rather than the south end, which everybody is familiar with,” Brooks told Dezeen.

“My first instinct was to respond to King’s Cross’ iconic railway station architecture, sculpting the site massing to create an animated silhouette. A language of two-story high arches creates a really generous, welcoming gesture at street level and toward the park,” she added.

The building is formed of a five-sided block, with no designated front or back, which rises to form two towers reaching 12 and 16 storeys respectively.

For its construction, the studio opted for a Design for Manufacture and Assembly approach, which saw 85 per cent of the building’s components prefabricated off-site.

At the centre of its angular plan, an open-air courtyard, complete with a reflecting pool, has been wrapped by sheltered walkways that provide a shared circulation space between the building’s private and commercial programmes.

“It’s a multifaceted building,” Brooks said. “Each facet of the pentagon has a particular identity or address to the space that it’s adjacent to.”

“This idea of making a very connected space at the base of the building, even though it’s a courtyard, is visually trying to connect all the sides of the plot to the city around it.”

“It’s a place of movement and light and also a kind of special quality because of the reflecting pool,” she added.

The building’s first two floors have been dedicated to 633 square metres of commercial and social spaces, which include a “community living room” that opens onto the courtyard at ground level.

A prefabricated lift system connects to the upper floors, where the 163 residential units benefit from both courtyard and street views.

A combination of rectangular and arched windows draws daylight into the building’s white-walled interior, complemented by private balconies and communal roof terraces.

Other projects developed as part of the King’s Cross regeneration include Google’s landscraper office building by architecture studios BIG and Heatherwick and an office block designed by Coffey Architects to recall the area’s industrial spaces.
