#9051. ICA Miami selects architect to renovate recently acquired building

Rendering of ICA Miami’s new building Courtesy Gensler

The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami (ICA Miami) has appointed the global architecture firm Gensler to renovate a 30,000-sq.-ft building the museum acquired in 2024, doubling its exhibition and public-programming space.

Steps away from its current venue in Miami’s Design District, the new wing is scheduled to open in late 2027—as the museum marks its tenth anniversary at its current location. Focused on expanding the free museum’s community outreach, the project will transform the ICA into a multi-site complex and house the first permanent display of its collection.

The museum’s new building formerly housed the De la Cruz Collection, a private museum that closed after the 2024 death of its co-founder Rosa de la Cruz. Since its $25m acquisition later that year, the site has mainly hosted the ICA’s educational programmes. It will close once construction begins. The renovation is part of a $40m capital campaign, supported entirely by private funds.

The new design will adapt the existing structure. “The building was developed to house a contemporary art collection,” Alex Gartenfeld, the ICA’s director and chief curator, tells The Art Newspaper. “But with the spaces we are constructing, we intend to enhance the museum’s story-driven narrative approach to the collection and exhibitions.”

Rendering of ICA Miami’s new building Courtesy Gensler

Eight new galleries will occupy the building’s first and second floors. Among them will be the museum’s first dedicated spaces for its growing permanent collection of more than 2,000 works.

“The programme between the two buildings is blended, but we will now have two full floors dedicated to our permanent collection,” Gartenfeld says. “Around every six months, we will refresh the collection display to reflect the collection’s emphasis and recent acquisitions.”

The entire third floor will be dedicated to public programming, including talks, symposia, lectures and performances. “Beyond adding galleries, this renovation will strengthen the ICA’s ability to support artists, expand learning and create a platform for exchange and belonging in one of the world’s most dynamic cultural cities,” says Bevin Savage Yamazaki, Gensler’s global culture and museums leader.

A reimagined façade with transparent components is key to the design. Gartenfeld says the façade aims to provide a connection between street-level traffic and the museum itself.

The renovations focus on visitor experience and accessibility as well. The lobby will be redesigned. And reconfigured outdoor areas will include social spaces, a sculpture deck and an expanded café. “We are aiming to create a more collective experience,” Gartenfeld says.

The museum expanded its exhibition space and reorganised its permanent collection for the first time in almost 100 years—with a special focus on Native American art

#9050. Artist Pablo Helguera Takes the Helm at New School’s Vera List Center for Art and Politics Amid an Electoral Earthquake

New York artist and educator Pablo Helguera, whose work has long focused on socially engaged practice, has been named director of the Vera List Center for Art and Politics (VLC) at the New School in New York, as well as director of the New School’s art collection.

He is an inside hire: since 2020 he has been an assistant professor of arts management and entrepreneurship at the school’s College of Performing Arts, where he oversees a master’s program. Before that, he spent 13 years as director of adult and academic programs at the Museum of Modern Art. Helguera succeeds Carin Kuoni, senior director and chief curator, who had led the center since 2004. Related Articles A New Exhibition Explores How Telenovela Tropes Reveal a Deeper Meaning in Art In 2022, Art Workers Continued to Unionize and Strike for Their Rights

“It feels like such a wonderful transition,” Helguera told ARTnews in a phone interview. “It’s exactly what I’ve done my whole career. I’ve been a programmer forever and there’s very few people of my species.” The VLC supports research, teaching, exhibitions, publications, and public programs. Its signature event is an annual public forum. At Kuoni’s initiative, the center adopts a new theme every two years; the current one is “Matter of Intelligence.”

“Pablo Helguera brings an extraordinary combination of artistic vision, intellectual curiosity, and institutional experience to the Vera List Center for Art and Politics,” JK Brown, chair of the Vera List Center advisory board, said in a statement. “His commitment to socially engaged art and the role of artists in shaping public life aligns deeply with the Center’s mission. As we welcome Pablo, we also celebrate Carin Kuoni’s remarkable leadership over the past two decades. She has built an institution of international significance, grounded in rigorous inquiry, artistic experimentation, and a profound commitment to social justice.”

Helguera has long been a fixture of the international art scene, and he has long been interested in exactly the kinds of intersections the Vera List Center explores. This summer, the Sheldon Museum of Art in Nebraska received a $100,000 grant from the Andy Warhol Foundation, partly to support “Pablo Helguera: Socialscapes,” a midcareer retrospective planned for 2027. “The Schoolhouse and the Bus,” his two-artist show with Suzanne Lacy, was part of Pacific Standard Time: LA/LA in 2018. While he was at MoMA, artist-writers Dushko Petrovich and Roger White sought him out as a contributor to their 2018 book As Radical, as Mother, as Salad, as Shelter: What Should Art Institutions Do Now? He conceived and directed “The School of Panamerican Unrest,” which included more than 100 public programs across 20 countries. He also founded Librería Donceles, a Spanish-language used bookstore that has traveled to 13 cities.

He has written two books, both published by Jorge Pinto Books: Education for Socially Engaged Art: A Materials and Techniques Handbook (2011) and Art Scenes: The Social Scripts of the Art World (2012). His curatorial credits include “Club Americano” at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (2017) and serving as “pedagogical curator” of the Eighth Mercosul Biennial (2011). His honors include a Guggenheim Fellowship, a Creative Capital grant, and fellowships and awards from A Blade of Grass, Franklin Furnace, and Art Matters.

At MoMA, he developed and led symposia, including an annual forum on contemporary art. He also conceived the Artists Experiment initiative, which brought artists including Nina Katchadourian, Michael Rakowitz, and Caroline Woolard into dialogue with the public through collaborations with MoMA educators. Before MoMA, he shaped public programming at the Guggenheim Museum and the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago.

The VLC was founded in 1992 and named for life trustee Vera G. List (1908–2002), an art collector and philanthropist. It has an annual operating budget of $1.1 million, with support from organizations including the Mellon Foundation, the Ford Foundation, and the Andy Warhol Foundation.

Helguera started in the role this week, at a dynamic moment in American politics. Democrats routed Republicans in national and state races across the country, flipping Senate and House seats and winning governorships in what had been considered deep-red territory. It was a realignment unseen since the aftermath of the Watergate scandal. Florida’s outgoing Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, called Election Day “close to an extinction level event.”

“I’m so lucky,” Helguera said. “We’ve lived through dark times for democracy, and this is an enormous event that allows us to think again: How do we rebuild trust in democratic institutions, and what role can artists play in helping us think about democracy and about what populism means? These questions are super-important right now. How can we ask them from a place of hope rather than the despair we have lived in for 10 years?”

The Doro C300 Pro V2 offers comfort, ergonomics and great arm rest adjustments.

We've reviewed a lot of office chairs over the years, and there's a brand we often come back to at the budget end of the spectrum. Sihoo is known for its fantastic-value M18, the cheapest ergonomic office chair we recommend, but it also makes some higher-end offerings. The Doro C300 Pro V2 is the one that's most impressed us, and it's now reduced by $70 from $509 to $439 on the Sihoo website.

That's a lot cheaper than most of the best office chairs for back pain, and the Doro C300 Pro has a wide seat, breathable mesh, lumbar support, lots of adjustability and fantastic armrests.

The Doro C300 Pro V2 sits firmly at the top of Sihoo's range of ergonomic office chairs and it's as good as many that cost over $100 more, as our Doro C300 Pro review notes.

The mesh material is great for breathability and has a good balance between firmness and spring. The lumbar support does its job, and the level of adjustability is impressive, particularly in the armrests, which move up/down, forward/back, tilt and can even more laterally closer or further from your chest.

There's also a footrest version, reduced from $559.99 to $459.99.

We recognise that the C300 Pro is not the most beautiful office chair, and, like all Sihoo chairs, it takes some patience with assembly. But once you've got it set up, it is very comfortable.

The highlight is the lumbar support, which is one of the more comfy that we've tested, helping to support the back's natural 's' shape without making you feel like it wants to break you into submission.

Most of the chair's adjustability is as you'd expect from a higher-mid range ergonomic chair, but the armrests stand out. They go up/down, forward/back, and tilt and, most impressively, move laterally in and out from your chest. This is no minor detail: it provides more options for how you sit and allows you to freely move your arms as you want.

Not in the US? See the best budget office chair deals in your region below. Once you've made your choice, make sure you know how to sit properly in a chair.

Whether you like your coffee black or with milk, the Black Friday sales are the best moment of the year to finally upgrade your home coffee making setup. The deals have begun already, and I've spotted a trio of great offers, including a massive £250 off the Sage The Barista Touch at Currys.

This is a Bean to Cup coffee machine, which means it grinds your beans as well as making the coffee. Fresh grounds are one of the keys to getting the perfect brew, and an all-in-one machine saves having to buy separate appliances and find the space and sockets for them.

See below for more details on this and other early Black Friday coffee machine deals available now.

The Barista Touch is a complete home coffee-making hub that maintains the look of a classic espresso machine. It has an integrated precision conical burr grinder, a ThermoJet espresso system and an auto steam wand optimised for latte art. The touchscreen makes it quick and easy to adjust water temperature, coffee strength and milk texture, and you can save up to eight personalised programs.

Traditionalists might turn their nose up at the Ninja AutoBarista as it foregoes the classic portafilter for a hands-off, push-button mechanism, but that does make make life easy on a busy morning. It has a steel conical grinder with a built-in digital scale to weigh your coffee and an automated Grind IQ feature that attempts to auto-calibrate settings based on flow and pressure. Beans go into the hopper, and coffee drops straight into the brew group inside the machine.

If you want a simple morning espresso without the distraction of digital displays and an infinite array of possibilities, the much simpler De'Longhi Dedica Style offers great value and a sleek, classic design. There's no grinder or programming, but it's a reliable, beautifully designed machine that can make two espressos at once and has a wand to froth or steam milk for cappuccinos, macchiatos or lattes.

#9047. French authorities investigate claim of fraud over Picasso plates and medallions on sale

Pablo Picasso with a silver plate, in 1957. The artist had commissioned François Hugo to produce repoussé metal pieces from his designs © 2026 Succession Picasso/DACS, London; © Photo: Edward Quinn, © edwardquinn.com

A criminal investigation amid a family crisis casts a dark shadow over the illustrious history of the French studio Ateliers Hugo, which produced jewellery and silverware created by major artists of the 20th century. According to a legal source, the court of Aix-en-Provence in the south of France has opened an investigation following a complaint by the Picasso family.

On 10 March, Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, representing the nine heirs of the Spanish artist, filed a complaint alleging “fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and concealment of these felonies”. The file does not name the alleged perpetrators, and their identity is not presently known. The following month the Picasso family published a formal warning in the Gazette Drouot, titled “Hugo silverware”. It urged “all art market professionals and buyers to exercise the utmost vigilance”, following the appearance of what it described as “a large number” of illegitimate silver plates and gold medallions, valued at millions of euros.

Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, the daughter of Pablo, has filed a legal complaint on behalf of nine family members of the artist about the allegedly unauthorised works © Studio Cabrelli

The title refers to Ateliers Hugo, a goldsmith based in Aix-en-Provence. It was founded in 1933 by François Hugo (1899-1981), the great-grandson of the famous French author Victor Hugo. In 1955 Pablo Picasso, who since 1947 had created a variety of ceramics in Vallauris on the French Riviera, commissioned François Hugo to produce plates and dishes from similar designs in fine metals, using the traditional technique of repoussé. Later, the workshop reduced them into medallions and earrings. With the help of his brother, the painter Jean Hugo, who introduced him to artistic circles, François made jewellery designed by Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, André Derain, Jean Arp, Jean Dubuffet, Roberto Matta, Jean Lurçat and Dorothea Tanning. In 1975, his son Pierre Hugo (1947-2023) took over the company. Pierre was followed by his son Nicolas (born 1989).

Members of the Picasso family and their lawyer, Jean-Jacques Neuer, who filed the complaint, declined to comment to The Art Newspaper. But their complaint alleges that “it has been discovered that the moulds of Picasso’s works were reused for unauthorised productions of silver and gold pieces, followed by duplicates, some of them bearing three times the same number, and unnumbered specimens”.

According to a source close to the investigation, the Picasso Administration, which represents the family, says it has discovered at least 17 complete or almost complete suspicious collections, amounting to hundreds of pieces. The first red flag was raised by the Museum of Old and New Art (Mona), a private Australian museum in Tasmania. According to this source, in May 2023 the museum informed the Picasso Administration of its doubts over plates it had bought at Sotheby’s in London. An auction catalogue of 13 October 2021 describes a “complete set of 24 silver plates” bearing the signature of the artist, completed with an additional “unnumbered proof of Visage aux mains”. The pieces were “accompanied by a certificate of authenticity issued by Pierre Hugo”. The lot was sold for £1.4m. Sotheby’s declined to comment for this story.

According to the legal files, the seller was the British dealer Mark Maurice, from a now dissolved gallery named Masterpiece. The source close to the investigation says the dealer allegedly produced documents showing that he had commissioned a set of plates and a set of medallions from the Ateliers Hugo between 2017 and 2020. Mark Maurice indicated he was “unable to respond” to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries “due to strict non-disclosure agreements in place”.

In summer 2023 the ceramics museum in Vallauris, Musée Magnelli, exhibited another collection of 24 silver plates as well as gold medallions attributed to Picasso.

In 2023, the Musée Magnelli in Vallauris exhibited plates and medallions attributed to Picasso Travelworld

According to the legal files, the Picasso Administration protested, having found that they bore no number, mark or punch, as legally required. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges these facts, but tells The Art Newspaper that the works exhibited at Musée Magnelli were so-called “author’s copies, made for the exhibition, duly indicating in the catalogue that they were not for sale”. He adds that he “recovered them and had them melted after the show”. Representatives for the museum did not respond to a request for comment.

In June 2023, as reported in the legal files, the French branch of the auction house Bonhams made a request to the Picasso Administration for the right to reproduce silverware for a catalogue. The auction house was planning a sale of 95 lots from the Ateliers Hugo collection, including works by Ernst, Derain and Cocteau, valued between €400 and €50,000 each. The most valuable were 59 pieces, “made by” or “after” Picasso.

On 26 September 2023 Bonhams was informed by the Picasso Administration that these pieces were considered to be “unauthorised” editions. The auction house then decided to “delay the whole sale”, just two days before it was due to take place. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges he “did initiate, in the wake of good results obtained at Bonhams UK, this sale of pieces”, produced, he says, by his “father and grandfather”. But, he adds, “When we were informed by dealers of the presence of possible duplicates, I agreed to withdraw the sale and collaborated with the Picasso Administration to identify them.”

Bonhams declined to comment, but according to the source close to the investigation, the lots attributed to Picasso were sequestered when a British financial company, Suros Capital, tried to recover them as collateral for a €256,000 loan. A spokesperson for Suros confirmed the operation to The Art Newspaper, adding that “it was secured against not only the Picasso pieces, but a range of assets which are progressively realised, so the company expects to recover the loan in full”.

In November 2023, according to the source close to the investigation, a representative for Bonhams France informed the Picasso Administration that a Spanish collector contacted the auction house to sell 24 silver plates, estimated at £900,000. Again, the auction house refused on the basis of Picasso Administration’s doubts about the objects’ authenticity. In the legal files, the Picasso Administration claims the same collector had sold another set of 24 silver plates and one of 24 gold medallions in private sales through Bonhams in London in 2022. Neither the British auction house nor the Spanish collector made any comment.

Nicolas Hugo, who says he has not been interviewed by the investigators, claims he has no knowledge of the proceedings and “is unaware of the content of the complaint” issued by the Picasso Administration. But, he says: “The criminal investigation can only deal with facts related to the time of my father and grandfather, therefore falling under the statute of limitations and concerning persons now deceased.” He adds that “the rights to reproduce the items disappeared with them, so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations”, and he does not have the legal status of a goldsmith. However, he says: “I have signed some certificates of authenticity, but only to confirm my father’s own signature.”

In interviews with The Art Newspaper, Nicolas Hugo describes himself as a “self-taught art dealer”. When he was around 20 years old, he started to work as an assistant in galleries in Paris, before moving to London. He is now an agent for several artists and a curator. In 2022, the French magazine Les Hardis described him as a “mix of British and Saint-Germain-des-Prés charm”. “My father became very ill in 2018,” he told the magazine. “I had an epiphany. I decided to take over the workshop. I immersed myself completely,” and started to train in manufacturing jewels.

“From 2019,” he tells The Art Newspaper, “I became involved in the history of his workshop and helped my father to showcase this heritage, for memorial and commercial reasons. I set up exhibitions in places like Barcelona or Vallauris and initiated this sale of the fonds d’atelier at Bonhams Paris. I have not taken over my father’s company and was not his partner.”

Nicolas Hugo says: “There have been some duplicates on the market, dating from my father’s period, but I have no idea who had made them in the workshop.” He says he has “no idea who put a collection on sale at Sotheby’s in 2021” and knows “nothing of the three sets proposed by this Spanish collector to Bonhams in 2022 and 2023”.

The criminal investigation is still at the preliminary phase. It comes at a time when the company is already in limbo. Pierre Hugo died in October 2023 and his five children have turned down his inheritance. Nicolas Hugo’s brothers and sisters declined to comment to The Art Newspaper due to the ongoing investigation.

However, sources close to the case say that Pierre Hugo’s heirs’ inheritance came with a €2.5m tax debt. According to these sources, three of the Hugo siblings said in police interviews they were “not at all” aware of the conduct of the workshop by their brother Nicolas, who had succeeded their ailing father in 2019. The sources said the three Hugo siblings were on alert after learning that Bonhams Paris declined to sell the collection from the Ateliers Hugo in September 2023. According to the same sources, when Pierre Hugo died a month later, the three siblings went to the workshop and took 21 moulds of plates that they decided to hand over to the Picasso Administration. Three moulds from the set were missing and they did not find those for the medallions.

According to these sources, the three Hugo siblings explained to the investigators that, “knowing that the rights of reproduction were extinct, they wanted to be sure this would be respected”. The siblings also asserted that they “did not want in any way to be implicated in these operations and made it clear to the Picasso Administration”, according to the sources.

Together with his wife Monique Mueller, the Swiss collector built one of the largest private holdings of Pre-Columbian, African and Oceanic objects in Europe

#9046. Georgia O’Keeffe Painting Found in Closet After 40 Years Heads to Christie’s With $ 3 M. Est.

When Christie’s holds its 20th Century Evening Sale in two weeks, one painting will hit the block with a curious story. The Georgia O’Keeffe painting Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930) only recently resurfaced after nearly 40 years out of the public eye.

Per the New York Post, the painting was found by a Rhode Island woman when she was helping her elderly aunt clear her East Village apartment. According to the 65-year-old woman, who the Post names only by her middle name, Betsy, she found the painting at the back of a closet under a row of fur coats. Related Articles Gloria Steinem's Life in Art What We Miss When We Flatten Georgia O'Keeffe Into a Feminist Icon

“I thought, wow, that’s that’s pretty wild,” she told the Post. “I wondered, ‘Is there any way I can keep this?’ … But once we started exploring what the value of the piece was, I realized that it’s worth more than my house.”

According to the woman, her aunt told her in 2022 off-handedly that there was an O’Keeffe painting in the closet as they prepped the house for home health aides. However, Betsy didn’t actually find the work until a few weeks ago when her aunt was put into hospice at age 98.

The aunt, who has since died, was once a Foreign Services worker. She recieved the painting as a graduation gift from her mother in 1963, when she purchased it from The Downtown Gallery on 51st Street for $3,800. As Betsy tells it, the painting hung in the apartment until the 1980s, when she noticed a guest “eyeing it a bit too closely.”

“I think she was fully aware of its value … she recognized that it was an expression of her financial position,” Betsy said.

The painting has since become a bit of an oddity for Betsy and her family, who says she hung it up “for chuckles.” “The men in the family who’ve seen this have commented, there seems to be a number of ‘vaginas’ in the picture,” she said

The painting carries a $2 million to $3 million estimate, and a portion of the proceeds will be donated to an unnamed educaiton institution. The rest will go towards Betsy and her family “for things like paying off the mortgage.” Fair enough.

In a lot essay, Christie’s described the painting as an “important early work” that is “likely the first iteration in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak, north of Taos Pueblo.” One of the other such works is in the collection of MoMA, while the other is in an unamed private collection.

#9045. Neri Oxman experiments with fabric pigment created by bacteria

Designer Neri Oxman has created a fabric dyeing concept where a bacterial solution is sprayed onto a 3D-knitted silk textile and left to grow a living culture producing faded indigo and pink pigments.

The project, called Vigils, was developed by the designer’s studio, Oxman, for designers, artists and collaborators to “create new forms of material and aesthetic expression”.

Tussah silk thread within the fabric is coated with “bacterially sensitive chemicals”, which act as “a bioreactor” once mixed with the spray.

The fabric then sits for 24 hours, during which the solution and chemicals begin to interact and eventually produce a living bacterial culture. This organism, “numbering in the billions of cells”, spreads across the fabric and converts amino acids into the pigments Indigo and Melanin.

For the process, the Oxman lab created a spray solution containing the BL21 strain of Escherichia coli (E. coli), a strain commonly used in biotechnology and synthetic biology research, and sprayed it onto a silk fabric.

Its growth pattern is directed by “where and how densely the designer directed the culture to grow” via the spray, according to the team.

The fabric is then washed and dried, removing the bacteria, but the pigment remains.

“The microorganisms respond to signals associated with the textile substrate, making biological activity an active component of the material process,” said the team. “Vigils is a research-driven exploration of biological textile colouration.”

“The project is intended to investigate the interaction between synthetic biology and material systems rather than to represent a fully optimised industrial dyeing process.”

The studio created a series of four capes to demonstrate the technique. They display the variations in the muted colours and patterns created by the bacteria.

The studio is presenting the process as a possible alternative to “resource-intensive” industrial dyeing processes.

“The result is not simply an alternative way of applying color: the biological process becomes part of the design itself, producing patterns and variations that could not be achieved through conventional dyeing and making each textile an expression of the process that created it,” said Oxman.

It has not undergone extensive Life Cycle Assessment, which measures its environmental outputs, and is still in the prototype stage.

Neri Oxman opened a New York studio in Midtown Manhattan in 2024 and unveiled an AI-designed skyscraper to demonstrate its computational abilities at the time.

The designer is known for her work in material ecology, but she also faced allegations of plagiarism in her PhD thesis completed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

We've already seen some great holiday adverts as the festive season begins, from the handcrafted stop-motion Levi's Christmas advert, to Prada's cartoon wonderland directed by former Disney animator John Pomeroy. Alas, the historic master of the genre has come up lacking.

In the UK, the arrival of the John Lewis Christmas advert was long seen as the unofficial start of the season. The department store chain features twice in our pick of the best Christmas adverts of all time. But its 2026 offering has sparked a fierce backlash over what people see as confused messaging, with some people even calling for a boycott of the store.

A post shared by John Lewis & Partners (@johnlewis)

Titled Gloria and Pickles, the 2026 John Lewis Christmas advert is an opulent affair. Set to a Sam Fender cover of The Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want, it sees National treasure Kristin Scott Thomas star as a wealthy grandma who can't find anything to entertain her spoiled grandchildren and stop them from messing up her huge, gloomy mansion.

The kids are, naturally, unimpressed by an ancient Fisher-Price Little Snoopy Toy. She's about to give them some cash when the wooden dog turns into canine Chat-GPT with the voice of Paul Whitehouse and admonishes her for the lack of imagination. "Do you want them to like you?" the toy asks her at one point.

Off they go shopping, passing through several sub-standard stores until arriving at John Lewis. There, Kristin spends a fortune on decorations to turn one of her many spare rooms into a festive party space, which convinces the kids to finally show her some affection.

The message is supposed to be that a personal gift is more in keeping with the spirit of Christmas than cold, hard cash. But what comes across is that, either way, spending money is the only way to get you grandkids to like you. Good luck if you can't afford to shop at John Lewis.

According to the creative effectiveness company System 1, the ad achieved 5.6 stars on its rating system, making it John Lewis's strongest-performing festive campaign since Excitable Edgar in 2019. Its testing found that 61% of viewers felt happy watching the advert, nearly twice the UK TV advertising average.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

That's not the impression you get from the comments on social media. Writing on X Piers Morgan (what's the opposite of a national treasure?) described it as "possibly the worst advert I’ve ever seen for anything".

There's some hyperbole there. It least it's not Coca-Cola's AI slop. But he has a point, and a lot of people agree. The family is unlikeable, the children entitled and overindulged, and the materialistic tone feels out of touch amid the cost of living crisis, reminding younger viewers how skint they are (everything from the dog to Kristin's outfits is shoppable). Even the colour grading is depressing.

John Lewis switched from Adam&Eve to Saatchi & Saatchi as its creative agency back in 2023. Unlike the whimsical ads of the past that became such an annual event, this piece feels cold and clinical. It's more obviously geared towards conversion, attempting to shape behaviour by guilt tripping grandparents.

Malika Favre and Kumkum Fernando blend music, mythology and '60s flower power.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Forty years ago, Montreux Jazz Festival brought together the great US pop artists Andy Warhol and Keith Haring to create the poster design for the annual event. The result was a vibrant fusion of styles celebrating jazz music and rhythm. Now, the festival has repeated the experiment for just a second time, uniting two acclaimed contemporary artists for a dream collaboration.

The 2027 poster design was created by the French illustrator Malika Favre and the Sri Lankan sculptural artist and designer Kumkum Fernando. The former's distinctive geometric graphic style merges with the latter's colourful retrofuturism in a striking maximalist design that channels diverse influences into the form of a divine being that represents music as a joyful, spiritual journey.

Montreux has a long history of artist-designed posters. Other previous contributors have included David Bowie, Jean Tinguely, Yoann Lemoine (Woodkid), Lakwena, Kévin Germanier and Christian Marclay.

Keith Haring designed for the festival twice. For his second commission, in 1986, he worked with Andy Warhol as a collaborator. The festival invited Malika to adopt a similar approach for her second contribution, ten years after her first design for Montreux.

While her 2017 poster stood out for its minimalism, the new design goes in the opposite direction. A densely packed arrangement of colour and shapes creates a fantastical figure that looks like a cross between a robot, sacred altar and a jukebox. In fact, the design is also being turned into a sculptural vinyl cabinet (see further below).

“I fell in love with the festival on my very first visit in 2017. The poster I created for that edition remains one of my personal favourites to this day. I knew it would be hard to match, so I wanted to take the opposite approach: to create a work bursting with colour, as maximalist as the first one was minimalist. Kumkum was the ideal artist for this,” Favre says of the collaboration.

The design draws on diverse influences, including South Asian traditions, retro-futurism and '60s counterculture. The flowers evoke the lakeside quays of Montreux but also the flower power movement of the hippie era, a nod to the fact that Montreux Jazz Festival was founded during the 1967 Summer of Love. The floral patterns also subtly outline lips, kisses and female faces – symbols of love, pleasure and sexuality that recur throughout Malika's artistic universe.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

“I had this vision of music blooming in Montreux, this feeling of the entire town coming alive during the festival,” Favre adds. “I wanted to convey that joy. The world is going through strange times, and a festival like Montreux is an opportunity to celebrate. For me, flowers also symbolise eroticism, an explosion of the senses and the pleasures found in music. I always like to tuck in something a little cheeky, and I thought I could bring that touch of a feminine sensuality. When I sent the first flowers to Kumkum he said, ‘Oh yes, that’s sexy!’”

From the outset, the idea was also to bring the poster’s divine entity into the world as a three-dimensional object, following Kumkum’s practice of creating futuristic, geometric sculptures. The result is a made-for-order vinyl cabinet with a dedicated turntable compartment and pull-out drawers for record storage.

“The spark came when we noticed the resemblance between the shape of certain religious altars and that of a jukebox, both sharing the same sense of symmetry,” Fernando says. “We imagined a kind of gateway into a sacred realm of music, a timeless entity, part retro-futuristic robot, part mythological being, that embodies music as a joyful, universal experience.”

The 61st Montreux Jazz Festival will take place on the Lake Geneva shoreline from 2 July to 17 July 2027.

#9042. Archaeologists Discover Vast Ice Age Cave Art Hiding in Plain Sight

Archaeologists have discovered one of the largest assemblages of Ice Age rock art ever recorded in the Iberian Mediterranean, shedding new light on population sizes and regional artistic expression during the Paleolithic. The 2019 find, made at the tourist attraction Cova de la Font Major in Catalonia, was described in the journal Antiquity this month.

Although more than half of the Paleolithic rock art recorded in Europe is in the Iberian Peninsula, it was long believed to be rare in the north-eastern part of the region. Comprising 280 figurative and nonfigurative rock engravings, the discovery at Cova de la Font Major has upended this assumption, suggesting not only a larger population than previously thought, but one with its own artistic traditions. Related Articles 12,000-Year-Old Clothing Made of Animal Hide Discovered in Ice Age Caves in Oregon British Museum to Loan 'Some of the Rarest Surviving Examples' of Ice Age Art to UK's 2025 City of Culture

As attested to by the numerous engravings and graffiti on its walls, have been visiting the Cova de la Font Major for at least 900 years. Although its main entrance collapsed at some point during the Roman period (2nd–5th centuries CE), an inscription dated 1199 indicates an entry in the second millennium CE, perhaps through a fissure or other access point.

In 1853, the Cova de la Font Major was entered through a private well, but only sporadic visits to it are recorded until 1956, when it was explored and surveyed by members of the Centre Excursionista Pirinenc. In 1957 the town council of Espluga de Francolí cleared the entrance to provide access to visitors, and in 1993 the cave was converted to a museum.

In 2011, researchers confirmed that part of the entrance, destroyed in 1957, had survived, leading to the inclusion of the site in a 2018 research project. The Ice Age engravings were discovered during the project’s excavation campaign the following year, when one of the authors noticed that among the various graffiti on the cave walls some looked Paleolithic.

“For more than six decades, thousands of visitors passed directly in front of the engraved surfaces, and in some cases inscribed names and dates over them, without the Paleolithic origin of the figures being recognized,” writes research co-author Josep Maria Vergès from the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA).

Located in series of small galleries within the cave, the engravings consist of depictions of various animals as well as groupings of abstract marks, including a particularly distinctive composition, comprising hundreds of loop-shaped incisions. Moreover, while uneven conglomerate rock like that at Cova de la Font Major is theoretically unsuitable for cave art, here the artists incorporated its irregularities into their compositions, using junctures of two different kinds of rock as ground lines for figures, for example, or turning a fissure into a water surface, as in one rendering of drinking deer.

“The Mediterranean art of western Europe is now enriched by a new body of rock art,” states Vergès, “which allows us to characterize in greater depth a Mediterranean graphic tradition with an identity of its own.”

A Brighton studio of Northerners, a 25-hour RPG and a free game engine. It’s set in 2002, so nobody has a smartphone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Plenty of Pokémon imitators have come along over the years, with the most brazen in recent years being Palworld. But look at 2023's Cassette Beasts, and you see how a creature-collecting game can offer a unique twist without following the same mascot-based formula. For one, it wasn't really about catching creatures but recording and then transforming into them yourself. Speaking to Bytten Studio's co-founder, art and game director Jay Bayliss, it had been important very early on to consider how Cassette Beasts would distinguish itself.

"We had the idea of fusion as a central mechanic, which Pokemon can't tap into because Pikachu is a mascot that you can't dilute by merging it with a thousand other beasts to get new beasts," he explains. "We also thought about focusing on the human characters, so maybe the beasts could be a reflection of the human characters, which led to the idea of transforming into them."

It also helped that Cassette Beasts aimed itself at a slightly older audience compared to every Pokemon game always having you start out as yet another schoolkid, though its British humour and sensibilities also stood out, which is something the Brighton-based studio is leaning even more directly on with its upcoming sequel.

Cassette Beasts 2002 is set in London (as well as its alternate world of Nodnol), but it aims not to give the tourist version of the capital, but a quieter Zone 6 suburb version of it, with the town of Elmwich.

"We don't lean into a certain Paddington-esque twee Britishism about it," Bayliss explains. "Crucially, we're Northerners living down South in Brighton; we don't really play with that twee Britishness. We enjoy portraying quite a mundane, crappy version of suburban English life. We're so bored of the Harry Potter-esque upper middle-class boarding school fantasy take on it. I think this version's more fun."

As the title's palindrome suggests, Cassette Beasts 2002 is also set in 2002. That appeals to me personally, much like one of my favourite indie games released earlier this year, Perfect Tides: Station to Station, because it taps into my formative teen years. "The early 2000s also mark this crossing point between the analogue and digital age," Bayliss explains. "The internet exists, but you don't have smartphones. People do have mobile phones in the game, but we haven't got the Panopticon of social media. For artists younger than me, they reflect on this ethereal time they just missed out on, just before we had the baggage of the modern world overwhelming you."

It was also important to reflect the era's aesthetic and fashion. "Skewing male, game developers often don't appreciate fashion, but if you go on TikTok and social media, people are very interested in noughties fashion," Bayliss explains. "There's a lot of interest in exploring that time that we don't discount, and that's reflected in the fashion sensibilities of the characters and the character designs themselves as well."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Perhaps a major visual shift with this sequel is a more 3D one. Well, it's a case of perspective, literally. The original Cassette Beasts, while presented in the traditional top-down perspective of classic Pokemon and other 8- and 16-bit RPGs, was actually made in a 3D engine, albeit with environments given pixelated textures to match its 2D character sprites. In Cassette Beasts 2002, the camera drops down so things are presented as a third-person 3D game, except its characters are still pixel-art sprites presented with a billboarding technique.

"We were like, what if we can design this game with higher resolution sprites, with eight directions so when you pan the camera around, it feels less awkward?" Bayliss explains. "From a technical point of view, you have to rethink how you're designing worlds, but suddenly the perspective and scale you have in these worlds is very different. If you took the first game and dropped the camera down, it would probably feel very small, so it changes how we sculpt and design the world."

Cassette Beasts 2002 is also developed with the open-source Godot engine, which more indies are turning to. Although Bayliss recalls the challenges of porting the game's predecessor, which was developed with Godot 3, the latest iteration, Godot 4, that the studio is using has greatly improved features, including porting and performance, that make it a more viable alternative to Unity.

"If you sign up to Unity, you're kind of on the hook for any changes that Unity makes, whereas with an open-source engine, if you don't like changes, you can change the engine," Bayliss explains. "I think the flexibility of Godot is what allows a team of two full-time developers to make a big 25-hour RPG. It's just a very uncomplicated engine - you make stuff, you put it in, it's in the game. If there's anything that you need to fix, you don't have to submit a bug report to the back-end team and hope they fix it in the next two years; you just go in and fix it yourself."

Cassette Beasts 2002 is releasing in March 2027 for PC, Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, and Nintendo Switch 2. You can wishlist it now on Steam.

#9040. Pratt's evolving courses reflect "broader shift in creative practice"

From architects using digital fabrication tools to how graphic designers can enhance their work with AI, Pratt Institute has responded to the increasing fluidity of creative careers by launching three new flexible programmes.

Pratt Institute’s School of Continuing and Professional Studies (SCPS) offers flexible programmes for both working creatives and lifelong designers who want to develop new skills without putting their careers on hold.

Its three certificate programs – Graphic Design, Fine Art and AI design – reflect how creative practice is rapidly evolving.

Pratt’s Graphic Design course focuses on the fundamentals of professional practice and creative production.

From covering typography and branding to composition and visual systems, students apply these skills across digital, print, motion and interactive media.

Its Fine Art course offers small, interactive groups where students curate a portfolio, complement another area of study or return to an existing creative practice. Interdisciplinary experts teach the course within Pratt’s dedicated art studios.

Pratt students explore artificial intelligence (AI) for research, visualisation, ideation and production within its AI Design course, while also considering questions of authorship, ethics and responsible design.

Here, Pratt treats AI as a creative tool rather than a replacement for creative thinking.

“The emphasis remains on human creativity, with technology extending what designers can explore and produce,” the organisation said on its AI course.

The organisation explained that the launch of its latest courses responds to how career paths are changing.

For example, designers are moving between studios and start-ups, consulting and collaborative research, and need to quickly develop new skills to keep up with technology changes.

“Creative careers are becoming more fluid, and education is changing with them,” said Pratt. “Continuing education at Pratt is no longer only about changing careers. For many creatives, it is a way to stay curious, deepen an existing practice and respond to an industry that is constantly changing.”

Pratt added that its courses also reflect a broader shift in creative practice.

For example, designers are increasingly expected to move between physical and digital environments, combine technical skills with conceptual thinking and quickly adapt as new tools and technologies emerge.

Each course covers these aspects and is designed to build on the skills the individual isn’t as strong in.

It added that designers also benefit from a community experience at Pratt. For example, designers, architects, artists, creative technologists and entrepreneurs learn alongside each other, exchanging ideas and forging professional connections that “extend beyond the classroom”.

Pratt’s courses are available in person at Pratt’s Manhattan and Brooklyn campuses and in hybrid formats, making it possible to fit study around work, everyday life and freelance projects.

For more information about Pratt’s courses, visit its website or contact scps-noncredit[at]pratt.edu.

#9039. Ex-husband of Brent Sikkema sentenced to life in prison over murder-for-hire killing

Brent Sikkema at Art Basel Miami Beach Photo by Joe Schildhorn / BFA.com

The former husband of the late New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, Daniel Sikkema, aged 56, has been sentenced to life imprisonment for organising Sikkema’s murder in 2024. A federal court in Manhattan handed down the sentence on Wednesday (4 November).

In May 2026, after a two-week trial, Daniel Sikkema was convicted on charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country. In addition to life imprisonment, he was sentenced to five years of supervised release.

Brent Sikkema, who was aged 75 at the time of his murder, was found stabbed to death at his home in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on 15 January 2024. According to prosecutors, Daniel Sikkema began planning the murder in 2023 in the midst of his divorce from the dealer, with whom he had been married for around 15 years and shared a son.

As the couple’s divorce proceedings became more acrimonious, Daniel Sikkema, who holds dual US and Cuban citizenship, recruited the Cuban national, Alejandro Triana Prevez, as the hitman. On the night of the murder, Prevez entered the late Sikkema’s residence and stabbed him 18 times. Prevez subsequently received $5,000 from Daniel Sikkema and was promised further payments.

Prosecutors said Daniel Sikkema made 11 payments to Prevez and Prevez’s partner in Cuba, using the identities of unwitting friends, employees and family members to conceal the transactions. Prevez was arrested by Brazilian authorities four days after the murder at a gas station on the side of the highway in the state of Minas Gerais, around 600 miles from Rio de Janeiro. He had stolen cash and jewellery in his possession. His case is being handled separately by a Brazilian court.

Brent Sikkema was born in 1948 in Morrison, Illinois, and studied at the San Francisco Art Institute before beginning his career. In the early 1990s, he founded Wooster Gardens in SoHo, moving the gallery to Chelsea in 1999. The business became Sikkema Jenkins & Co in 2003 following the involvement of Michael Jenkins and Meg Malloy.

The gallery is now known as Sikkema Malloy Jenkins and continues to operate in Chelsea. It has championed the work of artists including Kara Walker, Vik Muniz, Sheila Hicks, Jeffrey Gibson and Arturo Herrera. A representative for Sikkema Malloy Jenkins told The Art Newspaper that the gallery will not be providing any statement regarding the conviction or sentencing.

#9038. Paris Court Orders Sotheby’s to Return Nazi-Looted Pissarro Painting to Jewish Heirs

A Paris court has ordered the restitution of a painting by Camille Pissarro, allegedly seized by the Nazis during World War II, to the descendants of Jewish banker and art collector Salomon Flavian, reports Le Figaro. A group of his heirs sued Sotheby’s in Paris in September, saying they were improperly left out of an agreement struck with other members of their family

The case concerns the French Impressionist’s 1902 canvas Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée (Fishing dock and Duquesne basin, Dieppe, sunny afternoon), showing the port city in western France. Related Articles A Rare Albrecht Altdorfer Painting Heads to Sotheby's for $6.67 M. A Seagram Heir, a Bankrupt Hedge Funder, and More: Consignors for the November Marquee Sales Revealed

Sotheby’s London sold the painting in 2024 for £1.2 million ($1.5 million at the time). The auctioneer indicated that the work was being offered “pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian,” whose collection the Nazis seized in Paris in 1941. The house’s lawyers maintained in court that the heirs’ consent was gained through Mondex Corporation, which specializes in the recovery of art and other assets looted during World War II, reported the Art Newspaper. But seven plaintiffs maintained in court in September that only two relatives, Gilles and Nicholas Flavian, had signed the agreement and that the rest had not been consulted, per the newspaper.

In its Thursday decision, the court nullified all sales since the initial seizure of the painting, and ordered the return of the work. It concluded that the Flavian family established that Salomon had owned the painting, that it had been confiscated by the Germans, and that he had taken steps to recover his assets after the war. The court ordered Sotheby’s to inform the family of the identity of the buyer in the 2024 sale, or be fined €1,000 ($1,123) per day thereafter, reports Le Figaro, noting that the judgment applies immediately, even in the event of an appeal.

In an email to ARTnews, Mondex Corporation consultant James Palmer said that an appeal will be filed “forthwith.” Palmer argued that the archives of dealer Paul Rosenberg and the 1939 Pissarro catalogue raisonné “both clearly identify [British artist and collector] Edward Le Bas as the owner of the painting from 1939 to the early 1950s.” This means the painting could not have been seized from Flavian during the 1940s, he says.

“Of great importance is the fact that France currently lacks a formal restitution framework, which disadvantages both the state and claimants,” he added, contrasting France with existing adjudication bodies in the UK, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and the Netherlands, which, he said, “operate on a crucial general principle: that the benefit of the doubt is presumed in the claimant’s favor unless there is evidence to the contrary.”

Regarding Le Bas’s ownership, he continued, “These crucial facts were not commented upon by the court in its decision and can therefore be presumed to have been given no significant consideration, which is a flaw in the judicial assessment of the case. We are confident that when the vast amount of complex provenance research evidence is properly understood and considered that the court of appeal will reach a different conclusion.”

Apple's first-ever touchscreen MacBook is finally here! Find my hands-on impressions below, and scroll down for rolling coverage as reactions from critics and creators start to pour in across the web.

They said they wouldn't do it. A touchscreen MacBook has been rumoured since the dawn of time (well, the noughties), but, in a quote that's been infinitely dredged up across the internet over the last couple of weeks, Steve Jobs himself decried the concept as "ergonomically terrible". But Jobs also famously asked, "Who wants a stylus?" And the answer among millions of Apple Pencil users seems to be a resounding, "Us!"

And after a few days with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, I'm happy to report that this is very much a device—perhaps even the ultimate device—for creatives. But rather than the ability to touch the screen, it's all about the quality of that 'PROLED' display itself. Turns out there's a reason Apple decided to lead with that, and not touch, in the name of the device.

Simply put, it's the best laptop screen I've ever seen. With up to 2000 nits of peak brightness, 10,000,000:1 contrast, and P3 + Adobe RGB colour, this is a best-in-class display that puts every other OLED laptop screen I've used to shame. It gives creatives a portable reference-quality display, which means it recreates video, colour and contrast as faithfully as possible. Once you've used the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, everything else looks washed-out in comparison, and for that reason alone it's impossible not to recommend for creatives – so long as the small matter of the $2,899 starting price isn't a barrier.

When it comes to touch, as I've written before, in my testing I've found it to be a nice-to-have rather than a need-to-have. Now that we're all touchscreen natives (which wasn't so much the case when Jobs made those comments in 2010), certain navigational actions just feel right, even on a laptop. Scrolling through windows, pinching to zoom in on a photo or map, scrubbing through the timeline in Final Cut Pro; there are plenty of times when touching the screen feels more intuitive than reaching for the trackpad. And Apple's subtle UI tweaks, such as having navigational icons expand when touched, make the whole thing feel more natural.

But equally, there were plenty of times when I preferred to use the trackpad – particularly when a certain level of accuracy was required. And despite Apple claiming to have produced a newly designed hinge with greater stability, it still wobbles. There's just no getting around the fact that a touchscreen on a vertical display is less ergonomic than it is on a flat one.

From a design perspective, the new MacBook Pro isn't a game-changer – unless you really missed the illuminating Apple logo (another noughties mainstay). There are improvements here and there; the Dynamic Island takes up less space than the notch, and slightly smaller bezels result in slightly larger viewing areas. But perhaps the most meaningful design change is the reduction in weight. That OLED panel has allowed for a 14% weight loss – making the 14-inch model, somewhat ironically, lighter than the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air.

But everything pales next to the screen. The PROLED XDR looks incredible. If you're looking for the most impressive visual fidelity available on a laptop, here it is. You can touch it if you like.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is released tomorrow, with preorders available now. Prices start at $2899 for the 14-inch model, and $3399 for the 16-inch model.

Of course, it's a very pricey machine. But reportedly, Apple is trying to find ways to bring down the price in the future by using HMO thin-film transistor technology for OLED panels. It's a piece of tech also being considered by Samsung and LG to make OLED screens cheaper. Here's hoping.

What's that? You're looking for an ASMR unboxing of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display? Whatever floats your boat.

If you're tempted by that awesome new display (or, if you like, the touchscreen), you can go ahead and order the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display at Amazon right now, starting at $2899.

We were lucky enough to attend the launch of the MacBook PROLED with XDR display in Los Angeles last week. There, among other things, we saw... Apple CEO John Ternus signing iPhones? Sure. Okay, then.

Our sister site T3 is also waxing lyrical about the new MacBook Pro, but this time it isn't the touchscreen or the XDR display that's getting the most rapturous response – it's the reduction in weight:

"I brought my personal M3 MacBook Pro to the hands-on to compare it to, and hefting them both side-by-side, the loss of around 300g of weight between generations is really quite significant. On the one hand, you might not notice it explicitly... but everything adds up, and it makes a genuine difference."

It seems that even after a short time, there's something of a critical consensus: come for the touchscreen, stay for the display.

And the YouTubers' reviews are making their way online too. Here's renowned Apple fan/creator iJustine's take. Like many, she's a fan of the glowing Apple logo.

And here's our sister site Tech Radar with, again, a very similar take: "While all the talk is about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display being the first MacBook with a touchscreen, the touchscreen is arguably not its most interesting feature; it works fine, but macOS is still an operating system built for traditional laptop inputs. Instead, it’s the gorgeous tandem OLED screen and industry-leading battery life that should get you excited here."

The Verge's review is up, and it seems they share our opinion: the screen is incredible, the thinner and lighter design is welcome, and touch is... there. "Even if you love the touchscreen, you’ll use it a lot for a day or so and go back to using your laptop almost exactly the way you did before."

Hello and welcome to Creative Bloq's coverage of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. We'll be keeping this page updated with opinions from across the web, but for now, what do we think? In short, touch is nice, but it's that PROLED display that's the killer here. It's the brightest (and darkest) laptop screen we've ever used – and for creatives, having a portable reference-quality display could be a game-changer.

#9035. Trump Convenes Final Review for Triumphal Arch, Seeks Immediate Start on Construction

President Donald Trump’s planned 250-foot-tall triumphal arch could win approval as soon as Thursday, after he bulldozed a mountain of opposition to secure a final review by a federal commission. Approval would clear the way for construction to begin immediately, though a federal judge could still block the project, as some on Capitol Hill hope.

Washington, D.C., media reported that the Trump-allied National Capital Planning Commission began reviewing plans for the arch on Thursday afternoon, just two days after Republicans lost control of the Senate and the House of Representatives in seismic midterm elections. The commission is expected to approve the plans following lengthy public testimony. Meanwhile, the project’s opponents have called on the federal courts to halt it before construction can begin. Related Articles Arlington County Board Files Lawsuit to Stop Construction of Trump's Triumphal Arch After Resignation of Advisory Council, American Institute of Architects Weigh in on Trump's Arch

“The Court should not allow this lawless project to evade scrutiny,” Brian Schwalb and Jay Jones, the attorneys general of D.C. and Virginia, respectively, wrote in a joint court filing on Wednesday, as reported by the Washington Post.

The structure would rise at Memorial Circle, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, to a height that critics say would cast shadows over the surrounding memorial landscape at various times of day. In recent weeks, the president has reimagined the project as a “military complex,” complete with a sniper’s nest.

Trump first announced plans for the triumphal arch more than a year ago, presenting it as a necessary tribute to the nation’s 250th anniversary. A project of this magnitude would traditionally require congressional approval, which the president has not sought. D.C. lawmakers, historic preservationists, and veterans’ groups argue that the project has been illegally advanced and threatens the site’s solemn character.

In a lawsuit filed last month, the Arlington County Board argued that the arch would “directly obstruct[ing] the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that was deliberately created to symbolize the nation’s post-Civil War reunification.”

The Trump administration maintains that the arch is authorized by century-old plans approved by Congress to commemorate the nation’s reunification after the Civil War. Critics, however, have pointed out that the lawmakers’ plans called for a pair of columns, not a triumphal arch of the kind the president has likened to France’s Arc de Triomphe, “but better, more beautiful actually, much more beautiful.”

Mark Paoletta, a White House official who was appointed commission chairman in August, reportedly said on Thursday that the empty space at Memorial Circle “dishonors our veterans and leaves a key monumental gateway to Arlington that Congress authorized uncompleted.” He added that it was a “national disgrace” that such a landmark was not already standing, praising the president’s “historic vision.”

The Arlington County Board’s lawsuit, which names the National Park Service, as a defendant, accuses the administration and its official of failing to consider the arch’s potential risks to regional flight paths and its impact on emergency services.

“Using the Arch to store large stockpiles of ammunition and as a staging point for drones and snipers, so close to commuters and tourists, will dramatically worsen these public-safety harms and the risk of accidents,” the lawsuit warns.

#9034. Batek Architekten designs Berlin orthodontic clinic that looks more like a boutique or gallery

Avoiding the sterile appearance of most medical interiors, Berlin-based Batek Architekten used soothing shades of pastel yellow and matt silver to bring a sense of softness to orthodontic clinic Hey.

Described by its designers as “quietly playful”, Hey combines its two-tone palette with bold geometric elements.

These include a folded steel reception counter, a sculptural bench, and a criss-cross coat rail.

Treatment rooms feature translucent walls of glass-fibre-reinforced plastic, while lighting tubes trace graphic lines across the ceiling.

The result is a space that could be mistaken for a high-end fashion boutique or an art gallery.

“We decided early on to work almost monochromatically,” said studio founder Patrick Batek.

“A soft pastel yellow runs from the floor up across the walls, enveloping visitors and creating a warm, comforting atmosphere.”

Batek Architekten‘s scheme, overseen by Batek and architect Julia Jensen, evolved from a brief set by the client, doctor Julie Charlotte Angrick, who wanted a clinic where young patients would feel comfortable.

It was this that led Angrick to name it Hey, intended as an informal welcome.

“Most visitors are children and teenagers, and many of them come regularly over several years,” explained Batek.

“We wanted to create a place that takes away the fear of the clinical environment without being childish,” he told Dezeen.

“Instead of colourful decoration, we chose radical reduction.”

The same thinking shaped the visual identity developed by graphic design studio Bailey und Bailey, which includes a logo incorporating a smiley face emoticon.

The visual aesthetic didn’t come at the expense of functionality or hygiene.

Located in the north of Berlin, the 178-square-metre clinic occupies a former pharmacy. The architects completely cleared and reconfigured the floor plan, optimising the flow of patients through different spaces.

Textiled tiles line wet rooms and other surfaces that are likely to be touched often, while the yellow-toned floor was cast from a plant-based resin. This floor was the biggest challenge of the project.

“A surface like this needs a perfect substrate, because every irregularity underneath would become visible,” said Batek.

“Preparing the subfloor required great precision, but it was essential for the continuous yellow to work as one uninterrupted surface.”

The architects completed the design by picking out a few elements in red, matching the sign on the wall of the reception area.

These include room numbers, chairs and signs indicating toothbrushing areas.

Cabinets are integrated into the walls, allowing tools and equipment to be hidden away.

“The space is reduced but never cold,” added Batek. “Above all, it reflects the personality of the client and her way of working with young patients.”

The studio has previously also revamped the T7.2 dental clinic in Berlin and renovated a historic cinema in the same city.

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:

The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

The FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

#9031. Sweden Returns Benin Bronze Trove to Nigeria, Indigenous Remains to Bolivia

The Swedish government is set to return 40 sacred artifacts from the Kingdom of Benin to Nigeria, marking one of the largest repatriations of the so-called Benin Bronzes.

Nigerian media report that the artworks are expected to be received by a delegation from the Benin Palace in Lagos today, a development that Oba Ewuare II, the monarch of Benin, described as years in the making. Since ascending to the throne, Ewuare has advocated fiercely for the return of bronze sculptures, ceremonial objects, and ivory carvings—collectively known as the Benin Bronzes—from museum and private collections worldwide, with considerable success. Related Articles Buddhas and Dinosaur Bones Among Dozens of Smuggled Artifacts Repatriated to China Met Museum Repatriates Five Pieces of Looted Cretan Armor to Greece

“We have been trying, through my grandfather’s efforts, to bring back our artifacts,” Ewuare said in a statement. “My grandfather succeeded, my father succeeded more, and I think now history is obvious to everybody. We are doing our best to triple and triple all those efforts of our forefathers.”

The Kingdom of Benin was looted of roughly 5,000 royal and religious objects in 1897 by British forces on a punitive expedition through what is now Nigeria. Dispersed through illicit channels among museums and private collections worldwide, the artifacts have become emblematic of efforts by formerly colonized countries to reclaim their cultural heritage, as well as the broader—and often contentious—debate over the ethics of ethnographic collections. In recent years, public sympathies have seemingly shifted toward formerly colonized countries, prompting a wave of repatriations. Museums across the United States, as well as institutions in the Netherlands, Germany, and Switzerland, have returned Benin Bronzes and other ethnographic objects to their countries of origin.

The Swedish government also announced today that it will return 77 objects belonging to the Kallawaya people, including human remains, to the Archaeological Museum in La Paz, Bolivia. The remains were taken out of Bolivia illegally and remained in the collection of the World Culture Museum until 2023, when the Swedish government announced their transfer of ownership.
